title: KEYLIT  learn piano. The next key is already glowing.
pitch: Never guess which key is next. KEYLIT lights it. You play it. ChatGPT hears you on that same piano so anyone can start, on one live page.
about_excerpt:
Never guess which key is next. KEYLIT lights it. You play it. ChatGPT hears you on that same piano so anyone can start, on one live page.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Keylit 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Keylit 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Keylit 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 A chatbot can say “play middle C.” It cannot light that key, and it cannot hear whether you hit it. That is a useless piano teacher. 

 The WebMCP challenge asked for an app that gets better when a human and an agent share the same live page. I wanted that to be something anyone can use: learn piano on the keys in front of you. Not a lesson in a side chat. 

 I looked at how hardware instruments are laid out — dual layers, an LCD, generate-and-lock, a roll — but KEYLIT is not a clone of those products. No pads, no kits, no preset banks. The product is the glow: the next note is already lit. You play it. The agent hears you on that same piano. 

 What it does 

 KEYLIT is a sampled piano teacher on one live page. 

 
 Press teach me . Middle C glows cyan, with a Q on the key. 
 You play it — click, type, or a MIDI keyboard. The teacher hears that note and lights the next one. 
 Miss, and it stays put: TRY AGAIN · WANT D4 · YOU E4 . 
 hear it plays the next note in green so you can copy it. 
 When you can hold a chord, harmonize only works if your hands are already on the keys. 
 

 Lessons: first keys, C major scale, C major chord, Twinkle, Ode to Joy. Or the agent calls set-next-keys and invents a drill. 

 If the agent is not on this page, it cannot light a key or grade your hands. That is the point of WebMCP. 

 How we built it 

 Browser app: Vite, TypeScript, Web Audio, Web MIDI, and WebMCP on document.modelContext.registerTool . Samples are open rompler sets (Steinway, CP80, Wurlitzer), not a commercial library. 

 I used AI. I am not going to pretend otherwise. 

 
 Ideas and code: Cursor with Grok 4.6 Extra High Fast. Teacher loop, tools, most of the TypeScript. I directed, edited, and cut what did not serve the page. 
 Design: Claude Code, Opus 5. The rack, LCD, key glow, and making it sell instead of look like a bed. 
 Testing: Codex Luna Extra High. Click-throughs: teach me → C4 hit → wrong E4 miss → D4 advances. 
 

 The challenge allows AI. I did not name this CodexPiano or claim an official OpenAI product. The name is KEYLIT because the next key lights. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Native document.modelContext.registerTool still fails with SecurityError in a locked local browser, so the in-page Studio Agent falls back to local tools. Judges need the live HTTPS URL in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. That deploy, the public repo, and the demo video are still on me before the deadline. Samples and the grade-on-press path have to keep working on that origin, not only on localhost. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The lesson only moves when you play the glowing key. A wrong note does not skip ahead. Amber is you, cyan is next, green is the agent — on the same keyboard. Harmonize still refuses if your hands are empty. That is the product, not a chat overlay. 

 What we learned 

 A piano teacher that cannot see the keyboard is a paragraph. A teacher that shares the session is a product. WebMCP only pays off if the tool changes the same keys the human is looking at. get-lesson-state after they play is more useful than another chatbot tip. 

 “Inspired by” is not “copy the pads.” The new thing is the shared lesson. 

 What's next for KEYLIT 

 Ship the HTTPS demo, put the repo and LICENSE on GitHub, and record a under-3-minute video in ChatGPT’s browser: “Teach me piano.” Then freeze for judging. After that: more songs, slower drills, and a teacher that can invent a line and light those keys with set-next-keys .

title: E-ternal × WebMCP
pitch: An open-source ERP that works with your browser agent — same screen, same state. The agent drafts; only a human can approve. Built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An open-source ERP that works with your browser agent — same screen, same state. The agent drafts; only a human can approve. Built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Judge access: live demo at https://et-demo.kaiwu.com.tw — sign in as judge / webmcp-judge . Best experienced in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser (GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra) or Chrome 146+ with the WebMCP flag. Prior-work vs. challenge-period work is documented in HACKATHON.md in the repo. Inspiration ERPs are where small businesses actually keep their money, stock and tax obligations — and they are exactly the software agents are worst at: dense forms, hidden state, and one wrong click posts a journal entry. We didn't want an agent that "operates" the ERP by guessing its way through the UI. We wanted the ERP to tell the agent what it may do, show the human everything the agent does, and keep the one irreversible step — committing to the books — in human hands. WebMCP is the first standard that makes that shape natural: the tools live in the page the human is already looking at. What it does E-ternal is an open-source ERP for Taiwanese SMEs (quotes → orders → shipping, double-entry accounting, e-invoicing, VAT filing, HR/payroll). For this challenge every page now registers WebMCP tools on document.modelContext (ChatGPT's built-in browser) and navigator.modelContext (Chrome). A person and their agent then work on the same screen: Ask, don't click. "What did we sell this month, who still owes us money?" → the agent calls query_report , get_dashboard_summary , search_partners and answers with real ledger numbers. No scraping, no menu navigation. Draft together. "Draft a quote for Blue Harbor: 20 Control Hubs plus one maintenance plan" → draft_quote fills a live draft card on screen, field by field. Nothing is written to the ERP. The human can edit any line on the card; the agent reads the same draft back with get_current_view . One draft, two editors. Approve by structure. submit_draft suspends the tool call and shows an approval card. Only a human can click it. There is deliberately no tool that posts, approves or voids anything — that door was never registered, so it cannot be jailbroken. See everything. An on-screen activity panel streams every tool call the agent makes; a status chip shows which tools are registered for the signed-in role. How we built it apps/web/src/webmcp/ — a self-contained layer inside the existing React app: a modelContext wrapper (feature detection, name-keyed dynamic registration, AbortSignal unregistration), 12 tools with English descriptions and strict JSON-Schema inputs, a framework-free state bus (activity log, co-edited draft, approval requests), and the UI (draft card, approval card, activity panel — fully i18n'd, light/dark aware). Tools are recomputed from role × current page and re-synced on every change: logout ⇒ only describe_site remains; a sales account never sees finance tools. Domain guardrails live inside the tools: prices are untaxed integers, VAT is computed server-side from user-maintained tax parameters (never by the agent), ambiguous customer/product names return candidate lists instead of guesses. Also built during the challenge: full English i18n of the ERP, a one-command demo dataset, and the live deployment (Vercel + Supabase). Challenges we ran into Two APIs, one standard. Chrome exposes navigator.modelContext ; ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext . Supporting only one means "the API exists but the page never registers tools" on the other — we shipped a resolver that handles both. Discovery timing. Agents scan for tools at page load, before sign-in. We register a read-only describe_site tool at module load so the registry is never empty, and it tells the agent which tools appear after sign-in. Chrome 151 has no unregisterTool . Logout could leave tools behind. We switched to the spec's registerTool(tool, { signal }) and abort to unregister — verified in the browser. Roles that are read-only on the server. Our "general manager" role is read-only by design; the judge account had to be a finance role so the approval path can actually create the quote. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real agent (ChatGPT desktop, GPT-5.6 Sol) ran the whole flow on the live site with zero clicking: reporting → draft → human edit → approval → quote #6 created with server-side VAT. That is the demo video, edited for pacing only. The red line is architectural, not a prompt: judges can read the tool registry and confirm the missing doors. Everything is open source (LGPL-3.0-or-later) with a public commit history for the challenge period. What we learned WebMCP's real power isn't "an API for agents" — it is that the agent and the human share the same pixels. Once the draft lives on screen, trust stops being a prompt-engineering problem and becomes a UI problem, which we know how to solve. What's next Approval-gated tools for the other document types (orders, purchase receipts, HR requests), page-level context ( get_current_view reporting filters and selected rows), and undo for agent actions — all inside the same registry discipline. Reusable playbook (open source) We distilled this whole integration into an open-source agent skill so any team can make their own site agent-ready the same way: kaiwutech-TW/webmcp-skill (MIT) — the API reality check, the six browser traps we hit, the five structural guardrails (registry red-line, central validation, untrusted-content quarantine, idempotent submission, live schemas), and framework-free TypeScript templates. title: kata
pitch: Lets users teach a website a new agent capability by demonstration, then compiles that behavior into a safe, typed WebMCP tool.
about_excerpt: Lets users teach a website a new agent capability by demonstration, then compiles that behavior into a safe, typed WebMCP tool. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does KATA KATA is a system that allows users to teach a web application a new agent capability simply by demonstrating a workflow. Instead of requiring developers to manually write a dedicated API or WebMCP integration for every repeated action, a user performs the task a small number of times. KATA records the semantic application actions behind those demonstrations, compares the traces, identifies what stays constant and what varies, infers typed parameters, compiles the repeated behavior into a deterministic workflow, and installs it as a new WebMCP tool. For example, a researcher may repeatedly save a paper, assign it a priority, and add an “architecture” tag. KATA can recognize the common structure and create a tool such as: triage_architecture_paper(workId) An AI agent can then discover and execute that newly learned capability through WebMCP. The important distinction is that KATA does not record mouse coordinates or replay brittle DOM clicks. It records semantic application commands. The human UI and the agent both ultimately use the same command system, so a learned tool invokes real application behavior rather than a separate simulation. KATA also avoids generating arbitrary executable code. Learned workflows are represented as structured, validated programs built from a finite set of supported commands. Inputs are validated before execution, the complete batch is preflighted before mutation, and invalid workflows fail without partially applying actions. The deeper idea behind KATA is user-extensible application APIs: the API available to an AI agent no longer has to be completely defined by the developer ahead of time. Users can teach software the workflows that matter to them, and the application can safely turn those workflows into agent-usable capabilities. title: MOOD: A system for creative thinking
pitch: MOOD helps turn references and half formed ideas into a clear creative direction. The agent helps connect the dots, suggest what could work and refine it. You still make the calls.
about_excerpt: MOOD helps turn references and half formed ideas into a clear creative direction. The agent helps connect the dots, suggest what could work and refine it. You still make the calls. Like Comment Story Updates Cover Why I made MOOD The beginning of a creative project is usually the messiest part. You have a brief. Screenshots saved in five different places. References you love but cannot quite explain why yet. And very useful thoughts like "softer, but still bold" or "I know what I mean, I just can't explain it." That messy part is also where a lot of the actual creative thinking happens. I built MOOD because I wanted to explore what happens when an agent joins that process without trying to take it over. References become directions. Directions become decisions. Decisions slowly become a design system, and the agent helps along the way. The goal was never to let AI make the creative decisions. It was to give it enough context to be genuinely useful while I make them. What MOOD does A project starts with a brief and visual references , then moves through four stages: Stage What happens Explore Collect, organise and react to references Direction Turn those references into possible visual directions Refine Test choices, compare ideas and make actual design decisions System Bring the approved direction into colors, typography, principles and a reusable design system The System view is not a separate document generated at the end. It is a live projection of the selected direction and the decisions made along the way, so the different parts of the project cannot quietly drift away from each other. The same goes for the agent. It works with the same project state as the designer. It can understand which references were kept, which direction is selected, what has already been decided, what is locked and what still needs work. Then it can actually help. Why WebMCP This was the part of the project that really clicked for me. Creative work carries a ridiculous amount of context. A screenshot can show an agent what is on screen, but it does not explain why I kept one reference and rejected another. It does not know which decision I already approved. And it definitely does not know that changing one palette should update three different parts of the project. With WebMCP, MOOD can expose that context directly . The site currently registers 43 WebMCP tools , including 17 read only tools , through document.modelContext.registerTool() . They allow an agent to understand the live project before deciding what to do with it. A few examples: get_project_context get_selected_references get_selected_direction get_design_decisions get_design_system evaluate_palette create_suggestion update_palette navigate_to_phase So instead of guessing its way through the interface or asking me to explain the whole project again every time, the agent can simply ask MOOD . It can: inspect the current creative context understand the references behind a direction read existing and locked design decisions evaluate palettes and visual choices suggest changes with supporting evidence add or organise references create and refine directions update parts of the live design system move through the workflow itself And these are not shortcuts sitting on top of the product. WebMCP and the UI use the same underlying actions and the same state. If I change a palette in the interface or an agent changes it through update_palette , MOOD handles the result through the same system. Direction, Refine and System update together inside the running application. No separate "AI version" of the project floating somewhere else. The agent is not sitting next to the product. It can actually work inside it. The human part I really did not want to build another "AI does the creative work for you" tool. Taste is subjective. Context matters. And sometimes a suggestion can make perfect sense on paper and still just feel wrong. So MOOD treats suggesting and deciding as two different things. A suggestion contains: the reasoning behind it the references used as evidence the exact scope of the proposed change the mutation it would perform if applied The suggestion itself does not need to change the creative work. It can be inspected first, applied, rejected or simply ignored. Important design decisions can also be locked , so they cannot quietly be overwritten later. That separation became one of the most important ideas behind MOOD. The agent can contribute to the process without becoming the owner of it. You can disagree with the agent. That matters. The goal is not less human involvement. It is less time spent translating creative context back and forth . How I built it MOOD is built with React, TypeScript, Vite and Zustand , and deployed on Vercel. Project data lives locally in the browser. The architectural rule behind almost everything else is simple: There is one project state. The designer and the agent interact with the same thing. The visual interface and WebMCP tools dispatch the same domain actions against the Zustand store. For example, keeping a reference manually in the UI and calling keep_reference through WebMCP both update the same underlying project state. I documented that relationship in docs/action-parity.md , mapping: Human action → WebMCP tool → Domain action → Shared state That helped me make sure the agent was not getting special shortcuts that behaved differently from the actual product. Every WebMCP input is validated with Zod and exposed as JSON Schema . Mutating tools also return the current projectVersion , so changes to the shared state can be tracked consistently. I also built a WebMCP debug mode that exposes: API and registration state expected and registered tools available tool names execution results errors a guarded self test It started as something I needed while debugging and became one of the fastest ways to understand what the browser and the agent were actually seeing. The tricky bits 1. Deciding what an agent should actually be allowed to do Registering tools was not the hardest part. Deciding what those tools should be allowed to do was. There is a meaningful difference between: "What do you think about this palette?" "Suggest a better palette." "Change the palette." They sound almost identical in a conversation. Inside a creative product, they absolutely should not behave the same way. That meant thinking carefully about reads, suggestions and direct actions , and about where the human needs to remain in control. 2. Keeping one source of truth An early version allowed the System view to hold its own version of palette and typography. That worked until something changed somewhere else. The moment an agent updated a color, the selected direction and the generated design system could start telling two different stories. So I changed the model: the selected direction became canonical, and System became a synchronized projection of it. It sounds like a technical decision, but for me it was really a product decision. If a designer and an agent are genuinely working on the same project , they cannot be looking at two different versions of the truth. 3. Translating creative language into structure Creative feedback is rarely neat. It sounds more like: “This is too clean.” “I like this, but not for this project.” “It needs more personality.” Or the timeless classic: “Something feels a bit off.” Turning those kinds of thoughts into something both a designer and a browser agent can meaningfully work with turned out to be a surprisingly fun design and data modelling problem. What I learned I came into this project as a web designer first , and that shaped the way I approached MOOD from the beginning. One thing became very clear while building it: if you want a design system that actually feels specific to a project, a brand or an idea, the human part still matters a lot . AI is incredibly useful in the creative process, but on its own it can easily move toward something technically good and visually coherent, yet still very generic and basic. The harder decisions, the ones about taste, personality, context, what feels right and what does not , still need human judgement. Where I found AI genuinely powerful was in everything around those decisions. During Explore , it can connect references, spot patterns and suggest directions I might not have considered. Later, while shaping the design system, it can analyse choices, surface inconsistencies, suggest alternatives and help turn a direction into something much more complete, much faster than I could alone. That changed the way I started thinking about the relationship between human and AI. They are not simply two different ways of doing the same job. They are good at different parts of it. Human Agent Taste Speed Context Pattern finding Personality Analysis Creative judgement Alternative directions Final decisions A second point of view The designer still decides what the project should feel like. title: WebMCP Forge
pitch: Turn existing portfolios into agent-ready WebMCP sites with one script—scan, map, install, verify, and even use WebMCP itself to build WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Turn existing portfolios into agent-ready WebMCP sites with one script—scan, map, install, verify, and even use WebMCP itself to build WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP Forge scans an existing portfolio, maps its content, lets owners choose agent capabilities, and generates one install snippet. Five-step flow: paste a portfolio URL, scan the site, choose agent capabilities, install one snippet, then verify the live runtime. WebMCP Forge itself exposes WebMCP tools, so an AI agent can scan a portfolio, change capabilities, and generate the integration. ChatGPT discovers WebMCP Forge's 8 Site Tools and uses the builder through WebMCP to update the portfolio URL live. One ChatGPT request reads the current permissions, changes multiple capabilities through WebMCP tools, then verifies the updated state. WebMCP Forge doesn't merely generate WebMCP. The Forge builder itself is an agent-operable WebMCP application. Inspiration WebMCP immediately stood out to me because it changes an important assumption about the web. Most websites are designed entirely for people. An AI agent that wants to use one usually has to interpret the page, find the right controls, and interact with the interface almost like a person would. WebMCP gives a website a much cleaner option: it can explicitly describe the useful things an agent is allowed to do. While experimenting with that idea, I realized there was still a practical problem. Adding WebMCP to an existing website is straightforward for a developer who understands the site's code, but it is a much bigger ask for someone who built a portfolio in Framer, Wix, Webflow, or another site builder. A designer should not have to learn document.modelContext , JSON Schema, CSS selectors, or tool-calling conventions just to make a portfolio usable by an agent. That became the idea behind WebMCP Forge : Point it at an existing portfolio, let it understand the site, choose what agents should be able to do, install one snippet, and verify that the integration is actually live. I chose portfolios as the first use case because they are a good example of a website that contains useful structured information but is still primarily built for human browsing. Projects, experience, skills, education, contact information, and navigation all map naturally to useful agent capabilities. What it does WebMCP Forge provides a guided five-step workflow for turning an existing portfolio into a WebMCP-enabled site. 1. Point it at your portfolio The user enters the URL of an existing portfolio. WebMCP Forge fetches the site and analyzes its structure rather than asking the user to describe how the site was built. 2. Review what was found The scanner identifies useful portfolio content such as: projects skills work experience education navigation profile information contact information The interface shows a simple summary of what was detected so the owner can verify that the site was understood correctly. 3. Choose what agents can do The site owner decides which capabilities should be available to an agent. For example: learn about me browse my projects inspect a specific project search my projects show my skills read my experience read my education share my published contact information navigate my portfolio focus a particular project on the page The normal interface deliberately avoids exposing WebMCP implementation details. A portfolio owner chooses capabilities in plain language while WebMCP Forge handles the underlying tool definitions. 4. Install one snippet WebMCP Forge generates a small script tag that can be added to the website once. The runtime loads the site's published WebMCP configuration and registers the appropriate tools in supported browsers. The owner does not need to regenerate the integration every time a project or skill changes. The runtime reads the current live site rather than maintaining a separate copy of the portfolio content. 5. Verify the real installation I did not want the product to stop at "here is some generated code." WebMCP Forge can check the actual deployed website and report whether: the runtime is installed the configuration loaded correctly content mappings are still valid WebMCP is available in the current browser tools were registered projects, skills, experience, and education can still be found on the live site This gives the owner a concrete answer to a much more useful question: Is my website actually agent-ready? Why WebMCP fits this use case A portfolio already has two audiences. The first is a person who wants to look around the site normally. The second can now be an agent trying to answer a question such as: Which of this person's projects demonstrate backend development? Without WebMCP, the agent has to derive that information from the visual website or page structure. With WebMCP, the portfolio can expose a small set of intentional capabilities such as: list_projects get_project search_projects get_skills get_experience The portfolio remains the same website for a human visitor, while an agent gets a structured interface designed specifically for the task. Some tools can also affect what the human sees. For example, focus_project can bring a requested project into view instead of only returning text to the agent. That is the part of WebMCP I found most interesting: the agent and the person can work with the same live interface rather than having separate copies of the application. Use WebMCP to build WebMCP One feature I particularly wanted to include was making WebMCP Forge itself WebMCP-enabled . A compatible agent does not have to operate the builder by guessing where its buttons and switches are. The builder exposes its own tools for actions such as: setting a portfolio URL starting a scan reading the scan result reviewing available capabilities enabling or disabling a capability generating the installation checking verification status That means a user can work with an agent to configure WebMCP for another website. For example, the user could say: Scan my portfolio. Then: Do not expose my contact information. Then: Generate the integration. The corresponding WebMCP Forge interface changes as those tool calls occur. So WebMCP is both what the product generates and part of the interface used to generate it . How we built it WebMCP Forge is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui. The backend performs a bounded scan of a public portfolio rather than crawling the entire web. The scanning pipeline has two stages. Deterministic site analysis The first stage uses normal parsing and extraction to inspect things such as: page metadata headings navigation links repeated DOM structures semantic HTML internal routes contact links likely project collections platform fingerprints This gives the application a compact representation of the site before any model is involved. Semantic interpretation Some portfolio layouts are obvious to a person but difficult to identify from markup alone. For those cases, Google Gemini is used to interpret the extracted structure and map it onto WebMCP Forge's known portfolio concepts. The model does not generate arbitrary JavaScript for the user's website. Instead, WebMCP Forge owns a fixed capability catalogue and validates the structured result before using it. The application also has model fallback and retry handling so a scan is not tied to one model being available. Runtime The script installed on a portfolio is framework-independent browser JavaScript. It can: load the site's published configuration inspect the current page understand the active route read current portfolio content register allowed tools through WebMCP expose diagnostics for verification Normal portfolio visitors do not trigger a Gemini request when an agent calls one of these WebMCP tools. The portfolio itself remains the source of truth. Challenges we ran into Portfolio websites are not standardized The largest practical challenge was that two websites can present the same information with completely different markup. One portfolio may have a clear /projects page and semantic <article> elements, while another may be a single dynamically rendered page with generated class names. I did not want the system to depend entirely on model-generated guesses, so the scanner combines deterministic extraction with semantic interpretation. Avoiding stale portfolio data An early architectural temptation was to scan the website, copy its projects into WebMCP Forge, and have the generated tools return that stored data. That would have made the demo easier, but it would also mean the WebMCP representation became outdated as soon as the owner changed the portfolio. Instead, the configuration stores information about how to find the content , while the runtime reads the live site. title: WebMCP Design Studio
pitch: A studio where a person and an AI agent co-create flyers, posters and social posts on a live canvas. Agent-driven through WebMCP tools, images generated on-device via WebGPU.
about_excerpt: A studio where a person and an AI agent co-create flyers, posters and social posts on a live canvas. Agent-driven through WebMCP tools, images generated on-device via WebGPU. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every design tool is a wall of menus, and every "AI design" demo is a black box that hands you a finished picture. We wanted the third thing: a person and an agent at the same canvas, where the agent does the tedious work and the person keeps the final say. WebMCP made that buildable. A page can declare exactly what an agent may do, so the agent does not have to guess at the UI, and the human's consent can be part of the protocol instead of a dialog bolted on afterwards. What it does WebMCP Design Studio is a live canvas for flyers, posters and social posts. Say "make a spring yard sale flyer, Saturday 8am to 2pm, 14 Orchard Lane" and the agent creates the design, generates the artwork, sets the type and lays it out. Nothing is committed until you approve it. Every edit lands in a pending batch, approve-batch exists as a tool only while there is something to approve, undo appears with it, and a toolchange event fires as they come and go, so any agent can see the moment a human is required. Seventeen tools cover the whole loop: designs, elements, image generation on-device or through the fleet, background removal, restyling, export, memory of your preferences, and a production log that lets the agent tell you what the studio has made this week. A protocol feed shows every registration and call as it happens. How we built it Vite, React and TypeScript, with a fabric.js canvas. One ToolRegistry reconciles the design state onto document.modelContext when the native API is present and onto a spec-shaped polyfill when it is not, so the same tools work in ChatGPT's browser, in Chrome with the WebMCP flag, and everywhere else. The studio's own in-page agent drives the page through the same getTools and executeTool surface an external agent would, so the WebMCP surface is exercised by real traffic. The consent controls are also registered declaratively as a , the spec's second path. Images come from an on-device WebGPU model or from Sana on our fleet through the studio's own proxy; text comes from Bonsai 27B with an automatic fallback lane. It deploys as a static site on GitHub Pages with 205 tests behind it. Challenges we ran into Making consent a protocol object rather than a UI element took the most design work: the batch, the disappearing tools and the toolchange events had to agree exactly. The fleet side fought back too. Under load, the 27B text model crashed and the image lane timed out behind Cloudflare's 100-second cut, so we built a second text lane with automatic fallback, moved image generation onto a resident GPU path, and set honest timeouts everywhere. The demo itself was re-shot after the first cut used artwork from an unrelated production pack instead of the flyers the studio actually makes. Accomplishments that we're proud of The consent boundary lives in the tool surface itself, so any WebMCP agent inherits it. The app eats its own protocol. Image generation runs fully on-device when the browser can do it. And the studio is used for real work: its production log is a week of actual pieces, readable by the agent through a tool. What we learned Declaring capabilities changes how you design the app. Once every action was a tool with a schema, the pending batch and the approve step became obvious, and the UI got simpler rather than more crowded. We also learned that a demo built for agents is judged in the agent's environment: cross-origin, preflight and timeout behavior matter as much as the tools. title: Material Notes
pitch: a shared canvas for your bookmarks, notes, and ai
about_excerpt: a shared canvas for your bookmarks, notes, and ai Like 1 Comment Story Updates Material is an app to collect the things I'm thinking about: essays, tweets, videos, screenshots, and my own notes, and arrange them on an infinite canvas to think with them. why this is a strong fit for webmcp Material is a strong fit for webmcp because it turns an infinite canvas into a shared workspace between you and an agent. normally, all the context on a canvas stays inside the canvas. if I want to work with an agent, I have to leave it, copy dozens of notes and references into a chat, explain which ones I'm looking at and how they relate, wait for a response, then bring that response back into material and reorganize it on the canvas myself. every time I do that, I lose the spatial context I was working in — and usually the flow of thought that came with it. with webmcp, the agent can work from the same context I already have in front of me. it knows what's on the canvas, what I'm currently selecting, and how things are arranged, and it can work directly in that same space. how it makes the experience better the biggest change is that interacting with the agent becomes part of interacting with the canvas. I can select a messy pile of 30 references and say "group these by theme." the agent reads them, finds the themes, writes a synthesis for each cluster, and lays everything out. or I can select three cards that caught my attention and ask "what connects these?" I don't have to name them, paste their contents, or explain what I'm pointing at. selecting something is enough. that makes the interaction much more fluid. pointing, selecting, moving, and arranging are already how I think on a canvas. now those actions can carry context to the agent too, and its response comes back as part of the canvas rather than another piece of text I have to translate into my workspace. what people and agents can do together that wasn't possible the part I find most interesting is that I don't have to hand the canvas over to the agent or stop what I'm doing to give it instructions. we can work on the same thing at the same time. I might be moving things around, reading, and selecting a few cards that feel related without knowing exactly why yet. I can ask the agent what it sees in them, and it can read much more of the surrounding material than I would at once, find a pattern, write a synthesis, or reorganize the cards around that idea. I can immediately react to what it did — move something back, rewrite a sentence, select a different group — and continue from there. the human contribution is often directional and intuitive: this feels important, these things belong together, this is the thread I want to follow. the agent can take that partial signal and work across much more of the material at once. because we're working on the same canvas, the result doesn't arrive as an answer in a separate chat. it becomes part of the thing I'm already making. how I implemented it I registered eight tools with document.modelContext.registerTool, covering canvas state, selection, card content, creation, editing, and placement. reads come directly from a ref kept in sync with the live react canvas state. writes run through the same reducers as the UI and update state immediately, so there's no server round-trip. spatial operations are batched: the agent can place an entire cluster with one call containing all of its coordinates rather than issuing individual moves. the demo is intentionally ephemeral: the initial canvas is server-rendered from a postgres space and cached for 30 minutes, but all agent and user edits stay local and a reload resets them. the same eight tools run against persistent state in the authenticated product. title: Stadtoskop WebMCP
pitch: Stadtoskop uses WebMCP to let AI agents directly discover verified local events and venues, turning local culture into structured, conversational discovery.
about_excerpt:
Stadtoskop uses WebMCP to let AI agents directly discover verified local events and venues, turning local culture into structured, conversational discovery.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 




 
 InspirationInspiration 

 Finding something interesting to do in a city is still surprisingly fragmented. Events are spread across venue websites, cultural institutions, clubs and organizers. Stadtoskop started as an attempt to turn this fragmented information into a visual and playful way to discover local culture. 

 While building it, another question became increasingly important: How should AI agents discover local culture? 

 Today, an agent often has to search the web, interpret different websites and reconstruct information that already exists as structured data. 

 WebMCP offers a much cleaner approach. 

 What it does 

 Stadtoskop is a local culture discovery platform starting in Leipzig, Germany. It organizes events, venues and categories into structured data while keeping links to their original public sources. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, Stadtoskop adds an agent-accessible discovery layer. 

 Instead of scraping or visually interpreting the website, an AI agent can use WebMCP tools to search Stadtoskop directly — for example to find live music, cultural events or places matching a user's interests. 

 The goal is simple: 

 People explore the city visually. Agents explore the same city through structured tools. 

 How we built it 

 Stadtoskop already has a React Native frontend, a Node.js backend and a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database containing structured event and venue information. 

 The WebMCP integration exposes selected discovery capabilities as clearly defined tools. These tools connect the agent-facing web experience with the same underlying cultural data used by Stadtoskop. 

 This means the WebMCP layer does not create a second database or duplicate the discovery logic. It provides another interface to the existing Stadtoskop ecosystem. 

 Challenges 

 Local event data is messy. Names change, events repeat, venues move, and information can differ between sources. 

 A major part of Stadtoskop has therefore been about making discovery data reliable enough to be useful while still preserving the connection to official public sources. 

 The WebMCP challenge adds another interesting requirement: deciding which parts of that data model should become simple, useful tools for an AI agent instead of exposing the complexity of the entire system. 

 What's next 

 The WebMCP prototype is only the beginning. 

 The long-term idea is for Stadtoskop to become a local cultural discovery layer that can be used both by humans and AI assistants. 

 An agent could eventually answer questions such as: 

 “What can I do with my kids in Leipzig this weekend?” 

 or: 

 “Which bands playing in Leipzig during the next two weeks should I listen to?” 

 WebMCP provides a promising way to make that interaction direct, structured and useful.

title: Agent Ready
pitch: Can an AI agent actually use your website? AgentReady runs real agents through your raw UI and your WebMCP tools, scores the site 0-100, and publishes the gap. Measured: UI 0/3 vs WebMCP 3/3.
about_excerpt: Can an AI agent actually use your website? AgentReady runs real agents through your raw UI and your WebMCP tools, scores the site 0-100, and publishes the gap. Measured: UI 0/3 vs WebMCP 3/3. Like Comment Story Updates Benchmark Run Log Live Agent Traffic Scorecard Human Agent Cowriting Agent Ready Inspiration Everyone in the agent era repeats the same claim — "AI agents struggle to use websites" — and nobody measures it. Site owners have zero visibility into whether an agent can actually finish a checkout on their site, and WebMCP adopters have no way to prove the investment worked. We stopped arguing and built the measuring instrument. What it does AgentReady is the readiness benchmark for the agent-native web. It runs real AI agents against real task flows on a site twice — once through the raw UI, once through the site's WebMCP tools — and scores the site 0–100 from success rate, tool surface, and steps-to-complete, with a failure taxonomy (auth walls, popups, navigation loops, timeouts) explaining every miss. The benchmark's own dashboard is agent-native: 8 WebMCP tools let your agent query scores, compare sites, and co-write a readiness report with you in a shared on-page editor — it drafts, you edit by hand, and it reads your edits back through a tool before revising. Its queue_live_audit tool triggers a real serverless audit — headless browser, LLM agent, results into the database — that your agent then reads back. A demo store with 5 more tools (one cart shared between human and agent) is the reference implementation, and every tool call on the deployment streams to a live analytics view. Measured result on our own store: raw UI 0/3 (all timed out at 15 steps), WebMCP 3/3 in ~4 steps. How we built it Entirely on Cloudflare: the app runs on vinext (the Vite-based Next.js reimplementation) on Workers, D1 stores telemetry and audit results, Queues orchestrates audit jobs, Browser Run provides headless Chrome at the edge, and Workers AI (Llama 3.3 70B) is the audit agent. A small shim ( lib/webmcp.ts ) registers WebMCP tools via document.modelContext with a navigator fallback, instruments every execution for the live analytics view, and mirrors tools onto a page registry so headless auditors can drive the exact same tool functions. A local Playwright runner audits external sites with confidence intervals; a queue-consumer Worker runs the serverless audits. The demo video was produced by a multi-agent pipeline too: strategy, script, Playwright screen-capture of the live site, Kyutai pocket-tts narration, Veo b-roll, and a Remotion composition. Challenges we ran into vinext is explicitly experimental — our first deploys shipped an assets-only Worker (no server code) until we discovered the config needed an explicit main: "vinext/server/fetch-handler" . UI-mode audit runs take 12+ minutes, which blew past queue consumer wall-clocks when we batched runs into one message — the fix was one message per run. Workers AI sometimes returns parsed JSON objects where we expected strings, which silently killed our first serverless audits. Browser launch failures burned queue retries without recording anything until we made every failure write a result row. And securing an intentionally unauthenticated API (judges' agents must call it) meant same-origin audit restriction, a daily run budget, and payload caps instead of auth. Accomplishments that we're proud of The headline number is measured, not claimed: same site, same task, same agent — 0/3 through the UI, 3/3 through WebMCP. The bidirectional co-writing loop ( draft_readiness_report → human edits → get_report_draft reads them back) treats the page as a two-way channel between human and agent, not a tool facade. The benchmark audits its own demo store with one tool call, on camera, in production. And we kept the methodology honest: sample rows are clearly badged as synthetic, the real runs are labeled with their n, and the whole thing is MIT-licensed and reproducible. What we learned Agent-readiness is measurable, and the gap is bigger than the discourse suggests — our agent burned 15 steps and still failed on a UI it could clear in 4 steps with tools. A tool surface beats heroic UI parsing every time, and the score gap is the business case in one number. Architecturally: mirroring tools onto a page registry made the site testable by any headless browser, serverless constraints (queue wall-clocks, browser session limits) should shape job design from day one, and honest small-n data presented plainly is more credible than inflated claims. What's next for Agent Ready Audit real production sites (with permission) to grow the index into an industry readiness leaderboard. An embeddable "agent-ready score" badge and a CI check so a site's score updates on every deploy. Richer task suites beyond add-to-cart — search, auth flows, form completion, multi-step journeys. Durable Object browser-session pooling to parallelize serverless audits. And opening the instrumentation SDK so any site gets /live -style agent analytics by wrapping registerTool in one line. title: PixlPal
pitch: Imagine having an AI agent that uses Photoshop with you. PixlPal lets anyone edit photos. Just describe the changes you want in plain English.
about_excerpt: Imagine having an AI agent that uses Photoshop with you. PixlPal lets anyone edit photos. Just describe the changes you want in plain English. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The Problem with diffusion models AI image editing is getting popular because it allows people without any experience in using image editing software to create beautiful edits of their photos. However, the problem with AI image editing approaches right now is that they regenerate the photo . This approach is prone to mistakes such as the image generation model adding or removing certain details, or introducing diffusion noise. And since it "edits" by regenerating the whole photo, it leaves little control for the user to tweak certain image editing parameters themselves. It is not a true edit . PixlPal's Approach PixlPal believes that AI should instead use deterministic tools (like in photoshop) to truly edit the images directly. So I created a custom Rust engine that exposes tools/APIs for an AI agent orchestrator to edit photos. The coolest part: I added a segmentation model that agents can call so it can select specific objects to apply specific transformations to as well. Think of it like watching an AI agent use Photoshop or Lightroom while you watch and tweak, instead of having it one-shot regenerate the whole image. People and Agents working together PixlPal's approach also creates a better user experience because the user has more control over the editing process. With image gen models, this was impossible: they need to regenerate the image as a whole. It is not a "true" edit. But with PixlPal, users can tweak edits directly if they want. AI Agents and People working together. How we implemented WebMCP, and what it brings I already had a custom-built Rust engine to do image/pixel transformations set up, as well as tool definitions exposed to my built-in AI agent. For this challenge, it was just a matter of bridging those tools to WebMCP. WebMCP turned out to be a great complementary approach to the built-in agent. Users can now effectively "Bring Your Own Agent" (BYOA) to PixlPal, and their agents might have better specific context of their tastes and what kind of photos they like. Or if they're just more comfortable using their own agent, WebMCP allows users to use their own agent. Challenges we ran into Usually people want to apply changes only to specific objects instead of the whole image (think of the lasso tool). Without that capability, PixlPal was just a filter-applier rather than a true agentic image editor. At first, I thought this would mean needing to get an AI agent to use a lasso tool (very hard). Eventually, I realized I can just add an Image Segmentation Model as a tool-call for the agent. So the agent does a natural-language prompt to the segmentation model i.e. "select the red snack bag", and the segmentation model returns the exact pixels of the red snack bag, and then the agent can apply pixel transformations specifically to those pixels. Accomplishments that we're proud of Figuring out how to make AI agents select/segment specific objects easily. Creating a working product that lets anyone edits their photos. No background in professional editing needed. What we learned Human UI (clicking buttons, moving around cursors, drag and drop) are quite clunky for AI agents to interact with. In contrast, I think of WebMCP as like a UI for agents. WebMCP allows agents to easily navigate and use web apps and websites. What's next for PixlPal Image Segmentation Model is currently run client-side via WebGPU. This makes edits where PixlPal needs to segment a specific object slow unless the user has a GPU. In the future, I would like to host and run the segmentation model in the cloud. title: NEXUS
pitch: The continuity layer for the Agentic Web. NEXUS lets a user's intent continue across independent WebMCP websites, with failure recovery, rerouting, and explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: The continuity layer for the Agentic Web. NEXUS lets a user's intent continue across independent WebMCP websites, with failure recovery, rerouting, and explicit human approval. Like Comment Story Updates Websites end. Human intentions don't. WebMCP gives agents tools inside a website. NEXUS lets the user's intent continue beyond it. NEXUS is a WebMCP-first proof of concept that explores a missing layer of the Agentic Web: intent continuity across independent websites. The problem Human goals rarely fit inside a single website. An agent might successfully buy furniture from one provider, but the user's actual goal could be much larger: open an entire office, organize a trip, launch a business, or plan an event. When one website reaches the boundary of what it can fulfill, the user's intent should not disappear with it. What NEXUS does NEXUS preserves the unresolved part of a user's goal and allows an agent to continue it across independent WebMCP-enabled providers. The demo proves the complete lifecycle: Fulfillment → Intent Handoff → Recovery/Reroute → Human Approval → Goal Complete It also introduces an important trust boundary. A user who starts with a specific provider remains in Brand Mode . NEXUS cannot silently divert that user elsewhere. Continuing through other providers requires explicit authorization into Broker Mode . The agent can discover, plan and recover autonomously, while the human retains authority over consequential actions. Hero mission Our deterministic challenge is: Open an office for 20 people in Guadalajara before October 1, 2026 with a MXN 500,000 budget. The mission crosses five independent providers: OfficePro fulfills desks and chairs → 40% The user explicitly authorizes an Intent Handoff TechSupply fulfills computers → 60% FiberMX can provide internet, but installation is October 8 — after the deadline NEXUS records the failure and reroutes the unresolved requirement to NetBusiness NetBusiness can install by September 25 → 80% SecureNow finds a valid security solution but reaches a commitment-class action NEXUS stops at REQUIRES_HUMAN Only after explicit human approval is the installation requested GOAL COMPLETE → 100% Final cost: MXN 410,000 Remaining budget: MXN 90,000 Deadline: Satisfied Why WebMCP matters NEXUS is not an agent calling one centralized REST API. Each provider is an independent website exposing its own genuine WebMCP tools and owning its own catalog, pricing, availability and actions. The production demo spans: 16 native WebMCP tools 5 independent providers 6 HTTPS origins Cross-origin WebMCP discovery and invocation Explicit permission boundaries Failure recovery and provider rerouting Human approval before commitment-class actions We also validated the complete mission end-to-end using ChatGPT's WebMCP experience. What we learned The most interesting challenge was not tool invocation — it was preserving intent safely across website boundaries. NEXUS treats failure as a first-class state. FiberMX is not hidden when it misses the deadline. The failure remains auditable while only the unresolved internet requirement is rerouted. We also learned that agent autonomy and human control do not have to be opposites. Agents can discover, compare, plan and recover autonomously while humans retain authority at consequential boundaries. Execution NEXUS runs as a deterministic production proof of concept across six independent HTTPS origins. Production Lighthouse scores: 100 Performance / 100 Accessibility / 100 Best Practices / 100 SEO Agent Readiness improved from 39 to 66 (+69.2%) , while the WebMCP-specific check remained 5/5 . We deliberately did not fabricate REST APIs, OAuth, MCP servers, A2A endpoints, SDKs, or other capabilities simply to increase a generic readiness score. The idea WebMCP makes websites agent-ready. NEXUS explores what happens next: What if the user's goal is bigger than the website? One intent. Many providers. title: PixelAid
pitch: PixelAid is a free web app for turning oversized, fake, matted, or messy pixel images into transparent PNGs, stable palettes, and export-ready bundles. From AI all the way to game engines.
about_excerpt:
PixelAid is a free web app for turning oversized, fake, matted, or messy pixel images into transparent PNGs, stable palettes, and export-ready bundles. From AI all the way to game engines.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 I made PixelAid for the part of pixel art cleanup that kept wasting my night. 

 AI image tools can give you a cute sprite in seconds. So can a quick Photoshop pass, a screenshot crop, an old exported sheet, or a tool that says “pixel art” and leaves you with a giant blurry PNG. The image looks fine in a chat window. Then you open it in Aseprite, Unity, Godot, or your own engine and the whole thing falls apart: fake pixels, too many colors, weird transparency, a halo around the edge. 

 PixelAid starts after the image exists. It looks at the file, guesses the grid it was trying to be, cleans the background, reduces accidental colors, preserves useful details, and exports something you can inspect or keep working on. 

 What it does 

 
 Pixel snapping and grid alignment for pixel-perfect images 
 chroma and smart background removal 
 color space recognition and flattening (ai images typically generate > 10,000 unique colors whereas pixel art typically uses 8 - 32 colors. We use CIELAB and other color space algorithms 
 Resize and clustering work. There are a lot of algorithms in here to make the output art deterministic, repeatable, and correct. 
 Frame size detection - PixelAid understands whether your image is a static sprite, a spritesheet, or a framegrid of multiple animations. It also offers sprite animation previews and players so you can apply your pixel art fixes to animations too 
 

 How we built it 

 I have a much longer essay on how it works and the algorithms used internally: https://oscarsanchez.com/essays/ai-pixelart-is-broken/ but essentially the app itself a headless runner with a main algorithm owning the detection and then spreading to different algorithms based on what we need to do. The headless capability allows me to release PixelAid as a cli, a web app, and a desktop app. So you can use it however you want. The source is free and it's also on itch.io 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Detection is hard, getting colors to match is hard, sizing is hard. But colors are definitely the worst - if you ask AI to make an image of a white cloud, there will be 10,000 shades of "white" in that output. It may not seem significant, but if you have a character with red hair, yellow jacket, blue pants, green socks, brown shoes - that's already 5/8 colors you can end up with! 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 The headless app and ability to release in so many ways. Adding webmcp was really simple too! 
 

 What we learned 

 What's next for PixelAid 

 The algorithm can always be better. Image generation itself is not part of pixel aid either, and it can be.

title: Vide
pitch: An in-browser code-based video editor empowering AI agents to author timeline scripts, manage local media assets, and export MP4s via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An in-browser code-based video editor empowering AI agents to author timeline scripts, manage local media assets, and export MP4s via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Vide: In-browser Video IDE The 28 WebMCP Tools by Domain: Asset Metadata & Semantic Notes (3 tools): get_asset_metadata , set_asset_notes , search_assets — Attach and search semantic descriptions, mood tags, BPM tempos, spoken transcripts, and visual descriptions so the agent understands raw media files (e.g., matching "whoosh transition" to sfx_0294.mp3 ). File System Operations (4 tools): list_project_files , read_project_file , write_project_file , delete_project_file — Direct read/write access to project directory files and scripts. Script & Tab Lifecycle (8 tools): get_active_script , get_video_script , set_active_script_code , update_video_script , create_script , list_open_scripts , switch_active_script , save_active_script — Read, generate, and hot-reload DSL scripts with real-time agent reasoning banners. Engine & Playback Telemetry (3 tools): validate_script , get_scene_settings , control_playback — Perform dry-run syntax checks, inspect canvas dimensions/FPS, and drive timeline playback. Hardware Video Export (1 tool): export_video — Trigger client-side GPU video encoding with configurable codecs (H.264/AVC, AV1, VP9) and automatically save outputs to the project's export folder. Documentation & Knowledge Base (3 tools): search_vide_docs , search_vide_documentation , get_dsl_reference — Embedded vector-scored knowledge base for the agent to look up DSL syntax, math rendering, and composition rules on the fly. Multimodal Visual Inspection & QA (3 tools): capture_frame_screenshot , analyze_timeline , inspect_layers_at_time — Render in-memory frame buffers to base64 PNGs for multimodal vision models to visually verify text alignment, contrast, and layout, correcting bugs autonomously. Timeline Cues & Scene Navigation (3 tools): list_timeline_cues , seek_to_cue , add_timeline_cue — Manage timeline markers, gutter breakpoints, and playhead anchors across scenes. How We Built It Having no formal background in compiler design, AST manipulation, or custom DSLs prior to this project, I paired with ChatGPT and Gemini as collaborative engineering partners throughout development. We established that compiling a deterministic subset of JavaScript using Acorn was the ideal architecture—giving users familiar syntax with mathematical operators, while completely eliminating non-deterministic loops and security risks in the evaluation sandbox. Technical Stack: Framework & Routing: Full-stack local-first application built with TanStack Start , React 19, and Tailwind CSS v4. Agent Protocol: WebMCP Bridge exposing 28 structured tools over window.modelContext and message channels. Language Runtime: Acorn for AST parsing, evaluated in a deterministic sandbox with Valibot schema validation at every trust boundary. Code Editor: Monaco Editor with custom Monarch tokenizers, syntax highlighters, and DSL snippet completions. Engine & Export: Custom HTML5 Canvas 2D engine paired with Mediabunny for WebCodecs MP4/WebM hardware encoding and Web Audio API mixing. Storage & Hosting: IndexedDB with the File System Access API; deployed serverlessly on Cloudflare Workers . Challenges We Ran Into Deterministic Timeline Architecture: Translating declarative composition ( parallel , sequence , at , after , gap , offset ) into an immutable, time-addressable AST graph while preventing timeline keyframe collisions. Synchronizing Video, Audio, and Canvas Lifecycles: Ensuring Mediabunny's frame-exact video reader and the Web Audio context stayed strictly aligned during interactive timeline scrubbing and offline hardware encoding. Cross-Platform WebCodecs Audio Encoding: Overcoming platform-specific audio encoder limitations (such as Linux Chromium lacking AAC encoders) by implementing dynamic AudioEncoder.isConfigSupported fallback routing between AAC and Opus inside MP4 containers. Designing a Clean 28-Tool WebMCP Surface: Structuring a comprehensive tool suite that allows deep multimodal inspection without overwhelming the agent's context window. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of Zero-Server Video Encoding: Rendering 60 FPS 1080p MP4 videos with custom fonts and LaTeX math entirely within the client browser using WebCodecs and Mediabunny. Complete 28-Tool WebMCP Suite: Enabling multimodal AI models to discover assets, author scripts, visually inspect rendered frames, and export motion graphics autonomously. True Dogfooding: The entire demonstration and challenge submission video was 100% scripted, animated, composed, and rendered inside Vide itself. Local-First Privacy: Full file editing, local asset references, and MP4 generation without a single byte of user media ever leaving their machine. What We Learned How to design a clean Domain-Specific Language (DSL) and evaluate AST nodes deterministically. How to leverage the WebCodecs API and Mediabunny for client-side, hardware-accelerated video export pipelines. The transformative power of the WebMCP standard in replacing brittle visual UI scraping with structured, bidirectional tool interfaces between web applications and AI agents. What's Next for Vide Orama In-Browser Vector Database: Integrating Orama to provide client-side vector search and semantic similarity matching across asset transcriptions, visual descriptions, and DSL documentation with sub-millisecond local latency. Web Worker OffscreenCanvas Rendering: Offloading the entire frame rendering and WebCodecs encoding pipeline into background Web Workers for faster export throughput. Procedural Data Visualization Nodes: Built-in animated bar charts, line plots, and telemetry counter primitives. pitch: A shared release room where agents verify and prepare, but only humans ship.
about_excerpt:
A shared release room where agents verify and prepare, but only humans ship.

 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for ProofMesh WebMCP 

 Inspiration 

 Release decisions are scattered across CI, security, support, and private team context. Agents can reconcile that evidence, but backend-only agents remove the shared interface and screen-clicking agents are brittle. ProofMesh makes the release room understandable to both people and agents while preserving an explicit human decision boundary. 

 What it does 

 ProofMesh asks independent Engineering, Security, and Support agents to verify a launch claim, compares their evidence, and surfaces the contradiction needing the release owner. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can inspect the case, run verification, retrieve conflicts, and stage a proposed resolution. Every call updates the same page the user is watching. The agent cannot seal or ship the release: the owner reviews the proposal and clicks Approve & seal . Only then is a read-only decision-receipt tool registered. 

 How we built it 

 The React page registers four domain-level tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_release_case , run_release_verification , get_release_conflicts , and prepare_owner_resolution . Each has a focused description and JSON Schema input; read-only tools carry readOnlyHint . Registration is lifecycle-bound with an AbortSignal , reuses the existing verification API and React state, and dynamically registers get_decision_receipt after human approval. A visible activity stream records every agent action. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer state from pixels and repeatedly reread the page. A backend MCP server would lose the live, reviewable release-room context. WebMCP exposes domain capabilities inside the page while keeping actions visible and consequential finalization human-owned. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 The agent performs high-friction evidence work and prepares a concrete next step. The human sees the same evidence, edits or rejects the proposal, and owns the final decision. This inspect → verify → explain → prepare → human approve → receipt sequence was previously hard to make both reliable and accountable. 

 Challenges and lessons 

 The main challenge was resisting the urge to expose every button. We designed a small, permission-scoped surface, made read versus draft behavior explicit, and withheld irreversible approval from the agent. Agent-native does not mean agent-only; sometimes the safest tool is the one deliberately not registered. 

 What's next 

 Dynamic tools for release phases, signed receipts, permission-scoped cross-origin team frames, and evaluation against prompt injection and ambiguous finalization attacks.

A shared cat-behavior workspace where people and browser agents use the same profile, decoder, and journal through WebMCP

 WebMCP executes the existing decoder and saves the observation to the shared journal 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent-written observation appears immediately in the same local journal 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Miaunolog started as a cat-behavior interpretation app designed to combine vocalizations, body language, context, and cat-specific profile information. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to see whether a browser agent could use the same application state and logic as the human user, rather than relying on a separate demo or agent-only backend. 

 I was already working on Miaunolog when I received OpenAI's notification about the WebMCP Challenge on X. I thought the app was a natural fit to extend with WebMCP and submit to the challenge. 

 What it does 

 Miaunolog lets a user create a cat profile, interpret observed behavior, and save observations to a local journal. 

 Through WebMCP, a browser agent can access that same workflow using three tools: 

 
 get_cat_profile 
 interpret_cat_behavior 
 add_behavior_observation 
 

 The agent reads the real active profile, uses the existing Miaunolog decoder, and writes the result into the same local journal shown in the human-facing interface. 

 How I built it 

 The project was developed with AI-assisted workflows using Grok and ChatGPT for implementation, review, debugging, and iteration. 

 The app is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, TanStack Router, and Tailwind CSS. 

 The WebMCP integration uses document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The WebMCP layer is intentionally thin: it maps structured agent inputs to Miaunolog's existing internal domain model and reuses the existing decoder and persistence functions. 

 Profiles and journal entries remain in localStorage, while audio clips use IndexedDB. No separate backend is required for the challenge workflow. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was making WebMCP functional rather than decorative. 

 The agent needed to use the real application state, reuse the same interpretation logic as the human interface, and produce a write that immediately appeared in the existing journal. 

 Another challenge was preserving the behavior of the original decoder while creating an agent-facing English schema without changing internal IDs or stored data structures. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP makes it possible to expose application capabilities directly to browser agents without duplicating the application's logic. 

 The most useful pattern in Miaunolog was not giving the agent a second implementation, but letting both human and agent operate on one shared state and one decoder. 

 What's next 

 Future work could expand the set of agent-visible observations, improve longitudinal behavior tracking, and explore richer workflows across cat profiles, audio observations, and journal history.tion

title: Agent Chess
pitch: One verified chessboard. Two native interfaces. Humans and AI agents share every turn through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: One verified chessboard. Two native interfaces. Humans and AI agents share every turn through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Opening Board Human-agent exchange WebMCP explainer Legal-move guidance Why I built it I wanted to test WebMCP on a task where success could not be hidden behind a convincing-looking interface. Chess is a good test because every action has an objectively correct result. An agent must know where every piece is, whose turn it is, which side it controls and which moves are legal. Misreading one square can invalidate the entire game. A normal chess website is designed for human eyes and a mouse. An agent using that interface must reconstruct 64 squares from pixels and translate its move back into screen coordinates. That is fragile and unnecessary—the page already knows the exact position and legal actions. Obsidian Chess explores a different model: give the person and the agent interfaces designed for their individual strengths while connecting both to the same game. What it does The person plays through a visual chessboard. The agent plays through four page-defined WebMCP tools. For example, the person can select Take White and move the pawn from e2 to e4 . An agent waiting through wait_for_turn wakes up and receives the updated FEN, move history, role ownership, game status and exact legal moves. The agent selects one of those moves and calls move_piece , optionally adding an explanation such as “I’m contesting the centre.” The move immediately appears on the board. The SAN history, FEN, turn indicator and Human + Agent Trace all update from the same position. This is a complete playable experience rather than a mocked tool demo. A person can claim either colour, full chess rules are enforced, games can be reset, promotions are supported and invalid actions recover safely. The board works with a mouse, keyboard or touch. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Most agent tools perform one action and finish. A chess match is different: it is a long-running collaboration where control alternates between a person and an agent. A person might think for five seconds or five minutes. Without WebMCP, the agent must repeatedly inspect the screen and guess whether anything changed. With wait_for_turn , it can wait, wake when the person moves and receive the new authoritative state. WebMCP also lets the application expose precise capabilities without giving up control of its rules. The agent can inspect the position and submit a move, but the page still verifies side ownership, turn ownership and chess legality before changing anything. If the agent acts out of turn, submits an illegal move or moves before the person has chosen a side, the request is rejected without changing the board. The response includes a stable error code, the unchanged state and a specific recovery instruction. The person keeps the expressive interface that makes chess understandable. The agent receives structured state, exact legal actions and explicit permissions. Neither participant operates on a copy. Who this helps Obsidian Chess is immediately a playable human-agent game, but it is also a reference for developers building applications where people and agents share responsibility. The same pattern appears in purchase approvals, document reviews, scheduling negotiations, incident response and simulations. A person reviews information and makes a decision; the agent waits, observes the resulting state and continues from an explicitly permitted set of actions. These workflows often rely on screen interpretation, repeated polling or separate custom integrations. Obsidian Chess demonstrates another approach: the website exposes its existing state and domain actions directly while retaining control over validation and permissions. Chess makes this pattern easy to verify. A move is legal or illegal, turn ownership is unambiguous and every transition can be compared with the visible board. This is also what makes the project different from a typical AI chess demo. It does not add a chatbot beside a board or connect a hidden chess engine. The agent discovers the page’s tools, reads the shared state, chooses an action, explains it and waits for the person. How I implemented WebMCP The application is built with React and Vinext. chess.js is the authority for legal moves, check, checkmate, draws, castling, en passant and promotion. The page registers four tools through the browser’s model context: join_game announces the agent and returns the collaboration contract. get_board returns the authoritative position, ownership, history and legal actions. move_piece submits one schema-checked, turn-gated and rules-validated move. wait_for_turn waits for the agent to gain control of the next turn. Every response includes a protocol version, success state, stable status code, suggested next action and current game state. This gives the agent enough information to continue or recover without guessing. The waiting system uses a bounded long poll tied to a session identifier and state version. Duplicate waits are rejected, and resetting the game invalidates older waits so a stale call cannot act inside a new match. The visible Human + Agent Trace shows tool discovery, board inspection, waiting, moves, resets and errors. I also published evaluation.json and llms.txt guides so automated evaluators can follow a deterministic testing path. Challenges and lessons The hardest part was keeping two different interfaces synchronized across human thinking time. An early bug allowed the person to claim White but left pawn interaction in the wrong state. Fixing it required treating side ownership, turn ownership and the chess.js position as one transition instead of separate UI events. I added regression tests for opening pawn moves with humans playing either colour, alongside tests for wrong turns, promotions, castling, en passant, checkmate and resets. Reset behaviour was another subtle problem. A waiting call started during one match must never wake up and act in a different match. Session and version checks now return an explicit reset result to stale calls. I also learned that agent interfaces must explain failure as carefully as success. Returning only “illegal move” leaves the agent guessing. Returning ILLEGAL_MOVE , the unchanged position and a specific next action lets it recover safely. The result is one person, one agent and two purpose-built interfaces sharing one precise, verifiable game.
