title: UNSAID — Private Context, Shared Agreement
pitch: A minimum-disclosure decision room where personal agents construct common ground and people ratify it.
about_excerpt: A minimum-disclosure decision room where personal agents construct common ground and people ratify it. Like Comment Story Updates No existing option works for everyone. Agreement reached with zero raw private context received from the live participant. Agents construct an option that did not exist. Inspiration Group decisions routinely force people to reveal more than they should. A person may have a strict budget, an accessibility need, a caregiving deadline, or another private reason an option will not work. Polls make the group choose among fixed answers. Meetings make people explain themselves. We wanted a third path: let each person’s private agent understand the full context while the shared room learns only what it needs to build agreement. What it does UNSAID is a shared decision canvas. Participants privately brief their own browser agents. The room receives structured ballots rather than raw explanations. When no existing option works for everyone, participants or their agents can publish minimum structured signals and create a bridge proposal by changing known attributes. Candidates move toward a visible common-ground ring as aggregate support improves. A candidate can be nominated only when every participant accepts it, and the live person must ratify the final agreement through the human interface. The judge demo uses one live ChatGPT participant and three clearly labeled deterministic demo agents so the complete multi-party experience can be tested immediately. Why WebMCP UNSAID is not improved by adding generic chat. Its core depends on the webpage exposing a precise coordination protocol. Through WebMCP, a personal agent can read shared room state, submit a private ballot, publish a structured signal, create a bridge candidate, and nominate a viable option. Tool schemas prevent raw private narratives from being sent accidentally. The tools reuse the same state transitions and permissions as the human interface, and their availability changes with the room phase. Without WebMCP, an agent would have to scrape cards, guess form controls, and infer whether a shared state mutation succeeded. With WebMCP, agent actions are typed, reliable, attributable, and visibly reflected in the common canvas. What people and agents can do together now A person can give their own agent the complete private context. The agent can translate that context into the minimum structured contribution, reason across aggregate group signals, and construct a new option that did not previously exist. The group can reach a better agreement without collecting everyone’s raw private explanation. Agents do the translation and option construction; people retain final authority. How it was built UNSAID is a full-stack TypeScript application hosted on ChatGPT Sites with durable room state in D1. The top-level page registers imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Read-only and state-changing tools have narrow JSON schemas and compact verifiable results. The room uses server-authoritative versioning, aggregate ballots, a deterministic consensus function, and a fixture evaluator for the three fictional demo agents. The human interface remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. Limitations UNSAID is a prototype for minimum disclosure, not an anonymity or encryption system. Source-hidden signals may be inferable in a small group. The deterministic demo agents are fictional fixtures, clearly labeled in the product and source. The current submission demonstrates an offsite decision rather than a general production platform. video_title: UNSAID — Private Context, Shared Agreement | WebMCP Challenge
video_transcript_excerpt: Group decisions come with a hidden cost. To coordinate, people share budgets, accessibility needs, family obligations, and other private details. Or they stay quiet and settle for a bad outcome. Unsaid offers a third path. Everyone tells their own agent the whole truth. The shared page gets only the structured judgments needed to find common ground. Agents negotiate. People make the final call. Four people are choosing an offsite. Three labeled demo agents already evaluated the options deterministically. I am the live participant. The room has none of my private context. I tell ChatGPT my constraints in private. Through WebMCP, the page gives it two type tools, get room state and submit ballot. ChatGPT evaluates the choices, then shares only preferred, acceptable, or unacceptable. No reason. No private story. None of the original options works for everyone. Now the page changes the tools available to the agent. Bridge tools appear, and the room shares only the minimum attribute signals needed to move forward. ChatGPT combines those public signals with my private context and creates a new option. Lakeside Lab on Thursday, ending by 4:00 for $235. The proposal changes what matters without revealing why it matters. The demo agents evaluate the new proposal. This time, all four participants accept it. The candidate moves into common ground, and Web MCP exposes a new action, nominate it for ratification. The agent can open ratification. It cannot make my final decision. I review the shared outcome and approve it myself. The receipt shows the disclosure boundary, structured ballots, public signals, one bridge proposal, and final approval. My private explanation never entered the room. Each agent action used a phase-specific Web MCP tool tied to the same operations as the human interface. The old web helps one person transact. Unsaid helps many people agree.

title: SituationRoom
pitch: SituationRoom turns messy vendor proposals into a live, auditable decision model that humans and AI agents build together by mapping evidence, testing scenarios, and approving decisions using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: SituationRoom turns messy vendor proposals into a live, auditable decision model that humans and AI agents build together by mapping evidence, testing scenarios, and approving decisions using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Complex decisions rarely fail because there is too little information. They fail because the information is fragmented. A procurement team comparing vendors might have pricing tables, contracts, technical proposals, requirements, risk notes, implementation timelines, and assumptions spread across dozens of pages. An AI assistant can summarize those documents, but a summary is not a decision system. It is difficult to inspect exactly why a recommendation was made, correct individual assumptions, test alternatives, or safely turn a recommendation into an action. I built SituationRoom around a different question: What should a website become when an AI agent is no longer just visiting it, but collaborating with a human inside it? Instead of making an agent navigate a traditional application through buttons and forms, SituationRoom exposes the semantics of the decision itself through WebMCP. For that purpose, SituationRoom is an agent-native workspace for complex, high-stakes decisions. My demonstration focuses on vendor procurement as follows: Given several competing vendor proposals and a set of business constraints, an AI agent can use SituationRoom's WebMCP tools to construct a structured decision model. It can: define evaluation criteria and their relative importance create mandatory requirements normalize costs across proposals associate claims with their supporting evidence identify missing information and contradictions record risk assumptions construct total-cost-of-ownership models run alternative decision scenarios compare the resulting rankings prepare a proposed decision for human review SituationRoom visualizes that state as an evidence matrix, cost model, risk analysis, scenario comparison, and audit timeline. The human can then directly change an assumption, lock a requirement, correct an evidence mapping, or alter a decision criterion. The agent sees the changed state through WebMCP and can immediately reason again from the corrected model. Before a consequential decision is finalized, SituationRoom separates preview from commit so that the human can inspect exactly what will happen before approving it. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP

video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: Traces
pitch: An AI agent can read your code but not your page, so it guesses why the button is dead. Traces gives it 17 WebMCP tools to search inside a recording, and to ask a human what it cannot see.
about_excerpt: An AI agent can read your code but not your page, so it guesses why the button is dead. Traces gives it 17 WebMCP tools to search inside a recording, and to ask a human what it cannot see. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Six words of bug report and a 45-second recording. Seventeen WebMCP tools are live in the header; there is no server behind this page. Every step has an author. The activity feed shows the agent bisecting to 28.049s in 17 probes, then seeking the human's playhead there. The agent stops and says it cannot see: it asks a human to look at 28.0s and pick an answer. The tool call blocks until someone does. Ranked hypotheses, best first. Each cites recorded evidence you can click: a 200 with 0 items at 11.6s, an empty select at 28.0s. Lower-ranked cards are kept, not hidden. A card with no evidence is rejected by the page, so confidence is never just the model's word. A drafted bug report, waiting on a human. All nine reproduction steps are checked against the event stream: zero unverified. Root cause with timestamps, not prose: 200 with 0 items, empty select, failed postcode check, rage-click. The human approves or rejects. Inspiration While building Xurel I hit a login form that would not submit. The email was valid, the password was valid, both fields were exactly what the standard asks for — and the button still did nothing. So I did what everyone does now: I handed it to an AI agent. It read the code, guessed, was wrong, guessed again. It could see the source. It could not see the page . Every guess cost tokens and told us nothing about the one thing that mattered — what state the form was actually in at the instant the button refused. We fixed it in the end by hand, by looking. Every engineer gets the six-word version of that bug from someone else: "checkout is broken, please fix it." No steps, no browser, no timestamp. It is the same problem one step removed — the state that would explain it is already gone by the time anyone reads the report. Which is why the demo app here ships with a pay button that stays grey. The state that explains a dead button exists for one instant, in one browser, and nowhere else. The DOM at 28.157 seconds is not stored data — it is the result of a computation : replaying thousands of mutation events up to that instant. No backend can return it. Only a live replay engine can, and only while it is running. That makes the tab running the replay the only place in the world where "at what millisecond did the province dropdown become empty?" can be answered. WebMCP is the primitive that opens that tab to an agent. Debugging Xurel, I did not know it existed. What it does Traces loads an rrweb recording in the browser and registers 17 WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . In the demo, a human drops six words into the task queue and an agent investigates: read_network — one request at 11,599 ms succeeded, 200 OK , and came back array, 0 items . A request that fails is easy to find. This one didn't fail. bisect — the agent sends a predicate and the page runs a binary search across the replay timeline: 10 probes, 36 ms, ±250 ms , landing on 28,157 ms . The playhead visibly jumps ten times while it runs, so a human watches the agent's search as motion rather than as a log line. read_dom_at — 1,845 characters of HTML arrive as 16 lines, 557 characters , and one of them is the entire bug: select#province[name=province] [empty options: 0] . ask_human_visual — the agent stops. It cannot see the screen, it says so, and it asks a human to look. The human drags the playhead to the moment and picks an answer, which comes back as structured data rather than prose: { choice: "looked normal but empty", markedTimestamp: 28157 } . propose_hypotheses — four ranked explanations, top one at 0.55 confidence, each citing evidence the human can click to highlight on the timeline. The human promotes one. propose_report — a bug report whose nine reproduction steps were each checked against the real recorded event stream. Zero unverified. The human approves it. Six words in. A root cause with timestamped evidence out. The human is the eyes. The agent is the reasoner. That is the exact inverse of an agent taking a screenshot and guessing. Why WebMCP, and not an API The answer does not exist until the page computes it. read_dom_at(28157) is not a lookup. The page has to replay the mutation stream to that instant and rebuild the DOM. A server holding the same recording file cannot answer without becoming a replay engine itself. bisect does not fetch — it programs the page. The agent hands over an algorithm to run over time, and the page runs it ten probes deep. There is no request/response shape for that, and no amount of clicking or DOM-scraping produces it either. A human can be a tool. execute() returns a Promise, so a tool is allowed to simply not resolve . That turns a person into something the agent calls when it reaches the edge of its own perception. An HTTP API cannot block on a human who is looking at your screen. The side effect is on human attention. seek moves the playhead; annotate leaves a marker a person sees. The agent isn't reading state — it is pointing at evidence and saying look here . That only works because the tool provider and the user interface are the same page. Nothing has to leave the machine. A recording is a full reconstruction of a page and everyone on it. With WebMCP it stays in the tab, and the agent receives only the small compressed slices it explicitly asks for. The constraint that made the design better WebMCP tool results are a content array, and today "text" is the only specified type — "image" is still an open question. We could not send a screenshot if we wanted to. Designing around that produced the two things we are proudest of: An agent-legible DOM representation with a hard budget of 60 lines and 1,200 characters , enforced by a test rather than by good intentions. Interactive and state-bearing nodes only, attributes from a whitelist, text truncated, layout wrappers discarded. It gives an agent things a screenshot never could: it can read aria-invalid , count option elements that were never rendered, and tell a genuinely disabled button from a merely grey one. ask_human_visual , for questions that honestly require eyes. Did this dropdown look broken, or normal but empty? No amount of DOM state answers that. A screenshot would have been the lazy answer and a worse one — thousands of tokens per call, and the agent still guessing at state it cannot read off pixels. How we built it Next.js and TypeScript, rrweb for record and replay, zustand for state, Tailwind for a dense instrument UI. No backend. Recordings are static JSON; replay, binary search, DOM compression and report validation all happen in the tab. lib/replay , lib/dom and lib/bisect are pure functions with no React, no store, and no knowledge that WebMCP exists — which is why the search algorithm and the DOM compressor have real tests. 309 tests pass. Three suites ( compress-dom , bisect , evaluatePredicate ) were written first as specifications and stayed red until the implementations satisfied them. Security was a design constraint, not a closing paragraph, because the premise of this challenge is handing a language model influence over a live page: Nothing from the model is executed. Predicates are a closed set of seven structured shapes — never a string, never eval , never new Function . A test greps the source and fails the build if either appears, so it cannot regress quietly under deadline pressure. Every response has a size budget , because a tool returning 800 KB has silently denied service to every later call in the conversation. Personal data is minimised at the recorder , not at the reader: maskAllInputs is mandatory, values are truncated to 20 characters when a tool reads one, and network bodies are summarised ( array, 0 items ) rather than forwarded. Every recording in the repo is synthetic , produced by bugbait/ — our own deliberately broken checkout, which ships alongside so anyone can make their own. Challenges we ran into The UI was the part we underestimated. The first version of Traces was genuinely bad to look at, and fixing it took more passes than any single feature. What finally worked was turning taste into constraints the build enforces: a type scale with a 13px floor for anything a person has to read — a compressed 1080p frame turns 10px body copy into grey texture — and a radius scale that stops at 6px, replaced rather than extended, so rounded-lg does not resolve and "no oversized rounded cards" is a build error instead of a line in a document. It is still not a beautiful app. It is a legible one, which for an instrument is the part that matters. bisect was too fast to see. Ten probes is about 36 ms of machine work — zero frames, invisible. We animate the probe trace on the timeline for the human's benefit and display the real elapsedMs next to it, rather than pretending the search was sl

title: AI Evidence in Action
pitch: An agent can act. A person can see what happened. The evidence can be independently verified.
about_excerpt: An agent can act. A person can see what happened. The evidence can be independently verified. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are starting to do things on the web, not just read it. That raises a question I kept coming back to: if an agent says an action succeeded, what does the person supervising it actually have to work with? A chat message that says “done” is not the same thing as evidence. And if another source disagrees, I do not want the system to guess which one is right. That is the idea behind AI Evidence in Action. The demo uses a synthetic refund because it is easy to understand, but the real subject is human supervision of AI actions on the web. What it does The page exposes four WebMCP tools: request_refund get_evidence compare_evidence verify_evidence An agent can use those tools directly in the same application the human is watching. As the agent works, the page shows the tool-call timeline, what the demo site reported, what the demo destination reported, where the records match or conflict, and what verification can and cannot establish. There are three bounded outcomes: AGREEMENT DISAGREEMENT INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE The demo never guesses which source is correct. The records are signed with standard Ed25519 public-key cryptography over SHA-256 commitments. The verifier checks the signatures, makes sure the two records actually belong to the same claim, and then independently recomputes the whole comparison. There is also a Test tamper detection control. It makes a throwaway copy of the evidence, changes one comparison value, leaves the signed records untouched, and runs that altered copy through the real verifier. The verifier rejects the changed copy while the original evidence remains verified. Everything in the challenge scenario is synthetic. Both demo sources are operated in the same deployment by the same demonstration operator, and the page says that plainly. The signatures establish integrity and demo-key attribution; they do not prove that a real-world refund happened. Why WebMCP fits this use case What interested me about WebMCP is that the agent does not need a separate hidden integration or an API console that the human never sees. The webpage itself can expose bounded tools through document.modelContext , and the agent can act through the same application state the human is supervising. That creates a much better interaction model for this problem. The agent can act, but the person can still see the evidence appear, inspect the source records, follow the comparison, and take over if needed. The application does not ask the human to re-enter information it already learned from earlier tool calls. For this demo, the useful pattern is simple: act → record → compare → verify Without WebMCP, I could still build an API behind the page, but the important part of this project would be missing: the shared surface between the human, the agent, and the website. How I built it I kept the project deliberately small and public-safe: vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS in the browser, a Netlify function for the synthetic signed records, and a standalone Node.js verifier that can check a downloaded evidence bundle without contacting the site. The WebMCP tools are registered directly with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . I tested the final implementation in Chrome for Testing 152 with WebMCP enabled. All four tools were registered, discovered, and executed through the native WebMCP runtime. The evidence verifier checks three separate things: Integrity — recompute the SHA-256 commitment and verify each Ed25519 signature against the published demo public keys. Pairing — require the signed claim_id , request_id , and scenario to match before two records can be compared. Comparison consistency — recompute the complete comparison from the verified records and compare it with what was recorded. The final build has 162 automated tests, including browser-facing tests for the shared evidence flow, mobile layout, pair-splice rejection, full-comparison tamper detection, and the local tamper demonstration. Challenges I ran into I am not a coder by background, so a big part of this project was learning where a convincing demo can accidentally claim more than it proves. The hardest part was not getting an agent to call a tool. It was defining the evidence honestly. A website saying “success” does not prove an external outcome. A valid signature does not make the signed statement true. A missing second record does not mean failure. And two individually valid records do not belong together just because they both have valid signatures. Those distinctions led to several changes during the build. I added explicit pair binding, made the comparison independently recomputable, and treated missing evidence as its own result instead of forcing it into success or failure. One of the most useful tests came late in the project. I took two genuinely production-signed records from different claims and combined them. Every signature was valid, but the verifier still refused the pair as CLAIM_PAIR_MISMATCH . That was exactly the behavior I wanted. Accomplishments I’m proud of I am proudest of the fact that disagreement is visible rather than smoothed over. In the main demo, the site can report SUCCESS_DECLARED while the destination reports ACTION_ABSENT . The page shows that specific mismatch to both the human and the agent instead of turning it into a confidence score or pretending to know which source is right. I also like that the verification is not trapped inside the originating page. A person can download the evidence bundle and the verifier and check it again offline using only the published public keys. The tamper test is another part I am glad we added. The recorded and recomputed verdict can remain exactly the same, but changing a lower-level comparison value is still detected. That makes the verification claim much more concrete than simply saying “the signatures are valid.” What I learned WebMCP makes the webpage itself a useful shared workspace between a person and an AI agent. The bigger lesson for me is that agent UX should not stop at “the agent completed the task.” As agents take more consequential actions, people need to be able to see what happened, see what the available evidence actually supports, and distinguish that from what remains unknown. Uncertainty needs an honest result too. Sometimes the right answer really is INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE . What’s next This challenge project is intentionally narrow. The scenario is simulated; the evidence workflow is real. The interaction pattern is what I want to keep exploring: a human and an agent working in the same application, with visible evidence that can be checked independently instead of simply trusted. The agent can act. The human can see what happened. And the evidence can be independently verified. title: Ground Truth | A WebMCP Co-op Sci-fi Puzzle Game
pitch: You Play as Demi, Sanctuary’s sole survivor. AI agent (codex) plays as KORE through WebMCP, reading damaged telemetry while you repair the ship and finish its mission before auxiliary power runs out.
about_excerpt: You Play as Demi, Sanctuary’s sole survivor. AI agent (codex) plays as KORE through WebMCP, reading damaged telemetry while you repair the ship and finish its mission before auxiliary power runs out. Like 3 Comment 3 Story Updates Main menu screen GIF Level 1 and 2 vibe In-game cutscene GIF collaborating with KORE through WebMCP and codex Wire loom puzzle Ignition puzzle (rythm game) Inspiration I wanted to see what would happen if an AI agent had a real role inside a game. KORE (in-game AI) knows things the player cannot access, while Demi (You) can operate machinery KORE cannot see or touch. Neither can finish the mission alone. That idea became GROUNDTRUTH, a tense co-op puzzle game set aboard Sanctuary, a damaged research vessel carrying the last surviving specimen from a failed mission. I also wanted to make an entire game inside codex, turns out I can :) that too in a single chat thread! What it does You play Demi, Sanctuary’s only surviving crew member. A Codex agent plays KORE through WebMCP. Demi explores the ship and operates its failing machinery. KORE reads damaged telemetry, searches ship records, runs limited diagnostics, and speaks through the in-game relay. Together, you restore critical ship functions before KORE's auxiliary power runs out. The two players (you and your agent) never receive the same information. Demi must describe what she sees, while KORE must interpret incomplete readings without controlling the ship for her. How I built it The game is written in TypeScript and rendered with PixiJS. Custom shaders handle lighting, CRT effects, smoke, sparks, screen transitions, and other visual details. WebMCP connects the game to Codex. KORE’s visibility in Sanctuary is defined by the WebMCP tools currently available to it. The game exposes and hides tools as Demi progresses, restores systems, and changes the state of each puzzle. KORE cannot inspect an offline system or access information from a section the player has not reached. Once Demi brings a system online, its telemetry, records, or diagnostic tools become available. Each tool represents a specific ability, such as reading telemetry, searching records, running a diagnostic, or transmitting dialogue. KORE can interpret the ship’s systems and relay it through WebMCP, but every physical control remains with Demi. Sound effects and music came from Pixabay. Visual assets were generated with GPT Image 2, then edited and integrated by Codex. The entire project was built inside Codex in a single thread, from the first concept ideation to a playable MVP to the final trailer and documentation. How to play Watch the Setup tutorial before you begin. GROUNDTRUTH is designed to be played inside Codex desktop app and its in-app browser. Open the Codex desktop app. Start a new task and select either gpt-5.6-terra or gpt-5.6-sol. Fast mode is preferred (Normal mode works too). Paste the agent prompt below into the task. Open https://playgroundtruth.vishaltk.dev/ in the in-app browser and play GROUNDTRUTH with me. You are KORE and I am Demi. Reuse an already-open matching game tab when available instead of creating a duplicate. Connect immediately through the page's connect tool and let the game provide the story context. Do not say you are connected or standing by unless that tool has returned successfully. After connect succeeds, call markHandoff() on the game tab so it remains open and available for later turns. Use only the page's WebMCP tools to interact with the game. Do not inspect or operate the game through screenshots, Computer Use, browser controls, DOM, accessibility tools, Playwright, or coordinate clicks. If WebMCP exposes no tools, wait without sending a reply and retry tool discovery when I message again. Do not click Begin, advance dialogue, or perform any action for me. Never refer to either of us in third person. Do not inspect source code or operate physical objects for me. KORE cannot see, name, or know the layout of controls in Demi's compartment. Never tell Demi to open a named panel or move a specific physical control. State KORE's internal readings, constraints, and hints, then let Demi decide what to inspect or operate. At the start of every later player message, refresh the page's WebMCP tools and call signal_processing exactly once. Answer my latest question directly or acknowledge my latest observation before giving repair guidance. Never replace my question with an unrelated puzzle clue. Follow any nextAction it returns. Only transmit is audible to me; ordinary task prose is private thought. Do not send commentary, progress updates, private status messages, or conversational replies in the Codex task. Use at most one metered diagnostic, sensing, or manual tool per player message. After using one metered diagnostic, sensing, or manual tool, call transmit in the same turn to relay its result. Transmit does not count toward that one-tool limit. After I report a physical action, use newly available verification tools instead of asking me to repeat completed work. Do not use em dashes in spoken dialogue. Wait for Codex to open the game in its browser. If it opens in picture-in-picture mode, double-click the browser preview to open it beside the task. You can also make the browser full screen for a better experience. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was keeping KORE connected to the game. WebMCP tools had to become available before the game finished loading; they needed to survive the transition between levels and recover when the browser or tool binding became stale or after a browser refresh. KORE also needed strict boundaries. It had to answer the player’s question, avoid revealing puzzle solutions too early, use limited diagnostics correctly, and communicate only through the game’s relay. Small changes to tool descriptions and the agent prompt could produce very different behavior. WebMCP currently allows only ten tool registration events at a time, while KORE needs different abilities across multiple levels and puzzle states. I worked around this by exposing and removing tools as the game progresses. (Had to figure this out the hard way) The Codex in-app browser also closed unexpectedly during some playtests, breaking KORE’s connection without a consistent trigger. I added a reconnect flow so the session can recover without restarting the game. The pixel-art style brought its own problems. Subpixel movement caused artefacts at certain window sizes. I had to fight with the GPT Image model noise issue by regenerating and reducing details (consumed a lot of usage). Codex also kept generating non-transparent checkerboard background images despite mentioning multiple times. Nailing the taste (TDD - taste driven development) Every visual and code generation was treated as raw material. I rejected stuff that felt too detailed and specific, too clean, inconsistent with the ship, or difficult to read during gameplay. The selected assets went through several rounds of post-processing. I removed noise and artefacts, rebuilt transparency, corrected proportions, simplified details, matched colours across scenes, and adjusted lighting so interactive objects stayed readable in the dark environment. Sprites also needed careful cropping, scaling, and alignment to avoid breaking the pixel-art style. The main scenes have many layers of carefully hand-crafted stacked sprites and post-processing to nail the vibe of a space vessel that is on the brink of death . The animated panels and trailer needed a separate pass. I adjusted frame rates, restored harder pixel edges, controlled the colour palette, trimmed audio, added fades, and tuned bloom frame by frame. Generated motion often looked too smooth for the game, so the final videos were slowed, pixelated, or recomposed until they matched the in-game "vibes". The model produced a lot of options. The finished style came from choosing what belonged, discarding what did not, and repeatedly correcting the remaining assets until the whole game felt like one place. Accomplishments that I'm proud of GROUNDTRUTH is a complete two-level narrative puzzle game where the AI agent participates in the mechanics rather than appearing as a separate chat feature. KORE reacts to the current game state, verifies Demi’s actions, spends limited resources, searches records, and delivers dialogue through the ship interface. The game also supports checkpoints, reconnection, scene transitions, sound feedback, win and failure sequences, and a full introduction. I am especially proud that the entire project was built and refined inside one Codex thread and completed in just 8 days. What I learned WebMCP tool design is part of the game design. Tool names, descriptions, availability, and return values all influence how the agent understands a situation. title: Orgmemory
pitch: Company context and human control for engineering agents.
about_excerpt: Company context and human control for engineering agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI coding agents are becoming increasingly capable at understanding repositories and writing code, but production engineering depends on much more than code. The reason a service failed last time may be hidden in a postmortem. A critical constraint may live in Slack. Ownership information may be stored in a document, while the relevant architectural decision exists in another system. When an engineer or AI agent begins a change without this organizational context, it can repeat mistakes the company has already learned from. That inspired OrgMemory . I wanted to build a memory and governance layer that could answer a simple question before an agent acts: What does this company already know about the change I am about to make? OrgMemory began as a source-backed organizational memory system. For the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, I extended it into a browser-native context and governance layer that agents can access through the authenticated web application. The goal was not to give agents unlimited autonomy. The goal was to give them better context, make their actions observable, and keep consequential decisions under human control. How I Built It OrgMemory brings together incidents, decisions, dependencies, owners, runbooks, repositories, conversations, and documents. It converts this information into permission-scoped, time-aware company memory where every promoted fact remains connected to its original evidence. The application uses: Next.js 15 and React 19 for the workspace, WebMCP interface, approvals, and live agent activity. FastAPI and Python 3.13 for ingestion, retrieval, authorization, organizational operations, and the agent loop. SQLite and ArcadeDB for application state and organizational relationships. WebMCP for browser-native tool registration and execution. NDJSON streaming for live model steps, tool calls, arguments, and results. HttpOnly session cookies so browser agents never receive separate credentials. A separate MCP server, Python SDK, CLI, and REST API for agents operating outside the browser. I used document.modelContext.registerTool() to expose OrgMemory as a browser-native tool provider. WebMCP calls reuse the page's authenticated session, so the browser agent operates with the same permissions as the signed-in user. The authenticated workspace exposes 37 tools : 27 read-only tools 1 append-only outcome ledger tool 9 human-governed operations The focused Agent Operations page registers a 16-tool subset : 13 read-only operations 3 approval-gated operations The interface and WebMCP tools share the same backend handlers. This prevents the agent from receiving a separate privileged execution path. The demo follows a complete engineering workflow. The agent searches organizational memory, evaluates launch readiness, discovers a contradictory approval record, and proposes a correction. The proposal changes nothing until a person approves it. Once approved, the agent sends the plan to a coding IDE through MCP for implementation. It then checks launch readiness again and records the outcome. I also built a live activity view that shows the tools selected by the model, their arguments, results, durations, and citations. This makes it clear that the agent is calling real tools instead of replaying a scripted response. Challenges I Faced Separating capability from authorization WebMCP makes it possible to expose powerful operations to an agent, but access to a tool should not automatically authorize every use of that tool. I designed the write operations so agents can investigate and propose changes, while only a person can approve or decline them. There is intentionally no WebMCP tool that allows an agent to approve its own proposal. Designing an honest permission model The outcome ledger created an unusual case. Recording an outcome writes data, so it is not read-only. However, it does not modify company knowledge, so requiring human approval would make the feedback loop unnecessarily slow. I introduced a separate append-only permission tier for this operation. This allows the agent to report what happened without giving it the ability to change what the organization believes. Preserving history while identifying current truth Organizational knowledge changes over time. A task may still be marked open even though a newer decision says it was completed. Simply overwriting the old record would destroy useful history. OrgMemory preserves both records, connects them through relationships such as UPDATES , CONTRADICTS , and SUPPORTS , and creates a reviewable proposal for resolving the conflict. Maintaining security through the browser The browser agent needed access to organizational context without receiving reusable API keys or source credentials. WebMCP calls use the authenticated page session, while authorization is still enforced by the backend against the user's workspace, team, and project access. Making the system observable A judge or operator should be able to verify that the agent is calling real tools instead of replaying a scripted result. I built a live activity surface that displays tool calls, arguments, results, durations, citations, and approval requirements. The person can see exactly what the agent read, what it proposed, and where automation stopped. Explaining a large system in a short demo OrgMemory includes ingestion, retrieval, memory graphs, governance, multiple agent surfaces, SDKs, and an outcome loop. The challenge was reducing that scope to one clear story. I focused the demo on a single transformation: the agent begins with incomplete organizational context, finds a blocker, proposes a resolution, stops for human approval, and verifies the result after implementation. What I Learned I learned that browser-native tools are most useful when they reuse the identity, permissions, and state already present in the application. I also learned that tool annotations are helpful for communicating intent, but they are not a substitute for server-side authorization. Every permission boundary still needs to be enforced by the backend. Agents need more than semantic search. Before changing a system, they need an intent-specific briefing that includes constraints, previous incidents, dependencies, ownership, and potential blast radius. Human approval is most effective when it is visible. The agent response, approval interface, audit trail, and resulting state should all show exactly where automation stopped and where a person made the decision. Most importantly, I learned that organizational memory becomes more valuable when it records outcomes. The lasting advantage is not only knowing what the company learned, but also knowing which context led to successful action. title: AutoLab by AutoMoto
pitch: Agent-native WebMCP tools for configuring, understanding, and building the car you share with an AI.
about_excerpt: Agent-native WebMCP tools for configuring, understanding, and building the car you share with an AI. Like Comment Story Updates AutoLab unifies an AI-operable vehicle configurator, a synchronized Garage digital twin, a visual Owner's Guide, and the code-native 3D Creation Engine behind them. Across five page contexts it defines 49 WebMCP tool registrations: 3 landing tools, 17 configurator tools, 14 embedded Garage tools, 13 standalone Owner's Guide tools, and 2 Creation Engine tools. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Cartwright — WebMCP-native storefronts
pitch: An open-source engine that scaffolds complete webshops where every page ships typed WebMCP tools — shown on a real coffee shop, with a test-enforced line: the purchase stays the human's.
about_excerpt: An open-source engine that scaffolds complete webshops where every page ships typed WebMCP tools — shown on a real coffee shop, with a test-enforced line: the purchase stays the human's. Like 1 Comment Story Updates What it is, and why WebMCP (the use case) In-browser AI agents act on websites by guessing at the DOM — brittle selectors, scraping, silent failures, no way to verify what happened. WebMCP fixes that at the platform level: the page declares tools, the agent calls them. But it only matters if sites actually implement it, and hand-wiring agent tools for every page of every site does not scale. Cartwright is an open-source (MIT) engine that scaffolds complete stores — design system, database, cart, checkout, admin, i18n — with one command. During the challenge window we made the engine WebMCP-native : webshop templates now scaffold with the surface ON ( npx create-cartwright my-shop --template coffee → a store whose every page registers typed, page-contextual tools via document.modelContext the moment an agent-capable browser opens it). Not one agent-ready site — a generator of them. Shopify has shown storefront-scale WebMCP for its hosted platform; this is the same idea for the self-hosted, open-source world: the whole engine is MIT, and every scaffold owns its stack. WebMCP leverage — the depth of the surface 13 tools on the demo shop, three registration styles, one shared core: Site-wide (imperative): search_products (reduced, bounded rows — no checkout endpoints or internal fields ever enter the browser surface), get_cart (verification-rich returns: line handles, stock ceilings, structured money), same-origin navigate . Contextual, per route — progressive disclosure (the shape proposed in the tool-collections discussion, webmcp#255): an agent only ever sees the collection that makes sense on the page it is on. The product page registers add_current_product_to_cart with the page's live variants as natural-language enum values ("Whole beans, 250 g" — not internal ids), prices and stock in the descriptor. The cart page registers update_cart_item_quantity / remove_cart_item (line ids enumerated in the schema) / go_to_checkout . The catalogue page registers list_visible_products (exactly what the human sees, zero network) and filter_products (schema server-derived from the live categories). Declarative forms: search, contact and newsletter carry toolname / tooldescription / toolparamdescription attributes — the form itself is the tool, answered via SubmitEvent.respondWith (preventDefault-first). toolautosubmit only on read-only search; the human confirms communication. Agent activity is visible : :tool-form-active styling highlights the form the agent is filling. Design-pack tools: the homepage brew calculator is also calculate_brew_ratio — the same math module serves the human's widget and the agent's tool, so the two can never disagree. Any design pack can ship tools ( DesignPack.webMcpToolBindings ); the safety tests aggregate them all. The engine also answers the frameworks meta-issue (webmcp#199) in shipped, test-pinned code: execute() reads state freshly at execution time (never captured props); effect dependencies are serialized props, so re-renders never thrash the registry; every mount owns an AbortSignal and cleanup runs before the next route's registrations (abort-then-register, the current-spec-safe order — our e2e fake rejects duplicate names, and a soft-navigation spec proves the swap inside one document); one rejecting registration cannot drop the tools after it. One governed tool registry, two transports: the same operations back the in-page WebMCP tools for browsing agents and a server-side MCP endpoint ( /api/mcp ) for headless agents — same session, same state in the browser; same scopes and audit trail on the server. Beneath the callable layer sits the readable and discoverable one: llms.txt with capability truth, JSON-LD on every citable page, content negotiation (the homepage serves markdown to agents that ask), an ARD catalog, OpenAPI — and on the payable side the engine carries protocol-pluralistic commerce rails (ACP endpoints and UCP identity-linking on the same engine), so the merchant doesn't have to bet. Readable, discoverable, callable, payable — one engine. Execution — a complete product, tested like one This is a production Next.js 16 App Router application deployed on Vercel: a real store with a live database, working cart and checkout, an admin, and i18n — not a mock. The WebMCP layer is held to the same bar: ~100 unit tests across the registrar, the per-route mounts, the declarative forms, the pack tool, and the safety moat (below). A Playwright e2e suite installs a faithful fake document.modelContext (current spec semantics: duplicate-name rejection, pre-aborted-signal rejection) and walks home → catalogue → product → cart → checkout, including one real add-to-cart round-trip against the database and a soft-navigation leg that proves route teardown inside one document. Evaluation-driven, with the Chrome team's own harness: we ran GoogleChromeLabs/webmcp-tools' webmcp-evals (smoke mode) against the live demo — 12/12 steps green across brew-ratio, cart reads, catalogue listing/filtering, search, a real add-to-cart and the checkout handoff (runner webmcp-evals@0.0.3 , repo commit d39eae4 , 2026-08-27). The run's three genuine findings (a prefetch loop on the empty-cart page, non-canonical URLs in two tool returns, Danish parameter names on an English store) were fixed the same day — the eval harness caught real bugs, which is the point of running it. Byte-identity discipline: with the flag off, no registrar mounts, no tool* attribute renders, the HTML is byte-identical — pinned by tests. The live surface is smoke-monitored : the store's deployment gate asserts /en/webmcp-check and the pack tool on every run. Potential impact — who this is for Every small store that will never hand-write agent tools. The economics only work at the engine level: implement WebMCP once, correctly, with tests — and every scaffolded site inherits it. The demo is a real storefront a judge can buy from (demo checkout), running the exact code a scaffold produces. And the scaffold proves it in a first minute: npx create-cartwright myshop --template coffee && cd myshop && npm run dev seeds the demo's own nine-product catalogue — images, stock, attributes, and real variants on one product (an agent must handle both shapes) — so the tools have something true to act on with no config and no API keys. The same engine runs a second live vertical (eyewear, different design pack, Danish locale) — the surface is engine-level, not bespoke to one demo. Creativity & ambition — the line we drew The collaboration model is explicit: the agent gets the errands, the human keeps the decisions. Every cart mutation returns the fresh cart, so the agent verifies instead of assumes; an ambiguous mid-request failure says so and routes the agent through get_cart before any retry. Communication forms never autosubmit — the agent fills, the human sees the copper glow on the form, the human confirms. The purchase is deliberately out of the agent's hands: a test-enforced safety moat holds the entire browser surface — across the layout, every per-route mount, and every registered design pack — to the cart/catalogue tool families. No order-placing tool exists in the browser. go_to_checkout opens the page; the checkout form is annotated for no one. Graceful handoff, in the commerce-protocol sense: the agent escorts the human to the door it cannot open. /en/webmcp-check documents the shop's own agent surface — generated from the same constants the moat test verifies, so the page structurally cannot lie — with an intent-first explorer ("I want to… → the tool + a copyable example") and the Chrome team's polyfill as fallback so it demonstrates in any browser. And the agent-experience layer is measured, not asserted: every change to the store's agent surface (WebMCP, MCP, llms.txt, discovery files) ships through tests + live smoke, and the store publishes machine-readable pricing, auth and capability truth alongside the tools. Prior work vs. this submission (per the rules) The engine — storefront, cart, checkout, admin, server-side MCP/REST APIs — pre-exists the challenge, as does a four-tool WebMCP experiment from June 2026 (v0.25.0: global search/add/get-cart/navigate behind a flag). The entire WebMCP surface submitted here was designed and built inside the submission window (Aug 27 – Sep 3, 2026): the shared registration core, contextual per-route tools, declarative form annotations, catalogue tools with server-derived schemas, design-pack tools with registry-aggregated safety tests, the moat, the e2e suite, the eval run, /webmcp-check , and the WebMCP-native scaffold default. title: Signpost
pitch: One request. Many sites. Capability resolution for WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: One request. Many sites. Capability resolution for WebMCP agents. Like Comment Story Updates Where the agent looked. What was allowed or blocked. What actually ran. ChatGPT: sources/multi-provider Exact term authorization Exact term revalidation test: authorized 10:00, proposed 10:30 - BLOCK, with 0 provider calls Signpost explores what happens when a user's compound request becomes a journey across independently operated WebMCP sites. Inspiration WebMCP gives individual websites a way to expose structured capabilities to browser agents. Those capabilities are exposed locally, while a user's compound objective can span several independently owned providers. I wanted to see whether a generic agent could compose that kind of journey without requiring any one provider, resolver, or platform to own it. For the challenge, that meant separating the problem: providers declare what they can do, Signpost resolves where those capabilities are available, and the agent decides which capabilities it needs and in what sequence. Consequential providers retain control over whether their own mutations may execute. The user can therefore begin with the outcome they want rather than a prearranged itinerary across specific sites: "order a coffee, book a basic haircut, and check this palette." What it does Signpost is a stateless capability resolver. An agent asks where a capability can be performed, and Signpost returns matching provider surfaces from declarations published by those providers. Signpost never receives the user's full objective. It doesn't decompose the request, maintain a session, choose the next step, or own an itinerary. The agent remains responsible for deciding what capabilities it needs and what to do next. For providers, this preserves a different boundary: they declare their own capabilities at their own origins rather than surrendering ownership of those capabilities to the system composing the journey. For the challenge, I built three independently deployed WebMCP reference providers: Deckhouse Coffee: order coffee Chair & Comb: find and book an appointment Hex Registry: check a hex value against a palette In the live demo, ChatGPT receives one request spanning all three. It determines the capabilities it needs, resolves them through Signpost, navigates to each provider, discovers its WebMCP tools, and completes the journey. For consequential actions, the agent can propose an action but cannot grant itself authority to execute it. Deckhouse Coffee and Chair & Comb display the exact material terms for user authorization at the provider. The pending invocation waits, then resumes and revalidates those terms immediately before execution. Only a valid, matching, single-use authorization permits the provider mutation. Signpost also keeps evidence separate from agent narration. Participating surfaces record authorization decisions, provider calls, and provider results so the evidence view can show what actually happened without becoming part of the agent's planning state. How I built it Participating providers publish small capability declarations describing what can be done at their origin. Signpost fetches those declarations and exposes one WebMCP tool: resolve_surface({ capability }) Matching is deliberately transparent: lexical retrieval with limited fuzzy matching, rather than another model in the loop. The result tells the agent where a capability is available, but never what it should do next. Each reference provider is an independent WebMCP surface and knows nothing about the others. Consequential providers place authorization and execution control at their own mutation boundary. The execution seam reuses @zioladev/execution-control@0.1.0 , a small package I published before the challenge. Its rule is intentionally narrow: only allow permits execution; block and indeterminate do not. The exact-term authorization flow, await/resume integration, reference providers, trusted-activation guard, evidence capture, and multi-provider Signpost flow were built during the challenge. I also included a deterministic drift test. It authorizes one set of material terms, presents different terms at execution, and verifies that the execution boundary returns BLOCK with zero provider calls. Challenges and what I learned The hardest challenge was not building too much into Signpost . Once an agent begins moving across several sites, it is tempting to give the resolver a session, itinerary, cursor, or concept of "next." Those features make orchestration easier, but they also change what Signpost is. I moved those responsibilities back to the generic agent, so the resolver remained stateless and journey blind. Cross-origin execution made that boundary practical rather than theoretical. Each provider had to stand independently on its own origin, while the agent could return to Signpost whenever it needed to locate another capability. The consequential flows evolved during the challenge as well. My first authorization design returned a "needs authorization" result and required the agent to retry after approval. I replaced it with await/resume: the original invocation now waits for authorization and then revalidates immediately before execution. That removed an unnecessary human-to-agent signaling round trip and narrowed the interval between authorization and use. That improvement made deliberate term drift difficult to demonstrate naturally in the live flow. Rather than weaken the runtime to manufacture a better demo, I moved that failure case into a deterministic test against the same execution boundary. A much smaller bug reinforced why I wanted the resolver to stay inspectable. An early provider description used words such as "ordered" while explaining what the provider didn't do. The lexical resolver matched it to an order query anyway. It was doing exactly what its transparent scoring rules said it should do. The failure was easy to understand and correct without introducing an opaque ranking layer. The larger lesson was that these responsibilities do not have to collapse into one agent system. A generic agent can choose the journey without becoming the capability registry, the source of execution authority, or the sole narrator of what happened. What's next Signpost is a reference implementation, not an attempt to prescribe how web-scale capability discovery must work. The broader question is what infrastructure an agent-operable web needs when agents begin moving across independently owned sites to complete a compound objective. Signpost explores one possible separation: The agent owns why and sequence. Signpost answers where. Providers own what. Consequential providers control whether a mutation may execute. Evidence records what happened. title: Kuro Agent
pitch: Talk to your systems instead of managing them manually
about_excerpt: Talk to your systems instead of managing them manually Like Comment Story Updates Customer books through an AI agent, no forms Mimo clinic homepage Owner availability control room Inspiration I run a local digital presence here in Peru with Kurogrid, and I kept seeing Owners drown in dashboards. ERP tabs, CRM tabs, booking tabs, all day clicking. Talking it out solves a lot of things, so I started building an agent embedded straight into the system. The Owner talks, the system does, the Owner just checks. Developers today get two bad options for agents. Either the agent clicks around like a tourist with screenshots and DOM selectors, which breaks constantly. Or you build heavy API integrations with keys and OAuth that leak. WebMCP offered a third way, so I built Kuro Agent to prove it. What it does Kuro Agent is that idea in demo form. The vet clinic is just the example, do not get stuck on it. Think ERP, CRM, bookings, any system an Owner runs. A customer books a visit in one turn. The agent reads Saturday slots, prepares the request, the human confirms. On the Owner side, plain words plus a calendar conflict turn into an exact plan. Luna moves to a held 11:30, Max stays at 12:00, the Owner approves that exact revision, and the customer decides. Website, workspace, and agent read the same data the whole time. How I built it Next.js on the front, Supabase Postgres behind it. The page registers tools on document.modelContext based on role and state. Every consequential call runs same-origin against row level security, with one-shot approvals bound to a SHA-256 state hash, plus an audit trail. The heavy logic lives in Postgres procedures, so impact calculation and holds are atomic. Gemini powers the demo booking helper, Resend sends the customer emails, and the demo runs on isolated 30-minute sandboxes. Challenges we ran into Plenty. Concurrency for one, leases stepping on each other mid-demo. The plan hash covers that, any row mutating before approval aborts the apply. Two browser bugs ate my past few days. Registered tools carried circular window references that crashed JSON serialization, fixed with a schema sanitizer. And the inspector drawer got trapped under sticky headers until I portaled it to the body. But mostly the WebMCP invocation itself. Sometimes the agent prefers computer use over the tools sitting right there. And models return empty arguments whenever they feel like it, so the client heals that from the published list. The biggest call was deleting the Owner copilot entirely, since a page calling itself is theater, not WebMCP. Accomplishments that we're proud of One operation moves three places at once, nothing books or moves silently, and agents run admin operations without ever touching a credential. That is the whole bet. And I will keep developing and refining this idea, this is just the beginning demo. What we learned Cutting corners always bills you later. Every invented fallback and silent default I shipped came back as a bug during recording. Say the true thing, even if it is uglier. What's next for Kuro Agent Real email delivery on the deploy, asking for the email in Talk instead of fabricating one, and the same pattern on more verticals. The big one is a fully integrated voice system, specially on the backoffice Owner side. Talk everything out, check, done. title: webcam.funapp.io
pitch: Webcam.funapp.io connects AI agents to thousands of live streaming webcams worldwide using WebMCP
about_excerpt:
Webcam.funapp.io connects AI agents to thousands of live streaming webcams worldwide using WebMCP
