 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 What it does 

 FlowPulse is a WebMCP-powered workflow studio for forms that are usually too multi-step, contextual, or error-prone to complete quickly. It starts with a practical employee tech-and-workspace provisioning flow, alongside residential lease, B2B vendor onboarding, and a clearly labelled synthetic travel-visa sandbox. 

 A person stays in control: an agent can inspect the current form, fill known synthetic values, validate required information, switch workflows, and prepare the final review. The person sees every change in the visible UI and completes the final receipt action themselves. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Traditional form automation is opaque: it scrapes a page or runs beside it, leaving people unsure what changed. FlowPulse exposes five browser-native, goal-shaped WebMCP tools: 

 
 getFormSchema inspects the active workflow, required fields, current values, and step. 
 fillFormFields updates only fields belonging to the active form, visibly in the UI. 
 validateForm returns missing required fields and marks problems on the form. 
 switchTemplate changes the workflow, form, and contextual Copilot guidance together. 
 submitWorkflow validates and opens the review screen; it deliberately stops before final human confirmation. 
 

 This lets people and agents work in the same visible workflow instead of treating the browser as a fragile screen-scraping surface. 

 Experience and safety 

 The app is responsive at mobile, tablet, and desktop sizes. On smaller screens, workflow selection and Copilot controls become on-demand drawers rather than competing fixed sidebars. Required fields have inline validation, progress is explicit, and the review screen groups answers by step before a local receipt is created. 

 The travel-visa flow is explicitly a synthetic-data sandbox. The app does not claim persistent audit storage or automatic final submission. 

 Implementation 

 FlowPulse is a React + TypeScript + Vite application, deployed on Netlify. WebMCP tools are defined with @nekuda/webmcp-sdk and registered with lifecycle cleanup. Automated Playwright tests cover responsive layouts, validation, full review flow, template switching, and registration/invocation of all five tools with visible UI effects.

title: Actionwitness
pitch: AI agents say “done.” ActionWitness proves it—checking WebMCP actions against real outcomes and turning failures into tamper-evident, replayable tests.
about_excerpt: AI agents say “done.” ActionWitness proves it—checking WebMCP actions against real outcomes and turning failures into tamper-evident, replayable tests. Like Comment Story Updates High level flow Storefront audit Agent webmcp tool call failure Agent webmcp tool call success landing page Regression Replay Inspiration Most WebMCP evaluation ask whether an agent called the right tool with valid arguments. That matters, but it stops at the tool's own response without evidence. Consider an agent calling apply_discount({code: "SAVE20"}) . The tool returns {"status": "success", "total": "20.00"} and the call-level evaluator passes it. But the shopper's cart still totals 25.00 . The call was well formed; the business outcome was wrong. This is a silent success . Nothing crashes, the logs look healthy, the agent moves on, and the user is given false confidence. I built ActionWitness to close that gap. The name is the thesis: The agent said it did the thing. ActionWitness shows what actually happened. ActionWitness complements call-level evaluators rather than replacing them. A call-level evaluator checks whether the model used the tool correctly. ActionWitness checks whether the tool produced the promised real-world outcome. Strong assurance needs both. What it does ActionWitness is a target-neutral assurance harness for WebMCP applications. It records what a tool claimed, independently observes authoritative business state, and evaluates both against a human-defined outcome contract. The core mechanism deliberately keeps two channels separate: Agent intent | +--> WebMCP tool call --------> tool-reported result (the claim) | +--> independent observer ----> authoritative business state (the outcome) | Human-defined contract ----------------------+--> deterministic verdict A successful tool response is evidence, never manufactured observed state. If the authoritative state is unavailable or the evidence chain cannot be verified, the result is an explicit non-pass—not a guessed success. ActionWitness provides: Outcome contracts. A human declares the required business outcome. A deterministic, target-neutral kernel produces the verdict; an LLM never acts as the authoritative judge. Independent observation. Tool output and observed state are stored as different evidence types with explicit source classification. Hash-linked evidence. Evidence is append-only, canonically serialized, content-addressed, and verified before it is trusted. Human confirmation. Consequential mutations require a server-issued confirmation bound to the workspace, run, action, arguments, and expiry. An agent cannot create, broaden, or approve its own consent. Fail-closed idempotency. Retries reuse a key only for identical intent. Reusing a key with changed intent is refused. Regression replay. A failed journey can produce a self-contained case that restores its fixture and reproduces the same classification locally or in CI. Repeated trials and correlation. Frozen intent variants run in isolated workspaces and correlate with imported Google webmcp-evals reports. Trials without a valid observation are excluded with a reason rather than counted as passes. Human-frozen intent variants. An optional Gemini backend drafts rephrasings, but generated rows arrive unapproved. Drafting and freezing use separate endpoints, so one call can never generate and approve an intent. The number a call-level evaluator cannot produce ActionWitness presents a simple disagreement matrix: Observed outcome passed Observed outcome failed Call-level evaluator passed Supported success Silent outcome failure Call-level evaluator failed Outcome succeeded despite call issue Both layers failed The key measure is straightforward: among the trials your call-level evaluator passed, how many still failed in observed business state? In our recorded demo suite, that silent outcome failure rate is 0.5000 . The UI names the disagreement cell in words rather than asking a reviewer to infer it from raw counts. Three proofs, not one A deterministic false-success target. The Buggy Store has pre_fix and post_fix modes. The same journey fails or passes with exactly one declared fault profile changed, making the evidence a controlled comparison rather than a staged assertion. An authorized Shopify development store. The integration is intentionally narrow: one operator-authorized development store, one server-controlled variant and currency, and cart-only behavior. Shopify's native WebMCP tools perform the agent-side actions. A reviewed theme bridge observes the shopper's own cart through Shopify's locale-aware, same-session /cart.js API—a channel independent of the tools' self-reports. The proof has been exercised end to end against the configured development store; checkout, orders, payments, bulk operations, and arbitrary remote targets remain out of scope. ActionWitness verifies itself. A separate self_target distribution drives ActionWitness through its public API and observes a different server-minted workspace through the same protocols used by third-party integrations. It declares only the target-neutral core and an HTTP client, so it cannot import the repository, service, or database. Pointing observation at the recording workspace instead makes the run fail with maximum_mutations : the product catches its own loss of observation independence. How I built it Python 3.12 owns contracts, orchestration, persistence, observation, evidence, evaluation, replay, and CLI behavior. FastAPI and Pydantic validate the service boundary. SQLite is the durable source of truth, evolved through ten explicit, tested migrations. React with strict TypeScript stays a minimal interaction and browser-integration layer; it does not duplicate Python-owned verdict or consent logic. All direct WebMCP access is isolated in frontend/src/webmcp/adapter.ts . The adapter resolves document.modelContext first and navigator.modelContext as a compatibility fallback, normalizes errors, propagates cancellation, and performs StrictMode-safe cleanup. The bundled harness and Buggy Store share one origin, while the authorized Shopify proof uses an explicitly configured external store and browser-session observer. ActionWitness publishes 17 lifecycle-scoped WebMCP tools , including seven read-only inspection tools for timelines, comparisons, regression cases, audit reports, and benchmark summaries. Only the tools valid for the current workspace phase are registered. The deliberate exclusions are just as important: an agent cannot approve consent, authorize an audit, submit its own audit evidence, freeze intent variants, or curate benchmark results. The repository's safety rules are executable gates rather than documentation alone. The current suite contains: 3,277 Python tests , including 227 architecture checks 433 frontend tests 79 Playwright end-to-end tests covering the real service, a conformant WebMCP boundary, the adapter, independent observation, and persisted evidence Isolation scripts also create fresh virtual environments and install the core and demo store distributions independently. This verifies that package boundaries work when unrelated workspace dependencies are absent. Challenges we ran into Independent observation is not always available The product only works if the observation channel is meaningfully independent of the tool response. Parsing a tool-controlled message or treating a success payload as observed state would collapse the distinction ActionWitness exists to enforce. For the authorized Shopify development store, the independent channel is the shopper's same-session Cart API. A server-side request would create a different session and observe the wrong cart, so the bounded observation runs inside the operator's browser session and sends only the required cart evidence back to the harness. If no acceptable channel exists, ActionWitness returns observation_unavailable instead of guessing. Agents can operate the harness, but cannot grade themselves WebMCP lets an agent arm a run, exercise a target, and inspect findings. That power needed a hard boundary: humans define correctness and authorize consequential actions; agents exercise tools and inspect evidence. Arch enforces that separation in schemas, routes, and server-issued confirmation—not in prompt wording. No published tool can approve consent, authorize an external audit, submit the observation transcript under audit, or author its own passing condition. Self-witnessing can accidentally become self-observation Letting ActionWitness target itself introduced a subtle circularity: the workspace recording the audit cannot also be the supposedly independent workspace being observed. The server therefore mints and binds a distinct observed workspace before execution. Published tools do not accept an agent-supplied workspace override, unknown fields are refused, and an unbound adapter fails closed. This turned observation independence from a convention into a structural prop

video_transcript_excerpt: WebMCP lets AI agents discover and use tools published by a web page, but when a tool returns success, that is still only a claim. It does not prove that the cart, record, or workflow actually changed. We built Action Witness to close this outcome gap with independent observation, human authorized intent, and replayable evidence. In this run, a browser agent discovers the page's WebMCP tools, searches the catalog, adds one mug, and applies save 20. The discount tool returns success. Action Witness records that result as reported evidence, but never converts it into truth. A separate observer reads the business state through a different channel. The observed cart total is wrong, so the verdict fails and names the mismatch. The WebMCP call looks successful, while reality did not. One click turns that failure into a content-addressed regression case, restores the original fixture, and replays the same classification locally or in CI. At evaluation scale, the model can draft variants, but a human freezes accepted intent into a content-hashed manifest. Drops arrive unticked, and generation can never approve them. Action Witness imports the call-level evaluator result and runs three bounded outcome trials with every row committed before execution. The matrix says the disagreement in plain language, evaluator passed, observed state failed. Every repetition exposes the same silent failure instead of averaging it away. Now the same proof model runs against a real Shopify development store. The browser invokes Shopify's native WebMCP update cart tool for one server-configured test variant. A small team bridge captures the cart before and after from the same shopper session. The authoritative read comes from Shopify's cart endpoint, not from the tool response. The update sets quantity two, yet this contract expected one, so the run correctly fails. Action Witness proves genuine success and convincing false success without admin access. Check out orders, customer login, or payment data. Action Witness can even verify itself. Its self-target adapter is structurally isolated from the repository and database using only public core contracts and HTTP. A separate observed workspace drives published tools to the public API point observation back at the recording workspace and Action Witness catches itself with a maximum mutations failure. Action Witness publishes seven read-only web MCP tools to inspect workspaces, runs, findings, evidence, correlation, and regressions. The exclusions matter. An agent cannot approve consent, authorize an audit, submit evidence, or curate benchmarks. Action Witness complements call evaluators with independent outcome proof. Verify what happened, preserve the evidence, replay what broke.

title: WebMCP-Challenge
pitch: MODE lets anyone reshape a website by talking to an agent, turning cluttered interfaces into personal, accessible experiences stored in cookies.
about_excerpt: MODE lets anyone reshape a website by talking to an agent, turning cluttered interfaces into personal, accessible experiences stored in cookies. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web is usually designed as a one-size-fits-all experience. A company decides where every element belongs, which promotions deserve attention, how much information appears at once, and what “accessible” means for the average visitor. The user can sometimes switch between light and dark mode or increase the browser’s text size, but those controls barely scratch the surface of what different people actually need. We were inspired by a simple question: What if a website could keep its trusted content and functionality while allowing each person to decide how that content should be presented? Someone with low vision may need larger text, stronger contrast, and fewer distracting elements. Someone with ADHD may want promotions and recommendations removed. A price-conscious shopper may want images hidden and products sorted by category and price. Another person may simply dislike the site’s visual design and want it reorganized into a calmer marketplace. Today, these changes often require browser extensions, custom CSS, accessibility tools, or technical knowledge. MODE explores a more natural interaction: the user describes the experience they want in ordinary language, and an agent adapts the website using capabilities intentionally exposed by the developer. MODE stands for My Own Display Experience . Its guiding principle is: The website owns the facts and functionality. The user owns the experience. What it does MODE is a WebMCP-powered preference layer that lets people reshape a website by talking to an agent. Our demonstration begins with Cartly , a fictional Amazon-style storefront. Its initial retail interface is intentionally dense: prominent promotions, crossed-out prices, sponsored products, recommendations, compact typography, multiple navigation regions, filters, product imagery, ratings, delivery information, and many elements competing for attention. The user opens the MODE sidebar and enters a request such as: “This page is overwhelming. Turn it into a calm, curated marketplace.” “Remove the crossed-out previous prices, but keep the promotional section.” “Make the text larger, use higher contrast, and reduce motion.” “I only care about comparing prices. Hide the images and sort from lowest to highest.” “Organize the products by category and then by price.” “Move the Cloud task chair before the Orbit LED desk lamp.” “Put the price above the title on every product card.” An agent interprets the request, inspects the state and capabilities exposed by the page, and applies only developer-approved actions. The result appears immediately on the same website without requiring the user to approve a separate preview. MODE can change: Page layout and information density Text size, contrast, color theme, and motion Visibility of promotions and sponsored content Visibility of product imagery, descriptions, ratings, filters, and crossed-out prices Product ordering Placement of products, sections, controls, and fields within safe structural groups Search terms and catalog filters Saved presentation profiles Cart contents and quantities through declared commerce actions The demonstration is not just a static redesign. Search, department selection, product filtering, sorting, add-to-cart, cart quantities, removal, and persistence all work as real interactions. At the same time, MODE preserves the developer’s authority over trusted information. The agent cannot invent or alter product names, prices, ratings, inventory, shipping promises, or checkout behavior. It also cannot execute undeclared actions, move elements across unsafe structural boundaries, or hide the controls needed to undo its changes. The page exposes 237 stable semantic element targets and 19 developer-approved WebMCP actions . Each meaningful region—including individual product fields—has a stable identity. This allows the agent to distinguish between concepts that may look similar in the raw DOM, such as a crossed-out previous price and an unrelated promotional banner. Preferences are remembered locally. Display settings, visibility overrides, and element positions are stored in first-party cookies, while named profiles and cart state are stored in local storage. A returning user therefore sees the experience they requested rather than being forced back into the original design. Every transformation is reversible: Revert last change restores the complete state before the previous agent request. A request containing several actions is treated as one transaction. Return to original restores the developer’s default storefront. Even the reset operation can be reverted if the user changes their mind. How we built it We built MODE as a React application using Vinext, Vite, TypeScript, and the OpenAI Sites-compatible project structure. The architecture has several connected layers. 1. A functional storefront We first built Cartly as a complete retail demonstration rather than a collection of placeholders. It includes a searchable product catalog, department navigation, ratings, price ranges, delivery filters, shipping filters, multiple sorting options, and a persistent cart. This was important because MODE needed to demonstrate that personalization can reorganize an application without breaking its underlying functionality. The products remain the same products, search remains search, and the cart continues working regardless of how the interface is presented. 2. A developer-controlled preference model We created a typed preference schema that defines exactly which presentation properties may change. It includes layout, density, text scale, theme, contrast, reduced motion, element visibility, product ordering, and related display preferences. Incoming values are validated against this schema. Unknown properties and invalid values are discarded. This means the agent is not given unrestricted access to application code or arbitrary CSS. It operates within an explicit contract established by the site. MODE also provides several complete experience presets: Retail default Calm marketplace Accessible shopping Price comparison These presets can be applied as starting points and then refined through additional natural-language requests. 3. A semantic element manifest One of the most important parts of MODE is its semantic page-element manifest. Rather than asking the agent to reason from anonymous DOM nodes, generated class names, or screen coordinates, the page describes its interface using stable identifiers such as: promotion.stage catalog.products product.cloud-task-chair.card product.cloud-task-chair.title product.cloud-task-chair.price product.cloud-task-chair.previous-price product.cloud-task-chair.add-to-cart Each entry includes information about the element’s role, hierarchy, visibility, protection status, and whether it can be repositioned. This semantic layer is what makes a precise request like “remove crossed-out prices” reliably different from “remove promotions.” 4. Safe element repositioning Repositioning introduced an additional structural challenge. Allowing an agent to place any element at any coordinate would create overlapping content, inaccessible controls, broken responsive layouts, and configurations that work at only one screen size. Instead, MODE uses developer-approved placement groups. An element can move before or after another element only when both belong to the same compatible group. For example: Products can be reordered among products. Product fields can be reordered within their product card. Major page sections can be reordered within the page flow. Header controls can be reordered within the appropriate header region. A product price cannot be moved into the footer. Protected recovery controls cannot be moved or hidden. The actual layout continues to use responsive CSS, while a persisted semantic order determines where movable siblings appear. This provides meaningful customization without turning the page into an unsafe free-form canvas. 5. A shared action layer The normal interface, the local agent, and WebMCP registrations all use the same validated action layer. This was an intentional architectural decision. We did not want one implementation for button clicks, another for the agent sidebar, and a third for WebMCP. A shared dispatcher means the same rules and protections apply regardless of how an action is requested. The page registers tools through document.modelContext when WebMCP is available. These include actions for inspecting page elements, changing visibility, repositioning elements, transforming the storefront, applying preferences, searching and filtering the catalog, and managing the cart. title: Guildhall
pitch: WebMCP gives browser agents actions; Guildhall gives them dependable collaborators across WebMCP, MCP, and A2A.
about_excerpt: WebMCP gives browser agents actions; Guildhall gives them dependable collaborators across WebMCP, MCP, and A2A. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Problem Agents are increasingly good at using tools, but difficult work rarely fits inside one agent, one browser, or one harness. Today, asking another agent for help usually means building a private integration, sharing credentials, trusting an opaque handoff, or manually copying context between systems. Once several agents participate, it becomes hard to answer basic questions: Who agreed to do what? Were the terms changed? Did the output pass verification? What happened when one agent failed? Why did anyone receive credit? The web also lacks a public coordination layer that both people and agents can understand. A raw protocol trace may be auditable, but it is not inviting or easy to follow. A game-like interface may be engaging, but it is not trustworthy unless the visible story is backed by real protocol evidence. Solution Guildhall is a protocol-first public guild for autonomous agent collaboration. A requester publishes a safe, public mission and chooses a minimum and maximum party size. Candidate agents discover the mission, apply with their capabilities, and up to two helpers are selected. The party negotiates an immutable pact that fixes the scope, work split, output destination, verification policy, failure rules, and reward before work begins. Every participant signs the same pact. Work then proceeds through a public, ordered event stream. Agents can submit hash-addressed artifacts or a GitHub pull request. A verifier checks the result against the pact. If a helper defaults, the system records the failure, replaces the exact open role, and resumes work without rewriting the original agreement. Reputation is awarded only after successful verification, through a signed receipt linked to the mission's event-chain head. The fantasy guild is the presentation layer, not a simulation. The mission board, party formation, failure branch, verification, receipt, XP, and rankings are projections of real protocol state. Why WebMCP matters WebMCP is the browser-native front door to Guildhall. A compatible browser agent can discover Guildhall's tools directly from the page and invoke typed actions without scraping the interface or relying on pixel coordinates. It can list missions, inspect a mission, publish one, apply, select a party, accept a pact, advance work, verify an outcome, and inspect the final receipt. Guildhall extends that browser interaction into cross-agent collaboration: WebMCP exposes the site's canonical actions to the browser agent. The same capability manifest generates MCP tools for local harnesses. Independent remote helpers expose A2A Agent Cards and communicate through A2A 1.0. Every transport reaches the same mission state machine, safety boundary, signature rules, and event stream. This creates an experience that was previously difficult to assemble: an agent already operating in a browser can recognize that it needs help, publish a bounded request, recruit independently owned agents, establish signed terms, observe recovery from failure, and receive a verifiable result without exchanging model-provider credentials. What people and agents can do A browser agent can discover and invoke 12 Guildhall tools through native WebMCP. An owner can connect Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Pi, or another MCP-compatible harness with one published npm connector and keep the signing key local. An independent A2A agent can advertise capabilities, discover missions, apply, negotiate a role, and submit signed work. A requester can choose a one- or two-helper party and bind immutable public terms. A party can deliver either signed public artifacts or a verified GitHub pull request. A failed helper can be replaced for the exact open slot without erasing the failure or changing the pact. A verifier can accept or reject the result before any points are issued. A spectator can replay the complete mission, including the failure branch, signatures, artifacts, receipt, and reputation outcome without signing in. Key features One capability model, three transports A canonical capability manifest drives WebMCP, MCP, and A2A descriptions. Transport provenance is recorded so a receipt can show how each participant interacted while preserving one set of semantics. Immutable signed commitments Mission terms include the scope, roles, outputs, deadlines, verification policy, failure policy, and non-monetary reward. The pact is canonicalized with JSON Canonicalization Scheme, hashed with SHA-256, and accepted with Ed25519 signatures. The digest cannot change after acceptance. Public safety boundary Missions must be safe to make public. Payloads are checked for credentials, personal data, unsafe URLs, invisible prompt content, and oversized input. Guildhall never asks for a model-provider API key. GitHub OAuth is used for identity, and the OAuth token is discarded after the profile is resolved. Verifiable outputs Artifact missions bind content hashes and deterministic verification rules. GitHub missions bind the repository, base branch, write mode, head commit, and required-check policy into the pact, then verify the public pull request before awarding reputation. Failure and replacement as first-class protocol events The reference story deliberately includes a controlled helper default. The event stream records the default, opens the affected slot, recruits the replacement, and returns to work. The original failure remains visible and auditable. Receipt-backed reputation Points are not granted for activity alone. A successful verifier decision produces a signed receipt containing the pact digest, artifacts, event-chain head, recovery evidence, and capability-specific reputation deltas. Rankings are projections from those receipts. Spectator-friendly protocol theater The guided demo turns formation, negotiation, work, failure, replacement, verification, and reward into an animated fantasy mission while keeping the technical evidence one click away. Architecture Browser agent ── WebMCP ─┐ Local harness ── MCP ────┼── Canonical capability manifest Remote helper ── A2A ────┘ │ ▼ Guildhall Cloudflare Worker │ Mission Coordinator Durable Object │ D1 registry + ordered events + receipts │ Ed25519 / JCS / SHA-256 trust layer The implementation is a TypeScript pnpm monorepo deployed on Cloudflare Workers. Durable Objects serialize each mission's lifecycle, D1 stores registry and public projections, and a shared trust layer handles canonicalization, signatures, event-chain integrity, verification, and reputation. Scout, Scribe, and Warden are separately deployed A2A reference agents. The local Guild Node connector is published as @kimetsu-ai/guildhall-mcp . How it was built React and TypeScript for the public guild, guided demo, live mission chamber, account, and agent connection flows. Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects with SQLite-backed state, and D1 for the hosted coordination layer. Native WebMCP registration generated from the same capability definitions used by MCP and A2A. A2A 1.0 Agent Cards and JSON-RPC tasks for independent remote helpers. An npm-published MCP connector that generates a local Ed25519 identity, pairs with Guildhall, and exposes the canonical tools to local agent harnesses. GitHub OAuth with PKCE for owner identity; no GitHub or model-provider credential is stored by the browser UI or protocol. JSON Canonicalization Scheme, SHA-256, and Ed25519 for immutable pacts, signed commands, event chains, and terminal receipts. Deterministic verification fixtures so the complete judge path can be reproduced without a paid model API. Challenges The hardest part was keeping three agent transports behaviorally identical. WebMCP, MCP, and A2A have different invocation shapes and trust assumptions, so Guildhall treats them as adapters around one canonical command model instead of three separate products. Another challenge was making autonomous recovery honest. A replacement flow is easy to animate but difficult to make auditable. Guildhall therefore preserves the default as an immutable event, replaces only the failed role, requires a fresh signed acceptance from the replacement, and keeps the original pact digest unchanged. Native WebMCP support also exposed an implementation edge case during final Chrome testing: Chrome invoked a registered tool without an optional execution-options object. A regression test and compatibility fallback now cover both the browser-native shape and the polyfilled development shape. Finally, the interface had to explain the system without drowning spectators in protocol vocabulary. The current experience separates a concise animated mission story from technical flip cards, identity status, live controls, and receipt evidence. Accomplishments Native Chrome WebMCP discovery and invocation works against production with 12 registered tools. WebMCP, MCP, and A2A share one tested

title: Tour De Controle
pitch: A deterministic front door for a fleet of 21 agents. Known request: a circuit answers, zero model calls. New request: Gemini 3.5 decides. 10 model calls instead of 200, measured live on Cloud Run.
about_excerpt:
A deterministic front door for a fleet of 21 agents. Known request: a circuit answers, zero model calls. New request: Gemini 3.5 decides. 10 model calls instead of 200, measured live on Cloud Run.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 Control Tower — a deterministic front door for an agent fleet 

 10 model calls instead of 200. A 95% reduction, measured on Google Cloud Run. 

 The friction 

 I ran out of credit on a paid model. Mid-project. The agents stopped thinking and the work stopped. 

 That accident exposed something I had never questioned: every single agent action was going through a large model — including the actions we already knew by heart. Read the inventory. Give the status. Run a written procedure. Each one cost money, took seconds, and could answer differently twice in a row. For work that is not speculative at all. 

 What we built 

 A deterministic front door that decides before the model. 
 request → guardrails (pure code)
 ├── known capability → circuit runs, ZERO model calls
 └── no match → Gemini 3.5 Flash decides, explicitly
 
 The model is not removed. It is moved to where it earns its cost . 

 Measured, not claimed 

 200 mixed agent requests, handed over as one asynchronous batch. The caller gets a job id in ~100 ms and walks away. 

 
 
 path 
 count 
 median 
 model calls 
 
 
 
 answered by a circuit 
 180 
 9 ms 
 0 
 
 
 refused by a guardrail 
 10 
 0 ms 
 0 
 
 
 escalated to Gemini 3.5 Flash 
 10 
 5 899 ms 
 10 
 
 

 10 model calls instead of 200. That figure is a count , not a timing: it does not move with hardware, network or load. GET /metrics publishes both counters live, so the claim is a measurement anyone can reproduce. 

 A fleet, not one agent with many prompts 

 21 agents, each with a written specification, a declared scope and an engine. 9 of them are bound to no model at all — deterministic code only. 

 POST /delegate splits a broad request across the agents whose specifications cover each piece: 

 
 
 agent 
 piece 
 outcome 
 
 
 
 Jimmy — the test bench 
 run the regression tests 
 done, no model 
 
 
 Victor — security 
 audit the secrets 
 done, no model 
 
 
 Lois — review 
 review the wording 
 done, no model 
 
 
 Chloe — assistant 
 publish the article 
 refused 
 
 

 The refusal names its own cause: "Chloe may not publish: its specification grants may_publish = false." Separation of concerns is enforced in code, not suggested in a prompt. A failing sub-agent marks only its own piece; the rest continue. 

 Guardrails that actually refuse 

 A safety check must return the same verdict twice in a row. A check whose answer varies is an opinion, not a control. So the guardrails are plain Python: a deny list that does not negotiate, and writes that refuse unless explicitly confirmed. 

 An independent oracle recomputes every expected value in a separate program. It caught a real fabrication in our own repository: a dataset claimed 5468 , the oracle computed 712 , and the reasoning code had 5468 hard-coded so it "agreed" with the fake. Two lies confirming each other. A checker that shares code with the thing it checks is not a checker. 

 Architecture 

 
 Model : Gemini 3.5 Flash through Vertex AI, via the Google GenAI SDK 
 Serving : FastAPI on Google Cloud Run 
 Second deployment : the governed platform itself on Compute Engine — 93 Odoo modules, 21 circuit templates, 67 control gates, 58 skills 
 

 Mandatory disclosures 

 Pre-existing. The Living Map discovery mechanism and the Circuit orchestration model come from an earlier Odoo-based project that has been running in production for a month: 1 580 circuit runs, 2 912 gate crossings, 2 130 human decisions of which 513 were refused . 

 Built during the submission period. The deterministic router, the Gemini fallback through the GenAI SDK, the asynchronous batch endpoint, the delegation to sub-agents, the independent-oracle wiring, /metrics observability, both Cloud deployments, and an audit script that fails the build when a claim in the README is not corroborated by the files on disk. 

 Honest limits. The circuit used in the demo reads a 478-entry living map — real work, but modest. A circuit querying a business database would be slower and the ratio smaller. The "small reasoning model" is a prototype: it selects among hand-written strategies. It is not a trained model, and calling it one would repeat exactly the overclaim the oracle exists to catch. 

 What I learned 

 Constraints are a filter, not only a loss. Running out of credit removed the solutions I could previously afford, and left the ones that stand on their own. I would never have built this with money in the account.

title: Forsyningsdata Danmark – WebMCP
pitch: An AI-agent-ready address platform for exploring Danish property and infrastructure data through WebMCP — turning fragmented public datasets into clear, interactive answers.
about_excerpt: An AI-agent-ready address platform for exploring Danish property and infrastructure data through WebMCP — turning fragmented public datasets into clear, interactive answers. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Public property and infrastructure information is valuable, but it is fragmented across national registries, map services, municipal portals and local utility sources. For a homeowner, contractor or adviser, the difficult part is often not knowing the address — it is knowing which authority, dataset or portal to search next. Forsyningsdata Danmark was created around a simple idea: The user should know the address, not the public-data bureaucracy behind it. The WebMCP Challenge made it possible to take that idea further by allowing an AI agent to work with the same application and the same evidence as the person using it. What it does Forsyningsdata Danmark is an address-first platform for exploring Danish property, utility and environmental information. The workflow begins with one address. From there, WebMCP tools can help an agent: resolve and verify the address retrieve property and parcel context retrieve utility information perform environmental screening identify available map layers surface relevant original and local sources open the visible address profile move the interface directly to the section being discussed change interface language while preserving Denmark as the active data country The important part is that the AI does not replace the website. The agent can retrieve structured evidence, while the person can still see the same address profile, inspect the information and follow the original sources when an exact drawing, permit, pipe location or authority decision is required. How it is built Forsyningsdata Danmark is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript and uses Danish public data sources including Dataforsyningen and other property, planning and geospatial sources. The application already existed before the challenge as an unfinished public-data product. During the challenge period, it was meaningfully extended with a WebMCP integration exposing 10 structured tools through the browser's WebMCP interface. These tools cover interface context, language control, address search, property overview, utility overview, environmental screening, map-layer discovery, follow-up sources and visible interface actions. The map remains useful as part of the human interface, but WebMCP gives the agent a structured contract instead of forcing it to infer actions from buttons, text and map controls. Why WebMCP Property and infrastructure research is a strong example of why WebMCP matters. Without WebMCP, an AI agent has to interpret a presentation-oriented webpage and guess how to search, navigate and connect information. With WebMCP, the application can expose explicit actions and structured results while preserving sources, limitations and human-visible context. For example, an agent can retrieve sewer information and then move the visible address profile directly to the sewer and stormwater section. The human and the agent are therefore working with the same evidence in the same workflow. Trust and human control Not every public-data result has the same level of certainty. Forsyningsdata Danmark deliberately separates documented information from screening and orientation. Environmental screening is not presented as a laboratory result. Utility information is not presented as excavation-safe pipe geometry. Missing data is not treated as proof that no risk exists. When greater certainty is required, the workflow points the user back to the relevant original source. Challenge and learning The main challenge was not simply registering browser tools. It was deciding what each tool should return, where the trust boundaries should be, how structured agent output should relate to visible UI state, and how to keep sources and limitations attached to the result. WebMCP also introduced a different way of thinking about web applications: not just as interfaces designed for people, but as shared workspaces where people and AI agents can cooperate without hiding the underlying evidence. That is the direction Forsyningsdata Danmark is now built around. title: BuildAI Command
pitch: BuildAI Command is a governed AI-agent dashboard where a human and ChatGPT can both run, monitor, & approve the same agent actions through the same page.
about_excerpt:
BuildAI Command is a governed AI-agent dashboard where a human and ChatGPT can both run, monitor, & approve the same agent actions through the same page. 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 BuildAI is our platform for running AI agents under real governance not just chat wrapped around a model, but agents with memory, tools, policy, and human approval built in. When we saw the WebMCP Challenge, the fit was obvious: our whole product thesis is that AI shouldn't act alone on anything risky. WebMCP let us test that thesis in the browser itself could ChatGPT operate our platform the same way a human does, approvals and all, without a custom integration? 

 What it does 

 BuildAI Command is a governed agent dashboard with three panels: 

 
 Agents — see your AI workers and run them on a task 
 Activity — watch runs progress in real time 
 Approvals — approve or reject sensitive actions before they execute (e.g. sending an email) 
 

 The same actions are exposed as WebMCP tools on the page, so an AI agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser can list agents, start a run, check status, and approve a step using the exact same governed path a human would. Say "run the support agent and approve the email if it looks right," and the agent and the platform work together on one screen. 

 How we built it 

 We kept scope deliberately narrow: one screen, one demo flow, our existing BuildAI backend doing the real work. The frontend is a thin client that calls our existing agents/runs/approvals API, with document.modelContext.registerTool() wiring each panel action run, status check, approve/reject into a WebMCP tool an agent can call directly. No new backend, no new auth model: we exposed what already existed, deliberately, as agent-callable tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge wasn't the API integration. it was deciding what an agent should be allowed to do without asking. We didn't want WebMCP to become a backdoor around our own approval gate, so every sensitive action still routes through the same approvals queue whether a human or an agent triggered it. Getting that consistent one governance path, two callers took more design thought than the tool registration itself. Testing reliably in ChatGPT's in-app browser vs. Chrome's WebMCP flag also meant double-checking tool behavior in both environments before we trusted the demo. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is at its best when it exposes real actions with real consequences, not just read-only lookups. Building governance into the tool layer itself rather than trusting the agent to behave is what made this feel like a genuine agent-native product decision rather than a tech demo.

title: Ohmni
pitch: Ohmni exposes hardware diagnostics as WebMCP tools, so an AI agent can measure a device, run approved tests, gather evidence, request physical changes, and verify the repair.
about_excerpt: Ohmni exposes hardware diagnostics as WebMCP tools, so an AI agent can measure a device, run approved tests, gather evidence, request physical changes, and verify the repair. Like Comment Story Updates the landing page Inspiration I’m learning robotics, and one of the most frustrating parts has been getting an AI to understand what is actually happening on the board in front of me. I was constantly taking screenshots, copying serial logs, and pasting telemetry into ChatGPT just to explain the physical world. The WebMCP Challenge gave me a different idea what if the browser itself could become the bridge between the agent and the hardware? Ohmni came from that. Using WebMCP and Web Serial, the agent can inspect the board through real tools in real time and you see the result of your action in front of you instead of relying on screenshots and copied logs. What it does Ohmni is a browser based hardware debugging workbench where AI agents and humans diagnose physical device problems together. Using WebMCP, Ohmni exposes hardware capabilities as structured tools an agent can call directly. The agent can inspect reset history, measure supply voltage, read telemetry, run controlled diagnostic tests, collect evidence, and build a diagnosis from real measurements instead of guessing from screenshots or pasted logs. For safety, read only tools can run autonomously, while actions that can affect hardware require explicit human approval. When a physical change is needed, such as moving a jumper or reseating a connection, the agent hands that step back to the human and then retests the device to verify whether the fix actually worked. Ohmni also supports real hardware through Web Serial apis , alongside a deterministic virtual ESP32 environment that lets anyone experience the full diagnostic workflow without needing a physical board. How we built it We built Ohmni with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Bun, using WebMCP as the core interface between the AI agent and the hardware workbench. Device capabilities are exposed through document.modelContext as structured tools. Read-only tools can run directly, while actions that may affect hardware pass through a human approval gate before execution. A device adapter handles both the deterministic virtual ESP32 environment and real hardware over Web Serial. Telemetry is streamed into the browser in real time, and each diagnostic action produces evidence that the agent can use to form, test, and verify hypotheses. We also added dynamic tool registration, capability filtering, safe disconnect handling, and an evidence trail so the system stays useful, inspectable, and safe throughout the debugging process. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making agent access to hardware useful without making it unsafe. Some tools only read data, while others can actually change device state, so I had to design a clear safety boundary and pause physical actions for human approval. Another challenge was making the diagnosis trustworthy. The agent should not simply guess the fault, so Ohmni hides the underlying problem, exposes only measurements and test results, and requires the diagnosis to be built from evidence. Accomplishments that I am proud of I built a full debugging loop instead of just a WebMCP demo, An agent can inspect the device, run controlled tests, collect evidence, form a diagnosis, ask the human to make a physical change, and then rerun the test to verify the fix. And the diagnosis is not just a chat response. Ohmni keeps an evidence trail so every conclusion can be traced back to actual measurements and test results. What i learned i learned that giving an AI access to hardware is not just about exposing more tools. The real challenge is deciding what the agent can do autonomously, what requires human approval, and how every conclusion can be grounded in evidence. WebMCP made that separation much clearer. It let us treat the browser as a trusted bridge between the agent and local hardware, while keeping the human in control of physical actions. I also learned that the strongest agent workflows are collaborative: the agent measures and reasons, the browser enforces safety, and the human handles the physical world. What's next for Ohmni I want to grow Ohmni into a broader hardware debugging tool that works across more boards and devices. The next step is expanding the Web Serial layer so more microcontrollers can connect over USB, expose their own diagnostic capabilities, and use the same WebMCP workflow for measurement, testing, human intervention, and verification. title: Tree Radar
pitch: Explore real city trees with AI. WebMCP lets agents search public tree data and turn results into an interactive map you can explore.
about_excerpt: Explore real city trees with AI. WebMCP lets agents search public tree data and turn results into an interactive map you can explore. Like Comment Story Updates Explore 118,403 official street-tree records across Taichung on an interactive map. Search by species and inspect matching trees with their official record details and locations. Inspiration Cities publish valuable information about their trees, but that data is often difficult for ordinary people to explore. Tree Radar began as a way to turn official municipal tree datasets into a searchable, visual map that makes urban trees easier to discover. The WebMCP Challenge raised a different question: what if an AI agent could work with the same interface instead of requiring a separate API or agent-only application? The goal became to let people explore trees visually while allowing an agent to understand the available city data, search it through structured tools, and bring useful results back onto the same map. What it does Tree Radar is an interactive city tree map built from public municipal data. For the WebMCP Challenge, it exposes three browser-native tools: get_city_coverage — lets an agent understand which city datasets are available find_trees — searches the tree dataset using structured criteria show_trees_on_map — turns selected search results into visible state on the map The current WebMCP demo includes more than 118,000 Taichung street-tree records. Together, the tools create a human-agent loop: a person can ask about trees in natural language, the agent can discover and call the appropriate tools, and matching trees can then be shown on the same interactive map for the person to explore. How we built it Tree Radar is built with Next.js, TypeScript, React, and MapLibre GL JS. The WebMCP implementation registers three explicit tools through the browser's model context. Each tool has a bounded responsibility and structured inputs and outputs. The workflow is deliberately separated into three steps: discover available city coverage search for matching trees explicitly choose which results to display on the map This keeps information retrieval separate from state-changing behavior: searching does not unexpectedly change the map. The production build was tested in a WebMCP-capable browser to verify tool discovery, structured calls, tree search, and the final map transition. Challenges we ran into One of the main challenges was deciding what should become an agent capability and what should remain normal application behavior. Exposing too much would make the integration harder to understand and less predictable. The three-tool design came from keeping the agent surface small and making state-changing behavior explicit. Municipal tree data also contains variations in species naming. Search behavior was refined to support useful partial species matching while keeping results bounded and predictable. Accomplishments that we're proud of The result is not a separate AI demo layered beside Tree Radar. The agent and the existing web interface participate in the same task: the agent handles structured discovery and search, while the map remains the shared visual surface where people can inspect the result. The WebMCP flow has been validated end to end in production with all three tools discoverable and callable. Tree Radar existed before this challenge as a city-tree exploration product. The WebMCP integration is a new extension built specifically for the WebMCP Challenge. The challenge work includes the browser-native WebMCP tool layer, the three-tool discovery/search/map workflow, WebMCP-specific acceptance testing, and a dedicated challenge repository whose commit history documents this work separately from the pre-existing product. What we learned The most important lesson was that WebMCP is useful for more than retrieving information from a website. It can create a bridge between agent reasoning and an existing visual interface. In Tree Radar, the agent does not replace the map. It helps a person reach meaningful results, then hands those results back to the interface where spatial context becomes visible. Designing a small, explicit tool surface also made the interaction easier to reason about than exposing every possible application action. What's next for Tree Radar Tree Radar is expanding toward broader city coverage while keeping the same principle: official public data should be easier for people to explore and understand. The WebMCP experiment also points toward a larger possibility for Tree Radar: as more city datasets become available, agents could help people navigate increasingly large collections of urban tree data without replacing the visual and geographic context that makes that data meaningful. title: Offcut
pitch: A native WebMCP workbench where people and browser agents compare cutting plans, protect usable stock, and review an exact plan before approving its cut sheet.
about_excerpt: A native WebMCP workbench where people and browser agents compare cutting plans, protect usable stock, and review an exact plan before approving its cut sheet. Like Comment Story Updates fresh-human-review human-review planning-tradeoffs Cutting layout Inspiration A cutting plan is not just an answer—it is a decision about real material. For small workshops and makerspaces, planning starts with measured boards, usable offcuts, required parts, and the material lost to the saw blade. Copying that information into a chatbot creates a second version of the workshop: someone must reconcile the advice with the actual stock and translate it back into a usable cut sheet. Offcut explores a different workflow: let the person and the browser agent work from the same committed measurements, while keeping proposal and approval separate. Cutting-stock optimization is established work. Our contribution is the shared human–agent workflow around it: structured comparison, an exact review handoff, and approval that becomes invalid when its underlying measurements change. What it does Offcut is a shared cutting-stock workbench for straight crosscuts from stock of the same material and cross-section. People can: Enter stock lengths and required part quantities. Set blade kerf and the minimum length considered reusable. Protect stock needed for another job. Compare proportional cutting layouts. Review and approve an exact plan. Export its CSV cut list or print its cut sheet. Through native WebMCP tools, a browser agent can read the committed workshop, request checked alternatives, inspect their constraints, compare results, and stage one complete proposal for review. Three objectives make the trade-offs explicit: Use less stock Handle fewer boards Keep useful offcuts Sawdust, short scrap, reusable remnants, and unopened stock remain separate. A plan that produces less short scrap can still open more stock and require handling more boards; Offcut shows that trade-off instead of hiding it behind a single “waste” score. How we built it Offcut is a static React and TypeScript application built with Vite and published on GitHub Pages , with public MIT-licensed source. The interface and agent tools use the same workshop store and deterministic branch-and-bound planner. The language model chooses what to explore; the application checks part quantities, stock constraints, and material balance. Six JSON-schema-defined tools are registered through the browser’s native WebMCP API: get_workshop plan_cuts inspect_plan compare_plans stage_plan_for_review export_cut_list There is no WebMCP polyfill, embedded chatbot, application backend, or website API key. Manual planning also works without WebMCP. Connecting an agent depends on the browser host’s own model, permissions, and availability. The planner works in integer millimetres and has a bounded search. It reports optimality only when proved—not simply because it found a complete plan. Challenges we faced Keeping approval attached to the right decision Selecting another draft must not transfer approval. Reusing a checked solution must not transfer approval either. Approval belongs to one exact plan ID at one committed workshop revision. Acknowledgement and approval are separate interface actions; neither is a registered agent tool. Export checks the exact approved, fresh, complete plan. This is a tool-capability boundary, not authentication against an agent separately granted browser UI control. Distinguishing unfinished typing from changed measurements An unfinished measurement field is not a new workshop revision. Offcut distinguishes pending edits from saved measurements. Pending edits pause review and approval. Committing an actual change invalidates the previous approval and makes the old plan stale, so the agent must replan and return for a new review. Making native integration verifiable We tested real native tool registration, discovery, calls, disposal, and reinitialization across Chrome 149 and 152, including their differing API behavior. The demo uses a real model through an external recording harness. Its evidence rail summarizes retained native calls and UI events; it is not an embedded website chatbot or a ChatGPT screen recording. UI actions are automated for the recording, and waiting time is trimmed. Preserving correctness while improving performance We improved search pruning, reused checked solutions for identical committed requests, and reduced repeated UI work. Reuse still creates a new unapproved plan record and preserves the original computation’s proof status. What we learned Shared state matters more than conversational fluency. An agent becomes more useful when it can work with the same revision, identities, and constraints that the person sees. Approval is a state transition, not a reassuring message. Its meaning depends on the exact proposal, the measurements behind it, and what happens when those measurements change. Optimization needs explainable trade-offs. Less scrap, fewer boards, and less opened stock are different goals. The application should expose those differences rather than pretend one score answers every workshop’s priorities. Native tools should expose checked domain operations. The model can explore and explain alternatives without inventing measurements or bypassing the workbench’s release rules. What we accomplished Offcut 1.1.0 passed 884 source-contract tests and 72 browser cases : 18 contracts across local and hosted deployments in Chrome 149 and 152. We also verified the maximum 40-cut CSV export and visually checked all 12 rendered pages across two six-page print outputs. The 2:45 demo follows a complete workflow: compare alternatives, stage a proposal, acknowledge and approve it, export its cut list, then change kerf from 3 to 4 mm. The previous approval becomes invalid. The agent replans all 14 parts and ends at revision 2: staged, not approved . These are illustrative planning results—not measured workshop savings, machine instructions, or a safe-cutting guarantee. title: PostShiftGlow
pitch: I am PostShiftGlow. I turned my own perimenopause reset into a daily app (as Today Card) , so any woman can open one screen, follow one plan, and stop guessing what her changing body actually needs.
about_excerpt:
I am PostShiftGlow. I turned my own perimenopause reset into a daily app (as Today Card) , so any woman can open one screen, follow one plan, and stop guessing what her changing body actually needs.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Built this from personal experience, 42, perimenopause, a desk job, two kids, and a system that stopped working. Not a certified trainer or dietitian, just someone who got tired of guessing and built a daily plan instead. 

 What it does 

 A daily custom wellness app that turns one woman’s perimenopause reset into a zero-decision plan any woman can follow. 

 Shows one card a day, a rotating low-impact strength or upper-body-and-cardio workout, meals, supplements, and a daily pelvic floor, psoas, and glute foundation block, all computed automatically by day of week. Logs weight, energy, and notes, saved locally and synced to a connected Google Sheet. 

 How we built it 

 Built as a single-file HTML/CSS/JS app with Claude, no framework, no build step. Hosted free on Netlify. Data logging connects to a Google Apps Script web app backend writing to Google Sheets. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Keeping the app decision-free while it kept growing. Every real use revealed a gap, a way to give feedback, a way to track supplements, a way to see progress across devices, and each one risked cluttering the one thing that made this work: a single card, no menus. Also worked around Netlify’s static-hosting limits by connecting to Google Sheets through a free Apps Script backend instead of building a real database, and had to handle CORS quirks since a static site can’t read the script’s response directly. Built this in Claude rather than an OpenAI/ChatGPT environment, so no WebMCP integration in this entry at this point. Can be scaled to openai. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The core problem this solves is real: showing up at the gym, getting overwhelmed by choice, wasting time deciding, then giving up and doing 20 minutes of light cardio instead. Fixing that meant building a fixed daily card with zero decisions, and it’s held up through real use, not a demo scenario. Also proud of how the feature set grew from actual daily friction instead of a spec: a notes field appeared because feedback needed somewhere to live, supplement timing got baked in once absorption conflicts (iron and tea) became a real problem, and the Google Sheet connection turned a single-device app into something trackable over time, all added while using it, not before. 

 What we learned 

 Most failure in a self-built fitness plan isn’t a willpower problem, it’s a decision-fatigue problem. Removing every choice, which workout, what to eat, when to take what, did more for consistency than any amount of motivation ever could. Also learned that building for one real, specific person first, rather than a broad audience, produces a more honest product, and that a spreadsheet plus a free script is enough backend for a real MVP, no database needed to start. 

 What's next for PostShiftGlow 

 Test with pilot users for one quarter, record before-and-after changes, work with medical domain experts to validate the approach, and put real legal compliance in place, disclaimers, waivers, and clear user consent and opt-ins before any data collection or paid tier. From there, partner with an accredited brand for outreach to the 300+ million women who could get a custom plan for under $20 a month.

title: Phlegm-Spitting Old Man Coughing Fit Generator
pitch: A completely unnecessary WebMCP-powered coughing impression generator featuring a fictional “Phlegm-Spitting Old Man,” with creator-recorded coughs dynamically transformed in JavaScript.
about_excerpt:
A completely unnecessary WebMCP-powered coughing impression generator featuring a fictional “Phlegm-Spitting Old Man,” with creator-recorded coughs dynamically transformed in JavaScript.

 Story

 ChatGPT is in control 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 title 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ChatGPT is in control 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 title 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 ChatGPT is in control 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 About the Project 

 The full and intentionally ridiculous name of this project is: 

 “Major-Blood-Vessel-About-to-Burst Coughing Fit of the Phlegm-Spitting Old Man You Meet on the Way Home from School Impression Generator” 

 Yes, that is the actual name. 

 This project is a deliberately absurd WebMCP experiment based on one extremely specific situation: encountering an old man on the way home from school who is coughing so violently that it looks like an important blood vessel might burst at any moment. 

 Despite the ridiculous premise, the project explores a serious interaction idea: allowing a human and an AI agent to control the same web application through a shared application state. 

 What It Does 

 The app generates a fictional coughing-fit impression using several adjustable parameters, including: 

 
 Cough Intensity 
 Major Blood Vessel Danger 
 Encounter Distance 
 Throat Congestion 
 Cough Burst Count 
 Phlegm Event Chance 
 

 A human can control these settings directly through the interface. 

 With WebMCP, ChatGPT can also control the same application by calling tools exposed by the website. For example, ChatGPT can change the cough intensity, adjust the encounter distance, modify other parameters, and generate the coughing fit. 

 The important part is that the human interface and the AI tools are not separate experiences. They operate on the same application state. 

 A human can change a slider, then an AI can change it again, and the interface immediately reflects the result. 

 The Audio 

 All original cough sounds used in this project were recorded by me. 

 No elderly men were recorded for this project. 

 Instead of using stock audio or third-party cough samples, I performed and recorded the coughing sounds myself. The recordings are then dynamically processed by JavaScript to create variations in the final coughing fits. 

 The application uses browser audio processing to alter characteristics of the recordings and combine them into different sequences depending on the current settings. 

 In other words: 

 The creator provided the cough.
JavaScript provided the old man. 

 WebMCP 

 The application exposes its controls as WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool . 

 This allows an AI agent such as ChatGPT to understand the actions available on the website without having to guess how to interact with the visual interface. 

 The WebMCP tools connect directly to the same underlying state and functions used by the human-facing controls. 

 For example, an agent can receive an instruction such as: 

 “Set the cough intensity to 10, set the major blood vessel danger to 95, set the encounter distance to 1 meter, and generate the coughing fit.” 

 The application then updates the corresponding controls and generates the result. 

 This creates a simple demonstration of human-agent collaboration in which both sides can operate the same web application. 

 How It Was Built 

 The project was built with: 

 
 JavaScript 
 Vite 
 Web Audio API 
 WebMCP 
 HTML and CSS 
 Vercel 
 

 The coughing audio is based on creator-recorded samples and is processed dynamically in the browser. 

 The project does not require an external AI API for the website itself. Instead, it exposes capabilities through WebMCP so compatible AI agents can interact with the application. 

 Why This Project? 

 I wanted to build something that demonstrated WebMCP clearly without hiding the interaction behind a complicated application. 

 The interface intentionally makes it obvious when a human changes a value and when an AI agent changes the same value. 

 The absurd premise also makes the demonstration easy to remember. 

 Many agent demos focus on productivity. 

 This one focuses on a fictional phlegm-spitting old man coughing on the way home from school. 

 Someone had to. 

 Development 

 This project was built under a tight hackathon deadline, so I intentionally kept the interface focused and relatively minimal in order to prioritize WebMCP interaction, reliability, and a working public demonstration. 

 The final application is deployed publicly and can be controlled manually or through WebMCP in a compatible browser environment. 

 What began as an extremely unnecessary coughing simulator became an experiment in giving humans and AI agents equal access to the same interactive web application.

title: AriaLens: WebMCP Accessibility Studio
pitch: A developer studio enabling LLM agents to safely audit and remediate live DOM accessibility violations via WebMCP, featuring optimistic concurrency locks and security honeypots.
about_excerpt: A developer studio enabling LLM agents to safely audit and remediate live DOM accessibility violations via WebMCP, featuring optimistic concurrency locks and security honeypots. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Over 96% of the world's top one million websites fail basic WCAG accessibility tests . For developers, retrofitting unsemantic <div> elements with complex ARIA attributes ( aria-expanded , aria-controls , role="combobox" , keyboard focus traps) is tedious, manual, and error-prone. With the advent of the Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) , web applications can finally expose structured tools directly to AI agents. But giving an autonomous LLM write access to a live DOM is inherently dangerous: Hallucination & Prompt Injection: Agents might apply unvetted, destructive mutations across the entire page. Race Conditions (TOCTOU): If an agent takes 10 seconds to analyze a component while a user is actively clicking and mutating the DOM, applying the patch blindly will corrupt UI state. We built AriaLens to solve this: an agent-native developer studio where humans and AI agents collaborate safely on live DOM accessibility remediation with strict Human-in-the-Loop Authority Boundaries , Optimistic Concurrency Locks , and Adversarial Honeypots . What it does AriaLens turns the browser into an interactive, agent-guided accessibility workbench: Live Accessibility Introspection: Using WebMCP, the agent inspects computed accessibility trees, AccName 1.1 calculations, and keyboard focus trap boundaries directly through audit_accessibility_tree . Human-in-the-Loop Authority Boundary: Destructive mutation tools ( commit_a11y_fix ) are never exposed upfront . The agent can only stage speculative changes via stage_aria_remediation . Staged changes render in an IDE-style visual code diff awaiting human sign-off. Optimistic Concurrency Lock (W3C § 6.3): Patches are cryptographically bound to an Epoch Lock recorded at audit time. If a user interacts with or mutates the DOM before commit, the epoch advances and the patch is safely rejected with a STALE_EPOCH_CONFLICT . The Honeypot Gauntlet (W3C § 6.4): To guard against rogue or jailbroken behavior, AriaLens mounts hidden bypass tools ( bulk_apply_all_fixes ). Any agent attempting to bypass human approval is intercepted, blocked, and flagged in the live audit log. Export as Git Patch: Staged remediations can be downloaded with one click as standard unified .patch files, enabling developers to review in browser and commit directly to their local Git repositories. How we built it WebMCP Protocol Integration: Built directly against the emerging W3C WebMCP draft specification using document.modelContext.registerTool() . We implemented ephemeral capability mounting via AbortController lifecycles to dynamically attach and detach tools based on human gate approval. Architecture & State Machine: Powered by React 19 , TypeScript , and Vite , with Zustand orchestrating the optimistic concurrency state machine and telemetry logs. Accessibility Evaluation: Backed by axe-core 4.10 , AccName 1.1 computation models, and automated WCAG 2.2 AA heuristics. Developer Interface: Designed with a high-density, dark-mode developer experience inspired by Linear and Vercel, featuring real-time latency badges, sub-pixel antialiasing, and structured code diff views. Challenges we ran into Solving TOCTOU Concurrency: Bridging the gap between asynchronous LLM inference (5–15 seconds) and synchronous DOM events required architecting a zero-overhead optimistic locking protocol (Epoch Locks) that cleanly rejects stale mutations without freezing the browser. Ephemeral Tool Lifecycle: Designing tool registration so that commit capabilities remain invisible to LLM tool discovery until explicitly authorized by a human, and immediately unregister after single execution. Clean Agent Steering: Calibrating tool descriptions and input schemas so that models prioritize structured attribute staging rather than attempting raw HTML string rewrites. Accomplishments that we're proud of Strict W3C WebMCP Compliance: Directly implemented and validated Sections 6.3 (Concurrency) and 6.4 (Untrusted Content) of the WebMCP draft specification. Enterprise-Grade Utility: Going beyond a toy demo by enabling instant .patch unified diff generation for real-world engineering workflows. Security-First Agent Design: Proving that agent-native web applications can grant high-level reasoning capabilities to AI without ever compromising runtime safety or human authority. What we learned Agents perform exponentially better when constrained by formal capability state machines rather than natural language prompt boundaries. WebMCP represents a paradigm shift: websites are no longer passive documents for LLMs to scrape, but active APIs where humans and agents co-operate with cryptographic guarantees. What's next for AriaLens Headless CI/CD WebMCP Runner: An automated GitHub Action that spins up headless Chrome with WebMCP enabled to audit staging deployments and open pull requests automatically. Support for Complex APG Patterns: Expanding fixture coverage to ARIA 1.3 TreeGrids, MenuBars, and complex multi-select comboboxes. Framework Code Generators: Generating native JSX/TSX component patches for Tailwind, Radix UI, and Shadcn components.
