title: webmcp-foundry
pitch: WebMCP Foundry turns web-app actions into minimized, tested, authority-governed agent tools—and automatically withdraws them when their evidence becomes stale.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Foundry turns web-app actions into minimized, tested, authority-governed agent tools—and automatically withdraws them when their evidence becomes stale. Like Comment Story Updates GIF Code changed → evidence stale → WebMCP tool withdrawn. Foundry keeps the browser’s live agent surface synchronized with verified state. WebMCP Foundry Agents propose. Evidence qualifies. Authority promotes. WebMCP makes it possible for websites to expose structured tools to AI agents. But exposing a function does not answer a harder question: Which actions have actually earned the right to become agent-callable tools? WebMCP Foundry is a capability compiler and verification workbench for the agent-native web. It takes actions that already exist in a human-facing web application and turns them into minimized, tested, effect-aware, evidence-backed, authority-governed WebMCP capabilities . Instead of treating registerTool() as the beginning of the process, Foundry treats native WebMCP registration as the output of an engineering lifecycle : human action → candidate → contract → minimized inputs → effects + authority → verification → evidence → promotion → LIVE WebMCP tool If the underlying implementation changes, its old evidence no longer silently remains valid. Foundry marks the affected capability STALE and withdraws it from the browser's native WebMCP registry until fresh evidence qualifies it again. What it does The demo uses Ledgerly , an ordinary human-facing financial web application. Foundry discovers actions such as transaction search, notes, balance adjustments, fund transfers, and account deletion. It then determines what part of each action should actually be agent-controlled. For example, an initially over-broad action with four controllable fields is reduced to only two agent-visible inputs, while trusted session and identity state remain application-controlled. Foundry then verifies proposed capabilities using explicit contracts, observed effects, negative tests, and deliberately incorrect must-kill mutants . A check only contributes evidence if it can reject its assigned known-bad implementation. The demo shows the complete lifecycle: Discover actions from the human application. Minimize an over-broad interface from 4 inputs to 2 agent-controlled inputs. Find a concrete counterexample in an incorrect implementation. Block promotion because the evidence is FAIL. Repair the implementation and obtain fresh evidence. Refuse an agent's attempt to self-promote a consequential financial capability. Allow an appropriately authorized human to promote it. Register it through native document.modelContext . Execute the capability through the browser's native WebMCP tool registry. Change the underlying source, causing LIVE → STALE and automatic native tool withdrawal. The browser registry and Foundry state are continuously reconciled: LIVE ⇔ present in document.modelContext.getTools() Everything else — CANDIDATE, VERIFIED-but-unpromoted, BLOCKED, STALE or WITHDRAWN — must remain absent. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, Foundry would only be a verifier describing which actions could be safe agent tools. WebMCP makes the final step real. A capability that passes Foundry's gates becomes an actual browser-native tool. When its evidence becomes stale, Foundry aborts its registration and the tool actually disappears from the agent's available interface. That closes the loop between software assurance and the browser's agent surface. How we built it Almost the entire authoritative system is implemented in dependency-free Julia using only the standard library . Julia owns: capability and effect models authority policy contract minimization verification mutation testing deterministic gates stale-dependency analysis the hash-chained evidence ledger HTTP serving JSON handling the demo application the Foundry UI native-host acceptance grading JavaScript is intentionally limited to the browser boundary where WebMCP exists. A small bridge projects Foundry's LIVE manifest onto document.modelContext , maintains one AbortController per tool, reconciles getTools() , and reports native browser observations back to the authoritative Julia system. The development polyfill is explicitly separated from native WebMCP and cannot satisfy Foundry's native acceptance gate . Challenges One of the biggest challenges was avoiding a verifier that simply agreed with itself. We addressed this with external observations, explicit non-PASS verdicts, counterexamples, and must-kill mutants. UNKNOWN, UNGRADABLE and BLOCKED cannot silently become PASS. Another challenge was the experimental nature of WebMCP itself. During native testing we found that our Edge build exposed the expected document.modelContext API but differed from the current WebIDL expectation for one executeTool() input form. Foundry records that disagreement rather than hiding it. Deployment was another practical challenge. The public entry point now monitors the live Foundry and Ledgerly services and redirects judges to their current HTTPS origins. Accomplishments we're proud of A working native WebMCP lifecycle rather than a simulated tool registry. LIVE → STALE → native withdrawal driven by real dependency changes. Agent self-ratification of consequential capabilities is refused. Trusted/session-bound fields cannot be forged through the agent contract. Verification checks must demonstrate that they can reject known-bad controls. A replayable, hash-chained evidence and promotion ledger. A dependency-free Julia authority kernel with only a minimal JavaScript WebMCP boundary. Native WebMCP acceptance tested against the deployed application. What we learned WebMCP makes exposing tools easy. The difficult engineering problem begins one level earlier: What should be exposed, under what contract, backed by what evidence, and for how long does that evidence remain valid? We found it useful to treat an application's agent interface as a derived software artifact rather than a static list of callable functions. What's next The next step is to generalize Foundry beyond the Ledgerly demonstration: richer application adapters, CI integration, additional capability-effect models, and standards-backed normative provenance. The longer-term idea is for WebMCP to be one compilation target of a protocol-independent capability IR. WebMCP lets websites expose tools to agents. WebMCP Foundry asks why each tool is allowed to exist. It was a tight orchestrated ensemble of agents from OpenAI, Claude and Google! 5 hours short of deadline. My contribution was mainly the review of ideas from across my private repos to meet it and I chose this idea of all candidates. Another to review the video, audio and texts to be accurate and tolerable for viewing. title: Grant Scout + WebMCP
pitch: A live funding-search agent, now callable by agents directly via a real WebMCP tool.
about_excerpt:
A live funding-search agent, now callable by agents directly via a real WebMCP tool.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Grant Scout is a live, search-grounded funding research agent for solo, non-incorporated founders — every answer comes from a real SerpApi/grants.gov search, reasoned by Gemini, with real cited sources, never invented. 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Grant Scout already solves a real problem for a real audience (solo founders finding funding they can actually apply for). WebMCP lets us extend that from "a page a human visits" to "a real capability an agent can call directly" — without building a second, parallel, disconnected demo. 

 What's new for this challenge 

 The app's existing live search — the exact same pipeline a human visitor triggers by typing a question and pressing Send — is now registered as a real WebMCP tool via document.modelContext.registerTool() : 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "search_funding_programs" , 
 description : "Search for real, currently-open funding programs ..." , 
 inputSchema : { type : "object" , properties : { query : { type : "string" } } , required : [ "query" ] } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { 
 const data = await runQuery ( input . query ) ; // the SAME function the UI form calls
 return { answer : data . answer , sources : data . sources } ; 
 } , 
 } ) ; 
 
 An agent-native browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) can now call search_funding_programs directly and get back a real, live, cited answer — the identical pipeline a human sees, not a mock or a shadow path. The tool call drives the same visible UI state (pipeline ticket, rendered answer, sources) that a human's own search would, so the page stays truthful about what just happened. 

 Feature-detected: on any browser without WebMCP support, this code no-ops entirely — zero effect on the default experience. 

 What people and agents can now do together that was hard before 

 Before: a founder had to remember to visit Grant Scout, type their situation, and read the results themselves. After: an agent working on a founder's behalf — inside a WebMCP-aware browser — can call the real search directly as part of a larger task (e.g., "find me funding I don't need a company for, then draft an application checklist"), grounded in the same live, cited, non-fabricated results a human would get. 

 How it works (full stack) 

 Agent: Google's Agent Development Kit (google-adk), a single Agent with two live-grounding tools — SerpApi's Google Search API and grants.gov's public Search API, chosen deterministically based on whether the question signals US federal funding.
Reasoning: gemini-flash-lite-latest reviews only the real returned results and cites every claim to a real source URL.
Backend: Vercel Python serverless function (frontend/api/chat.py).
Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4.
WebMCP: frontend/components/gs/TryIt.tsx registers the tool in a useEffect , sharing its query-execution logic with the human-facing form via a single runQuery function — one pipeline, two callers. 

 Try it live 

 https://grant-scout-jayblast.vercel.app — the human UI. The WebMCP tool registers automatically in any WebMCP-capable browser visiting the same page. 

 Repo: https://github.com/jayblast-spec/grant-scout (see frontend/components/gs/TryIt.tsx for the tool registration)

about_excerpt: A video editing sandbox built equally for humans and AI. Like Comment Story Updates The problem We built Perpetual because video editing is often the bottleneck for builders, researchers, and creators. Existing AI editors usually hide the timeline behind a prompt, or place a chat box beside a normal editor. We wanted a person and an agent to seamlessly tag-team inside the same project. What we built Perpetual lays out an ambitious concept for browser-based video editing with a canvas, timeline, media library, project management, and shared history. A person edits through the interface. An agent edits through WebMCP . Both use the same editing harness , so every change stays visible, editable, and reversible. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is central to the product architecture. The agent can inspect projects, index local media, search speech and shots, cut frame-accurately, arrange clips, edit overlays, generate media, and add kinetic captions. Tool availability follows the project lifecycle. Strict schemas, confirmation steps, activity feedback, and shared undo keep agent actions controlled. Challenges Video editing is stateful, while tool calls are independent, and thus a sequence of valid edits can produce the wrong result. We addressed this with shared project state, attributed action history, and atomic commands for operations like timeline arrangement. We also built local media persistence, Blob relinking after reload, and validated segment IDs that connect media understanding to real time ranges. What we learned The action history is useful beyond undo. Perpetual can distill a completed editing session into a reusable recipe/workflow : its intent, method, conventions, and adaptation rules. An agent can apply that approach to new footage without copying a fixed timeline. Where this goes The same harness can init projects, run agents in parallel, and record outcome for evaluation, training or RL. Video is our first environment; motion graphics and canvas-based design can use the same core Perpetual paradigm. title: BuildVsBuy.ai
pitch: BuildVsBuy.ai is a live build-vs-buy canvas. Humans and WebMCP agents share one decision model — weights, future stress, honest overrides — with every call in the tool log.
about_excerpt:
BuildVsBuy.ai is a live build-vs-buy canvas. Humans and WebMCP agents share one decision model — weights, future stress, honest overrides — with every call in the tool log.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Prototypes got cheap. Decisions didn't. 

 I kept seeing the same mess: someone ships a little tool for fun, then hits auth or scraping and freezes on build vs buy. ChatGPT will write you a confident paragraph. Ask again and you get a longer paragraph. You're still doing the math in your head. 

 I didn't know this domain well when I started. I just didn't want another essay. I wanted the page to move when the agent did something, and I wanted to see the call in a log so it couldn't just agree with me. 

 What it does 

 BuildVsBuy.ai is a decision canvas in the browser. You and the agent share one model. Nine WebMCP tools. Cards, weights, a future-stress banner, an override with a gap and a liability list. 

 If it says Build dropped, the log has to show a rerank. If the log didn't change, it guessed. 

 The demo walk: 

 
 Auth. You admit you're shipping a prototype fast. Build usually falls last. 
 Switch to scraping. "What if HIPAA and 50k users?" That's a simulation. Baseline cards stay put. 
 You still want to own the crawler. It pins Build, shows how far that is from the math, and lists what you're taking on. 
 

 Numbers on the axes are my estimates for the demo. Not vendor quotes. Not financial advice. 

 How I built it 

 Vite, vanilla JS, no backend. Vercel. 

 Tools live in src/webmcp.js ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). Math lives in src/decision.js . The UI just redraws a snapshot. Human sliders and agent calls hit the same execute path, tagged human or agent so the log isn't lying about who did it. 

 I also wrote two smoke scripts so I wasn't debugging this only through ChatGPT's mood that day. 

 What I learned 

 Soft instructions do not save a live agent. It will skip the rerank. It will invent cards. It will pin Buy because some flag wasn't set. 

 The stuff that actually held on camera was refusing the bad call in the tool itself. Prompt text is decoration. 

 Also: WebMCP is useful when the page is a real store, not when you ask the model to "look at the screenshot." 

 Challenges 

 Recording almost killed me. Same session, Prompt 2 did the right tool and nothing moved because the weight was already 10 so we skipped rerank. Prompt 4 looked like Buy won because override wouldn't pin Build unless core IP was already true. I fixed both in code. I was not going to sit there and whisper hints on camera. 

 Keeping simulate as a projection (not rewriting live context) was another fight. Agents love to "just set HIPAA" and pretend the future already happened. 

 I cut saved accounts, live pricing, and a third industry. Ten days. The loop had to work: ask, tool, visible state, honest disagreement.

title: Post-Purchase Resolution
pitch: When a purchase goes wrong, WebMCP helps an agent find the right Shopify order and prepare a resolution—without taking authority away from the customer or merchant.
about_excerpt: When a purchase goes wrong, WebMCP helps an agent find the right Shopify order and prepare a resolution—without taking authority away from the customer or merchant. Like Comment Story Updates Post-Purchase Resolution Shopping agents know how to buy. What happens when something goes wrong? Post-Purchase Resolution is an agent-native post-purchase support experience built with WebMCP + Shopify . Instead of forcing a customer to search for an order number, navigate support menus, or explain the same problem several times, the customer can simply describe what went wrong in natural language. The agent can then discover the website's structured WebMCP capabilities, find the correct purchase, read authoritative Shopify state, and prepare the next step. But there is one deliberate boundary: The agent can help. It cannot silently become the customer or the merchant. The customer keeps customer authority. The merchant keeps merchant authority. Shopify remains the external source of truth. 🎥 Demo Watch the full demo In the demo, a customer reports that a Portable 4K Action Camera — $149 arrived damaged and would not turn on. The customer never provides an order number. From that natural-language request, the agent discovers the site's WebMCP tools, finds the correct authenticated purchase, reads its return eligibility, and prepares a resolution. Then: Agent prepares → Customer commits → Merchant decides → Shopify records the truth. 💡 Inspiration AI shopping experiences are becoming increasingly capable before checkout. Agents can search. They can compare. They can recommend. They can help people buy. But commerce does not end at checkout. Products arrive damaged. The wrong variant is delivered. Shipments arrive late. Customers need exchanges, returns, replacements, or refunds. And that part of the experience is still dominated by: order numbers support menus forms ticket queues policy pages repeated explanations disconnected customer and merchant workflows That led us to a simple question: If the web is becoming agentic, what should happen when the purchase itself goes wrong? We did not want to build another chatbot floating on top of an ecommerce site. We wanted the website itself to expose meaningful, structured capabilities that an agent could understand and use safely. That is where WebMCP became the core of the product rather than an add-on. ✨ What it does Post-Purchase Resolution lets a customer describe a purchase problem naturally. For example: “The action camera I bought recently arrived damaged and won't turn on. Can you find the purchase and tell me what I can do? Don't submit anything.” The customer does not need to know the order number. The agent discovers the site's available WebMCP tools and can use: find_order get_order prepare_resolution The experience then separates responsibility between three actors. 🤖 Agent The agent can: understand the customer's intent locate the relevant purchase read authoritative order information inspect return eligibility prepare the appropriate resolution The agent cannot commit the commerce action through WebMCP. 👤 Customer The authenticated customer decides whether to actually request the return. That action occurs under the customer's own Shopify Customer Account authority. 🏪 Merchant The merchant receives the pending request in a separate decision desk. Only the merchant can approve it. 🟢 Shopify Shopify records the authoritative lifecycle of the return. The website does not invent its own version of commerce state. 🔥 Why WebMCP matters Without structured site capabilities, an agent often has to reason from presentation: inspect UI interpret text locate controls infer what a button means navigate DOM state hope the page still looks the same Post-Purchase Resolution instead exposes explicit business capabilities. Customer intent ↓ ChatGPT / Codex ↓ WebMCP Site Tools ↓ find_order get_order prepare_resolution ↓ Authoritative Shopify data This means the agent does not need to guess that a certain button or piece of text represents an order lookup. The site tells the agent exactly what capability exists. And just as importantly, it tells the agent what capability does not exist. 🔐 The capability boundary This became one of the most important design decisions in the project. The WebMCP surface intentionally contains: ✓ find_order ✓ get_order ✓ prepare_resolution It intentionally does not contain: ✕ request_return ✕ approve_return ✕ refund That is not an unfinished feature. It is the authority model. The agent can find, read, and prepare. The customer commits. The merchant decides. This allowed us to design the experience around collaboration instead of maximum agent autonomy. More agent capability is not always better. The right capability at the right boundary is better. 🛍️ A real end-to-end scenario One of our clean validation runs used a fresh Shopify purchase that was never hardcoded into the application. The application discovered the purchase automatically. The customer then followed the complete flow. Fresh purchase ↓ Agent discovers purchase ↓ Agent prepares resolution ↓ Customer explicitly requests return ↓ Shopify Return = REQUESTED ↓ Merchant reviews request ↓ Merchant approves ↓ Same Shopify Return = OPEN The critical part is that the same external Shopify Return object is preserved throughout the lifecycle. The application is not maintaining a parallel pretend state. Shopify is the system of record. 🧪 Real Shopify proof We verified the architecture against a Shopify development store using test payments and real Shopify Order/Return objects . A clean flow demonstrated: Step Result Fresh order discovered without hardcoding ✅ Customer-scoped purchase ✅ Agent mutation tool exposed No Customer requested return ✅ Shopify Return created REQUESTED Merchant reviewed same Return ✅ Merchant approved ✅ Same Shopify Return updated OPEN Duplicate Return created No Refund automatically performed No This distinction matters. The agent did not manufacture a UI result. The state transition existed independently in Shopify. 🗣️ Natural-language WebMCP verification We also tested the WebMCP experience through ChatGPT/Codex Site Tools. The user described a damaged purchase without giving an order number. The agent discovered and used: find_order get_order prepare_resolution It found the correct purchase and prepared the resolution. Nothing was submitted. An independent Shopify check confirmed: Return created by agent: NO Refund created by agent: NO Approval event: NO We then repeated the experience using a spoken request in a new chat with no previous order context . The observed flow was: Spoken request ↓ ChatGPT agent turn ↓ Website Site Tools enumerated ↓ find_order ↓ get_order ↓ Correct purchase found The spoken request asked only to find the purchase and explain the available option. The agent did exactly that. It did not stage a resolution unnecessarily. That gave us an interesting proof of intent-sensitive tool selection. 🏗️ How we built it The product is built around four distinct layers. ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Customer / ChatGPT / Codex │ └──────────────┬──────────────┘ │ WebMCP │ ┌──────────────▼──────────────┐ │ Post-Purchase Resolution │ │ Vercel-hosted application │ └──────────────┬──────────────┘ │ ┌────────┴────────┐ │ │ Customer Account Admin API API │ │ │ ▼ ▼ Customer action Merchant action │ │ └────────┬─────────┘ ▼ Shopify External source of truth WebMCP The site registers structured tools through the browser's model context. The final tool surface is deliberately small: find_order get_order prepare_resolution Shopify Customer Account API The authenticated customer flow uses Shopify Customer Account authentication. This keeps order discovery scoped to the currently authenticated customer's purchases. The customer action uses customer authority. Shopify Admin API Merchant approval uses a separate server-side Admin authority. The Admin credential is never exposed to the browser or agent. Vercel The public application and server-side API routes are deployed on Vercel. Secrets remain on the server boundary. 🔑 Authentication and authority Customer authentication uses OAuth/OIDC with PKCE. The customer session is used to query purchases belonging to that authenticated customer. The architecture does not permit arbitrary customer order enumeration from the customer flow. The merchant side uses a separate operator access control in the current implementation. That merchant access layer is intentionally distinct from customer authentication. Current limitation: The merchant decision desk uses an operator credential rather than full merchant OAuth/identity. We document this explicitly rather than presenting it as something it is not. 🛡️ Security by capability design Security was not treated as a final checklist item. It influenced the WebMCP architecture itself. Important boundaries include: customer-scoped order retrieval no arbitrary order lookup from authenticated customer flow S

title: SkyRingAI-WebMCP
pitch: Run your AI receptionist from ChatGPT with secure analytics, transcripts, appointments, and preview-before-publish configuration updates.
about_excerpt: Run your AI receptionist from ChatGPT with secure analytics, transcripts, appointments, and preview-before-publish configuration updates. Like 3 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Small-business owners using an AI receptionist accumulate valuable context across call analytics, transcripts, appointments, and assistant settings. Answering a question like “Which qualified callers need follow-up?” normally means navigating several screens and then switching to another workflow to act on the answer. Conventional browser agents must guess at controls and page state, which is brittle and especially risky when changing a live voice assistant. What it does SkyRingAI-WebMCP turns the authenticated SkyRingAI customer portal into a structured, agent-operable workspace. After the existing Supabase session resolves an active customer, the portal registers seven private WebMCP tools: get_dashboard_summary search_call_history get_call_details list_upcoming_appts get_assistant_config preview_assistant_update publish_assistant_update A customer can ask ChatGPT to summarize performance, find qualified calls, inspect a bounded transcript, list upcoming appointments, read the full receptionist configuration, and propose changes. Configuration changes use an explicit preview-before-publish workflow: the preview returns field-level differences and a short-lived ID; only a separate publish request saves the reviewed change. The production demo uses a dedicated non-admin judge account with isolated fictional records, a disposable VAPI assistant, and a live inbound demo number. The public repository contains the complete WebMCP contracts, seven-tool implementation, registration lifecycle, fixture provider, tests, and runnable sanitized demo—not the private commercial SaaS. Why WebMCP WebMCP is a strong fit because the useful unit is a trusted business operation, not a page click. An agent receives bounded tools with explicit schemas, read/write annotations, and authentication-derived scope instead of guessing how to traverse a dashboard. This lets a person and agent combine analytics, call discovery, transcript review, appointment context, and controlled action in one conversation. Tool inputs cannot select a customer or tenant. Stored transcript and database text is treated as untrusted, phone output is masked, and ranges, transcript size, pagination, and configuration fields are bounded. How we built it The tool layer is organized around a provider interface. The portal resolves the authenticated Supabase user and active customer, constructs a provider bound to that trusted context, validates tool inputs, repeats customer filters on production reads, and normalizes privacy-bounded results. An abortable lifecycle removes every private tool when the authenticated session ends. Assistant updates first read the complete current configuration so list replacements can preserve stable IDs. Greeting-only changes use the existing direct assistant path. Every effective non-greeting change must complete the authenticated N8N preview workflow before a publishable ID exists. Publishing accepts only that short-lived preview ID, and the server resolves the customer again before saving and requesting the downstream VAPI update. Challenge-period enhancement SkyRingAI existed before this challenge and briefly experimented with one small public, read-only WebMCP pricing tool plus declarative form annotations. During the submission period I built a substantial new authenticated customer-portal capability with Codex: seven tools spanning dashboard analytics, call search, bounded transcripts, appointments, complete assistant configuration, and preview-before-publish updates. I added the customer-scoped production provider, validation and privacy boundaries, lifecycle cleanup, controlled N8N mutation path, automated tests, dedicated production judge tenant, and separate open-source challenge repository. This expands the early experiment into a coherent, working business operations workflow. How I used AI and Codex ChatGPT is the runtime conversational control surface. VAPI powers the voice receptionist, and N8N powers the existing non-greeting configuration generation and update workflow. Codex was the primary engineering collaborator for architecture inspection, scoping, implementation, debugging, tests, security hardening, production verification, and open-source packaging. Lovable helped provision and verify the isolated production judge tenant through its connected Supabase and existing server integrations. The feature was tested live through ChatGPT from another machine. Accomplishments Seven authenticated WebMCP tools working in production. Customer identity derived from the trusted session, never a tool argument. Bounded outputs, masked phones, safe errors, strict schemas, and untrusted-content hints. Human-reviewable, single-use preview-before-publish assistant mutations. Real N8N preview/publish integration for non-greeting changes. Verified RLS isolation and a dedicated fictional judge environment. Runnable fixture-only open-source edition with no production credentials or customer data. Passing automated tests and production build. What I learned The most important lesson was that exposing more tools is not automatically better. Agent-native product design is about creating trustworthy operational boundaries: give the agent enough structured context to be useful, keep identity outside caller-controlled input, label untrusted data, constrain outputs, and separate “show me what would change” from “make the change.” What's next After the challenge, I plan to expand customer-controlled WebMCP workflows while keeping the same authentication, tenant, privacy, and preview-before-publish model. Likely next areas include controlled follow-up actions, broader analytics questions, and additional assistant lifecycle operations. about_excerpt:
A privacy-first workspace where AI agents can search, analyze, and edit your notes directly in the browser — powered by WebMCP, with your data staying local.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, but the web is still difficult for them to interact with reliably. 

 We wanted to explore a simple question: 

 
 What if a web application could expose its own capabilities directly to AI agents? 
 

 That led us to build AgentDOM — a privacy-first knowledge workspace where the application itself exposes useful actions to agents through WebMCP . 

 Instead of forcing an agent to scrape the UI, guess what buttons do, or rely entirely on external APIs, AgentDOM gives agents structured tools for working with the user's knowledge. 

 What we built 

 AgentDOM is a browser-based workspace for creating and managing notes and knowledge. 

 The key difference is that the application is agent-ready . 

 Through WebMCP, AgentDOM exposes capabilities that an AI agent can discover and use directly from the web application. An agent can work with the user's knowledge through structured tools rather than treating the page like an opaque visual interface. 

 The project is designed around privacy as well: knowledge can remain within the user's browser instead of requiring a traditional backend to store everything. 

 This creates a different model for AI + web applications: 

 Web App → exposes capabilities → AI Agent → performs useful work 

 rather than: 

 AI Agent → scrapes/interprets UI → tries to control Web App 

 How we built it 

 AgentDOM was built as a modern web application with a local-first architecture. 

 We created the knowledge workspace and then integrated WebMCP so that the application could expose agent-facing tools alongside its normal human-facing interface. 

 The agent interaction layer allows compatible AI agents to discover the available capabilities and invoke them using structured inputs and outputs. 

 We also kept the architecture lightweight and browser-focused so that the project could demonstrate that an application does not necessarily need a large backend or complex agent infrastructure to become agent-ready. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 WebMCP changes the relationship between websites and AI agents. 

 Instead of every agent having to independently figure out how a website works, the website can explicitly describe the actions it supports. 

 For AgentDOM, this means the application can provide tools specifically designed for working with knowledge. 

 This makes agent interaction more predictable, easier to reason about, and potentially much more reliable than UI automation. 

 What we learned 

 Building AgentDOM taught us that making an application agent-friendly is not simply about adding an AI chatbot. 

 The more interesting part is designing the interface between the application and the agent . 

 We learned to think about: 

 
 What capabilities should an application expose to an agent? 
 What should the tool inputs and outputs look like? 
 How can agents interact with structured application state? 
 How can we keep the human experience simple while making the application machine-readable? 
 How can local-first applications participate in the emerging agentic web? 
 

 WebMCP also made us think differently about the web itself: websites can become active participants in agent workflows rather than simply being pages that agents navigate. 

 Challenges 

 One of our biggest challenges was figuring out how to bridge the gap between a normal web application and an agent-facing tool interface. 

 We had to think carefully about which application capabilities should become tools and how an agent should interact with them. 

 Another challenge was keeping the experience useful for both humans and agents. We didn't want to build something that was only impressive in an agent demo; the application still needed to work naturally as a normal web workspace. 

 We also had to work within the limitations and emerging nature of WebMCP while building a practical demonstration around it. 

 What's next 

 AgentDOM is an experiment in what an agent-ready web could look like. 

 We want to explore more sophisticated tools, richer agent workflows, and ways for more web applications to expose their capabilities directly to agents. 

 Our goal is simple: 

 
 Make the web easier for agents to understand and safer for users to control.

 Shopping online is still fundamentally designed around humans . 

 We search through products, open multiple pages, compare specifications, check reviews, evaluate prices, add items to our cart, enter delivery details, and finally complete the purchase. 

 But as AI agents become increasingly capable, we asked a different question: 

 
 What if an AI agent could actually use an e-commerce website instead of simply talking about it? 
 

 That question inspired us to build CARTOS — an AI-native e-commerce experience powered by WebMCP . 

 We built a complete shopping application backed by a real-world Amazon product dataset containing 123,133 products . 

 Our goal wasn't to build another chatbot that recommends products.

- The final purchasing decision

This creates a clear boundary:

> **The agent does the work. The human makes the final commitment.**

Traditional websites expose information primarily for **humans**.

title: Nearcast WebMCP
pitch: Nearcast is a WebMCP-powered cross-border hazard map that helps people and AI agents explore authoritative wildfire, severe weather, and earthquake data across Canada and the U.S.
about_excerpt: Nearcast is a WebMCP-powered cross-border hazard map that helps people and AI agents explore authoritative wildfire, severe weather, and earthquake data across Canada and the U.S. Like Comment Story Updates Map Overview Focusing on a specific region Human + Agent Shared State Cross-Border Hazard Comparison Inspiration Nearcast began as a Canadian iPhone app that pulls official hazard data. Hazard maps are exactly the kind of interface generic browser agents struggle with: hundreds of clustered markers, a dozen filter combinations, geographic bounds, a selection, and six agencies' worth of heterogeneous records. WebMCP lets the page say what it can do instead of making the agent infer it from the DOM. What it does Nearcast WebMCP shows current wildfires, weather alerts and earthquakes across Canada and the United States on one MapLibre map, normalized from six official sources (ECCC, NRCan CWFIS, Earthquakes Canada, NWS, NIFC, USGS) with explicit attribution and freshness. Every source fails independently; if a feed is down the app says so and keeps working. It exposes eight WebMCP tools that read and mutate the same application state the human is looking at: get_current_view — map bounds, zoom, filters, selected hazard, counts, source freshness get_visible_hazards — concise list of what is on screen after all filters set_focus_area — move the map to regions ( ["BC","WA"] ), bounds, or a point set_hazard_filters — countries, hazard types, minimum weather severity, minimum magnitude focus_hazard — select a hazard exactly like a human click (highlight, pan, details panel) get_hazard_details — full record with agency classifications and the official link compare_regions — deterministic counts for provinces/states create_situation_context — structured facts for an area; the agent writes the prose An Agent Activity panel logs every tool call, so people can see what the agent did. Why WebMCP fits this use case Map applications hold large amounts of visual state. Screen-scraping and clicking is brittle and slow. WebMCP gives the agent typed, described operations while keeping human and agent in the same visible workspace : the human zooms and clicks, the agent reads that through get_current_view , changes filters or focus, and the human sees it happen and refines by hand. Better UX Instead of manually toggling countries, filtering hazard types and scanning hundreds of markers, the user says "Focus on British Columbia and Washington and show only wildfires and important weather alerts" — and still sees and controls the resulting map. Verified live in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser with GPT-5.6. What humans and agents do together Human: explores visually, selects incidents, validates context, controls decisions. Agent: manipulates filters, compares regions, retrieves structured details, surfaces relevant information, writes the narrative. Application: authoritative normalized data, deterministic geographic calculations and counts, visual state — and never a "you are safe" claim. How we built it React + TypeScript + Vite + MapLibre GL (OpenFreeMap basemap, no tokens). One TypeScript Lambda behind API Gateway HTTP API with six source adapters ( Promise.allSettled , per-source timeouts, stale-snapshot fallback), a shared hazard model, and severity translation kept alongside raw agency classifications. CloudFront serves the SPA from a private S3 bucket (OAC) and routes /api/* to API Gateway so everything is same-origin; Terraform provisions all of it. Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() and wrap the app's own store actions — the same functions a click uses. No AI API keys anywhere: WebMCP is the AI integration. Challenges Government feeds are inconsistent: CWFIS's national fire layer is temporal (189k rows; only rows whose validity window includes "now" are current), most NWS alerts have no polygon (placed at Census county centroids and flagged approximate ), Earthquakes Canada is pipe-delimited text. Keeping severity honest: earthquakes and US wildfires have no agency severity, so we expose magnitude/hectares plus a clearly labelled display significance instead of inventing one. Demo robustness: per-source failure handling, stale snapshots, and a clearly labelled demo-data mode. Accomplishments Live cross-border six-source hazard workspace; eight well-described tools; shared state proven by get_current_view reflecting manual pans and clicks; 44 unit tests; reproducible Terraform deployment; verified end-to-end in ChatGPT's built-in browser. What we learned Tool descriptions and strict schemas matter more than tool count. Deterministic, structured outputs (counts, ids, source status) let the agent explain without hallucinating, and a visible activity log makes the collaboration legible to people. What's next Evacuation orders (BC first), air quality, time-windowed regional summaries, and Chrome origin-trial enrollment. Safety Nearcast is an awareness tool, not an emergency service. It always shows the issuing agency, timestamps and the official link, and reminds users to follow local emergency authorities. Built With amazon-api-gateway amazon-cloudfront amazon-web-services aws-lambda maplibre-gl node.js openstreetmap react terraform typescript vite vitest webmcp Try it out hazards.securitygeek.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo project. I designed the product and the human + agent experience, chose the government data sources (reusing what I learned building the Nearcast iPhone app), and built and deployed the full stack: React/MapLibre front end, TypeScript Lambda API, Terraform on AWS, and the eight WebMCP tools. I used Claude Code as a pair programmer throughout and tested the tools live in ChatGPT's desktop browser and Chrome. Biggest lesson: good tool descriptions and deterministic, structured outputs matter far more than tool count. title: Verdiqt
pitch: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict.
about_excerpt: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI made building software cheap. It did not make building the right software cheap. People now ship a SaaS product in a weekend, and find out at launch that nobody wanted it. Verdiqt moves that painful discovery to before you write the first line of code. You put your idea on trial, and a court decides whether it deserves to live. What it does You file a case: your SaaS idea in a sentence, or a link to a public GitHub repo you already built. Then the courtroom goes to work, and you watch every step happen live: The case file. The court reads your idea and writes it up: who it's for, what problem it solves, what to search for. The investigation. Real research across five real communities : Hacker News, Reddit, GitHub, Stack Overflow, and Product Hunt. Every finding appears on screen with a link to its source, and every source reports honestly: gathered, failed, or empty. If the first search comes back thin, the court automatically widens its search. The deliberation. Six AI judges each take one question: "Is the pain real? Is anyone actively looking for this? Who already exists? Who would pay? Can you reach these people? Can you build it fast enough?" Each judge delivers their score the moment they finish, you literally watch the bench board fill in, one verdict at a time. The ruling. A presiding judge reads the entire case file and rules: BUILD, PIVOT, or KILL —> with a score out of 100, the reasoning behind every number, and exactly one recommended next step (a real, cheap test you can run this week). A full trial takes about a minute. And if you refine your idea and try again, the court remembers: the evidence you marked as important and the previous ruling follow your case, so every iteration builds on the last. How we built it Zero cash out of pocket. The whole product runs on free tiers and hackathon credits: one small server runs the website and the research pipeline, the AI judges run on free model APIs, and when one provider's daily quota runs dry, the court automatically switches to a backup provider mid-trial and keeps ruling. Constraints became design: the court paces itself under rate limits, shows its deliberation while it works, and never wastes a token. The model argues; the code rules. Anti-hallucination isn't a prompt, it's enforced in code. Judges may only cite evidence the court actually gathered: invented citations are stripped automatically, and a high score that loses its citations gets capped. When public evidence is thin, the judge is allowed to use domain judgment but the ruling must say so, out loud, in the rationale. Uncertainty is never dressed up as certainty. Privacy without accounts. No sign-up. Your browser gets an unguessable key; only its fingerprint is stored. Your cases are yours, anyone else asking for them gets an identical "not found.", don't worry. Challenges we ran into Running a multi-stage AI pipeline on free tiers meant treating every token and every request as scarce... the wait-and-retry pacing, the provider failover, and the one-at-a-time trial queue all exist because of it. And WebMCP is new enough that the tool contract itself was a design problem: we learned that the workflow belongs inside the tool descriptions, so agents teach themselves the journey. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, evidence-cited validation trial in about a minute. A deliberation you can actually watch. A surface that serves two audiences at once... humans get a courtroom, agents get a toolbox, and each can see the other working. What we learned Never think you have enough time to build something. What's next for Verdiqt GitHub sign-in to put your whole repo graveyard on trial at once, re-trials over time to watch a verdict change as markets move, and Reddit's expanded API access for even deeper community evidence. title: NetLab
pitch: A browser-based network simulator where people and AI agents troubleshoot the same live network together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A browser-based network simulator where people and AI agents troubleshoot the same live network together through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Website opened inside ChatGPT Browser ChatGPT Diagnosing with the help of WebMCP tools NetLab Network Creation NetLab exposed WebMCP Tools used by ChatGPT ChatGPT highlighting the faulty node in network through the highlight_node tool ChatGPT fixing the faulty node through the WebMCP Tool Inspiration Network simulators are great for learning because you can experiment with routers, IP addresses, gateways and routes without needing physical networking hardware. But when something breaks, the experience is still very manual. A topology may look perfectly fine while one incorrect gateway or missing route prevents two machines from communicating. You then have to open devices one by one, inspect their interfaces and routing tables, run tests, and work backwards until you find the problem. That felt like a good place to explore WebMCP. Instead of building another chatbot inside a simulator, I wanted to see what would happen if the simulator itself became understandable and operable by an external AI agent , while the user continued working in the same interface. That became NetLab . What NetLab does NetLab is a lightweight browser-based network simulation lab. A user can: create PCs and routers connect and disconnect devices configure IPv4 addresses and CIDR prefixes configure default gateways configure router interfaces add and remove static routes load working and intentionally broken network labs run connectivity tests see the forward and return packet paths inspect exactly where and why routing fails The networking behavior is handled by NetLab itself. It has a deterministic client-side simulation engine for IPv4 addressing, subnet logic, gateways, directly connected networks, static routing and bidirectional reachability. In other words, the language model does not decide whether a network works. ChatGPT reasons about the result; NetLab decides the result. Why WebMCP fits this use case A network simulator contains much more state than what is immediately visible on the canvas. Two routers may look correctly connected while their interface addresses or routing tables make communication impossible. Without structured access, an agent would have to inspect the UI, open individual devices, read form fields, understand what each control represents and then attempt to operate the application through the interface. With WebMCP, NetLab exposes meaningful networking capabilities directly. The current site tools are: get_topology get_device_state test_connectivity highlight_device add_static_route remove_static_route This allows ChatGPT to work with the actual network state rather than infer it from screenshots. For example, in the included Broken Static Routing Challenge : PC-01 cannot reach PC-02. ChatGPT reads the live topology. It runs NetLab's connectivity simulator. It inspects the relevant router. It identifies the missing return route. It can highlight that router directly in the user's canvas. When asked, it adds the missing static route. It runs the simulator again and NetLab verifies that connectivity now succeeds. The important part is that the human and the agent are not working with separate copies of the network. They are both operating the same live lab state . If the human changes the network manually, the next tool call sees that change. If the agent modifies a route, the user immediately sees it in the same inspector. How I built it I first built NetLab as a normal network simulator before adding WebMCP. The application uses a visual topology canvas for manipulating devices and connections, while the network itself is represented as structured client-side state. The simulator implements the core Layer-3 logic separately from the UI so that both human actions and agent actions can reuse the same behavior. At a high level: Human UI → Application actions → Shared lab state → Network simulator and: WebMCP tools → Application actions → Shared lab state → Network simulator This was important because I did not want a separate "AI version" of NetLab's behavior. The WebMCP tools are registered using the imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Read tools expose concise networking state instead of React or framework internals, and write tools reuse the same application actions used by the normal interface. Everything currently runs client-side. NetLab does not require a backend or an embedded AI model. Challenges The first challenge was scope. It would have been very easy to turn this into an attempt to recreate Packet Tracer, which was neither realistic nor necessary for the idea I wanted to demonstrate. So I deliberately kept the networking scope focused on PCs, routers, IPv4, CIDR, default gateways and static routing. This was enough to make troubleshooting real without pretending NetLab was a full network emulator. The second challenge was keeping the simulator trustworthy. Connectivity needed to come from deterministic network logic rather than from the AI. That meant handling forward and return paths, subnet checks, next-hop resolution, static-route matching and useful failure conditions correctly. The third challenge was WebMCP itself. Tool design mattered more than simply exposing lots of functions. I kept the surface intentionally small and domain-specific so an agent could clearly understand when to inspect the network, when to run a simulation and when to make a routing change. Testing was also interesting because WebMCP is still emerging. I verified the tools directly in Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled and then tested the full human-agent workflow inside ChatGPT's in-app browser. What I learned The biggest thing I learned from this project is that making a web application "agent-native" is not the same as adding AI to it. The useful part is deciding which pieces should remain deterministic application logic, which capabilities should be exposed as tools, and where the human should stay in control. For NetLab: the simulator owns networking truth WebMCP exposes structured capabilities the agent reasons over those capabilities the human still sees and controls the live workspace That division ended up being much more interesting than simply asking an LLM to operate the UI. What's next NetLab is intentionally a small Layer-3 simulator today, but the same interaction model could extend much further. Future versions could explore switches, VLANs, ARP, DHCP, NAT, dynamic routing protocols and richer challenge generation. More interesting to me is the collaborative side: an agent could generate troubleshooting labs, guide a learner without directly giving away the answer, explain packet behavior step by step, or validate a network design while the user continues modifying it manually. For this challenge, I wanted to get the core idea right first: a network simulator where a person and their agent can inspect, troubleshoot and change the same executable environment together. I also designed and implemented the six site tools that let ChatGPT inspect, diagnose, highlight, modify, and re-test the same live network used by the human. about_excerpt:
A high-performance URL shortener written in Go using Fiber v3, PostgreSQL, and Redis. Now with WebMCP
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Go Link Shortener started as a small, fast URL shortener built around a simple idea: creating and resolving short links should require as little friction as possible. 

 When I discovered WebMCP, the project became a natural experiment for a different question: 

 What if an AI agent did not need to inspect the page, understand the layout, and simulate clicks just to use a web application? 

 Instead of building a separate chatbot or a remote MCP server, I wanted the existing website itself to expose its capabilities directly to AI agents while remaining fully usable by humans. 

 The result is an agent-native URL shortener where the same application can be used through its normal UI or through structured WebMCP tools. 

 What it does 

 Go Link Shortener allows users to create custom short URLs, redirect visitors efficiently, and collect click analytics. 

 With WebMCP enabled, the website exposes three capabilities directly to AI agents: 

 
 create_short_link — creates a short URL using the existing HTML form and server-side validation. 
 resolve_short_link — returns the destination behind an existing alias. 
 get_link_analytics — returns aggregate traffic information such as total clicks and the latest click timestamp. 
 

 This enables interactions such as: 

 
 "Create /webmcp pointing to the WebMCP documentation." 
 

 or: 

 
 "Where does /webmcp redirect, and how many times has it been opened?" 
 

 The agent can discover and execute the appropriate tools without visually locating controls or automating clicks. 

 How I built it 

 The backend is written in Go using Fiber v3 , with PostgreSQL as the persistent datastore and Redis for fast URL resolution. 

 I deliberately kept the existing server-rendered architecture instead of introducing a frontend framework only for WebMCP. 

 For link creation, I used the Declarative WebMCP API . The existing HTML form is exposed as the create_short_link tool, so both humans and agents go through the same validation and persistence code. 

 For read operations, I used the Imperative WebMCP API through: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( . . . ) 
 
 Two read-only tools are registered when WebMCP is available: 
 resolve_short_link
get_link_analytics
 
 They call lightweight JSON endpoints implemented in the existing Go application. 

 The integration is implemented as progressive enhancement. If a browser does not support WebMCP, the website continues working normally. 

 Privacy and safety 

 The original application records redirect events for analytics, including information useful for internal traffic analysis. 

 I intentionally designed the WebMCP interface to expose only aggregate information. 

 The get_link_analytics tool returns: 

 
 total clicks 
 latest click timestamp 
 

 It does not expose raw IP addresses, User-Agent strings, referrers, or individual click events. 

 Read operations are also explicitly marked with readOnlyHint: true , giving agents additional information about which actions are safe to execute without modifying application state. 

 Challenges I faced 

 One of the most interesting challenges was that implementing the tools themselves was not enough. 

 WebMCP requires the document to run in the appropriate browser security context, so I had to configure origin isolation using: 
 Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp
 
 I also added configurable support for the WebMCP Origin Trial token so the application can participate in the browser experiment without hardcoding environment-specific credentials. 

 Another challenge was deciding where WebMCP should stop. 

 It would have been easy to create a parallel API layer, duplicate validation in JavaScript, or rebuild the UI using a frontend framework. Instead, I kept the existing application as the source of truth and exposed only the capabilities an agent actually needs. 

 That kept the implementation small, maintainable, and aligned with the progressive nature of WebMCP. 

 What I learned 

 The biggest lesson was that making a website agent-friendly is very different from adding AI to a website. 

 There is no LLM inside Go Link Shortener. 

 Instead, WebMCP gives external agents a structured contract describing what the website can do. 

 This changes the integration model from: 
 Agent → inspect DOM → understand UI → simulate clicks
 
 to: 
 Agent → discover tools → execute structured action
 
 I also learned that good tool design matters as much as implementation. Tool names, descriptions, JSON schemas, read-only annotations, error handling, and privacy boundaries directly affect how reliably an agent can interact with the application. 

 What's next 

 The next steps would be to expand the agent-native interface with capabilities such as: 

 
 listing and searching previously created links 
 safely deleting or disabling short links 
 richer aggregate analytics 
 expiration dates 
 QR code generation 
 authenticated link management 
 

 The important part is that these features can continue using the same architecture: normal web functionality for humans, structured WebMCP capabilities for agents. 

 Go Link Shortener remains a simple web application. 

 It just no longer assumes that every visitor using it has fingers.

title: LineLab — Rehearse the Rush
pitch: LineLab lets event organisers rehearse crowd flow before doors open. A WebMCP agent tests safe fixes, compares outcomes, and waits for human approval before any plan is committed.
about_excerpt:
LineLab lets event organisers rehearse crowd flow before doors open. A WebMCP agent tests safe fixes, compares outcomes, and waits for human approval before any plan is committed.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 LineLab — Rehearse the Rush 

 LineLab helps event organisers rehearse a crowd rush before real guests arrive. 

 An organiser enters simple event facts such as guest count, doors, security staff, registration desks, pre-registration rate, backstage crew, and programme timing. LineLab then models the flow from gate to hall, identifies where people will get stuck, and lets an AI agent safely test possible repairs. 

 The important part: the agent can prepare, compare, and stress-test a plan, but it cannot make the final change. The organiser must visibly review and approve it. 

 The problem 

 A concert, college fest, or conference can become chaotic when too many people arrive at once. Registration may be slow, a QR scanner may fail, security may be understaffed, or the stage may not be ready when doors open. 

 Usually, organisers find out about these problems only when the real crowd is already waiting. 

 LineLab lets them ask: “What happens if this goes wrong?” before the event starts. 

 How it works 

 
 Enter a fictional event scenario. 
 Run a baseline rehearsal to see the current average wait, maximum queue, and bottleneck. 
 Ask the agent to create several safe draft repairs. 
 Compare the before and after results in plain language. 
 Stress-test the chosen plan against a disruption, such as a QR scanner failure or an arrival surge. 
 The organiser approves the final plan themselves. 
 

 For example, LineLab may show that Registration is the bottleneck because guests arrive faster than the team can check them in. It can then test a QR express line, arrival windows, a manual help desk, an extra entrance, or staff reassignment — and explain the trade-offs. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 A normal chatbot can suggest “add more staff” without understanding the actual event state. 

 LineLab exposes structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , so a WebMCP-enabled agent can work with the real scenario inside the product instead of guessing where buttons are on the screen. 

 The agent can: 

 
 inspect the event flow and limits; 
 configure a fictional scenario; 
 run the baseline rehearsal; 
 create a draft repair; 
 compare outcomes; 
 stress-test a disruption; 
 commit a plan only after visible human approval. 
 

 This makes the agent useful, testable, and accountable. The organiser stays in control. 

 How we built it 

 LineLab is a Next.js and TypeScript web application with an interactive event-flow model. The model uses fictional data only; it does not use personal data, contact real venues, or make bookings. 

 We built the interface around plain-language explanations because an event organiser should not need to understand queueing theory to understand a problem. Instead of only showing numbers, LineLab explains what each result means, why a bottleneck occurs, and what would change in a proposed repair. 

 Challenges and what we learned 

 The biggest challenge was avoiding a fake “AI demo.” We wanted the product to do more than display a static answer. Each repair is calculated from the current scenario and must respect practical guardrails such as volunteer limits, doors, security, registration capacity, and pre-registration. 

 We also learned that human approval is not a small detail. The best agent experience is not an agent that silently changes everything; it is an agent that shows its reasoning, makes the trade-offs clear, tests failure cases, and lets a person make the final call. 

 What’s next 

 Future versions could support richer venue layouts, staff shift planning, accessible routes, live check-in signals, and post-event learning — while keeping organisers in control of every real-world decision.

title: Release Sentinel — WebMCP Proof Arena
pitch: Give AI agents real power without giving them the final word. Release Sentinel lets agents act through WebMCP while a deterministic Gatekeeper retains release authority.
about_excerpt: Give AI agents real power without giving them the final word. Release Sentinel lets agents act through WebMCP while a deterministic Gatekeeper retains release authority. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP solves an important problem for agentic websites: instead of forcing an AI agent to guess at a page's DOM, a site can expose explicit, typed tools. But that creates a second question: How do you give an AI agent enough power to be genuinely useful without also giving it the authority to approve its own actions? For consequential systems, that distinction matters. An agent may need to investigate, challenge, repair, or prepare an action — while approval must remain somewhere else. Release Sentinel explores that boundary using software release approval as a concrete test case. Our principle is simple: agent acts → Gatekeeper decides → human verifies What it does Release Sentinel is a WebMCP-powered security lab for AI-assisted software releases. A vulnerable software release begins at NO_GO . The AI agent receives useful capabilities through WebMCP. It can inspect the release, inspect the trust boundary, run bounded attacks, compare gate revisions, find and minimize counterexamples, propose remediation, rebuild a candidate, and request fresh verification. What it cannot do is authorize the release. The demo first lets the agent try the available attacks against the authority boundary. Advisory GO votes, replay attempts, forged authority, evidence tampering, severity downgrades, blocker deletion attempts, and prompt injection still do not give the agent release authority. So the agent has to solve the real problem instead. It compares the production gate against an independent Coverage Arena reference oracle, identifies an observed security escape, minimizes it, and creates a bounded remediation proposal. That proposal is explicitly PROPOSAL_ONLY . The candidate is then rebuilt to a new SHA-256, fresh evidence is generated, and the deterministic Gatekeeper performs verification again. Only the Gatekeeper can return the final GO or NO_GO . A human can independently verify the resulting proof context, but human verification is not release authority either. How we built it The browser registers exactly 12 typed WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . They are divided into three capability classes: READ — inspect release state, trust boundaries, coverage, and proofs CHALLENGE — run attacks and find counterexamples PROPOSE — request bounded remediation and rebuilding There is intentionally no set_verdict , force_go , arbitrary shell execution, arbitrary filesystem access, evidence editor, policy-disable tool, or Gatekeeper override. That absence is tested as part of the security contract. Inputs use strict schemas with bounded enums and forbidden extra fields. The agent selects package-owned identities rather than supplying arbitrary source code, fixture paths, or executable content. We also built run_attack_suite as browser-side composition instead of adding a more powerful server endpoint. It reads the bounded attack catalog and invokes the same registered attack capability repeatedly. The browser gets better ergonomics without expanding server authority. The release decision itself remains in a separate deterministic Go Gatekeeper using signed, hash-bound evidence. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making the security model understandable. An earlier version of the Proof Arena was technically accurate but difficult to read. A judge would encounter concepts such as proof-context binding, overblocks, and PROPOSAL_ONLY before understanding the story. We added a guided demo and plain-language narration without weakening the security model. Another challenge was resisting convenient shortcuts. For example, implementing the attack suite as one powerful server endpoint would have been easy. Instead, we kept the server surface narrow and composed the workflow in the browser over the existing bounded tools. That required more work, but better demonstrates the architectural value of WebMCP. Accomplishments that we're proud of The final system demonstrates a useful agent that remains structurally unable to authorize its own success. The agent can attack the release gate, identify a real weakness, propose a fix, rebuild the software, and request verification — yet final authority remains outside the WebMCP capability plane. The project also includes: 12 typed WebMCP tools strict bounded schemas agent-readable recovery errors browser-side capability composition an independent Coverage Arena a deterministic Go Gatekeeper signed and hash-bound evidence source-hash transition visibility a Human Proof Checkpoint frozen trust and coverage kernel manifests Python, Go race, browser, and WebMCP contract verification What we learned WebMCP is not only about making browser agents more capable. The more important architectural question is which capabilities should never become authority . Typed tools make agent interaction clearer, but tool design also defines the security boundary. The capabilities that are deliberately absent can be just as important as the capabilities that are exposed. We also learned that browser-side composition is a powerful WebMCP pattern: useful agent workflows can become more ergonomic without automatically creating broader server privileges. What's next Release approval is our test case, but the pattern is broader. Any consequential website may need agents that can act without being allowed to authorize — for example administrative systems, payments, infrastructure, or other sensitive workflows. The next step would be turning this pattern into a reusable primitive: capability classes plus a verifiable assertion that final authority is not reachable from the WebMCP capability plane. title: Generative Learning
pitch: Generate the learning. Not the canvas. A professional learning surface for AI tutors to personalize the lesson, pace, and guidance for each learner - step by step, on a shared interactive canvas.
about_excerpt: Generate the learning. Not the canvas. A professional learning surface for AI tutors to personalize the lesson, pace, and guidance for each learner - step by step, on a shared interactive canvas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates GIF Chess Generative Learning GIF Triangles Generative Learning Chess Learning Professional Canvas Triangles Learning Professional Canvas Inspiration In 2021, I filed a patent for a web interaction layer where websites declare supported actions so external agents (bots) can interact with them without relying on the visual UI. At the time, I was focused on automation where the browser could effectively stay in the background . The agent could perform actions without the user needing to watch every step. WebMCP made me revisit the same idea from the opposite direction: What happens when the visual interface is not something to bypass, but something the human and AI need to share? Many web tasks can happen while the page is hidden or barely looked at - purchasing, form filling, data entry, even some document operations. But visual learning is different. You cannot meaningfully learn chess, manipulate a triangle, inspect a circuit, or reason about spatial relationships while the learning surface is hidden. The learner needs to see it, act on it, and understand what changes. So I specifically looked for learning domains where the visible interface is essential to the task itself . AI can generate great explanations, diagrams, and canvases - but learning often needs a professional environment that stays in place . That led me to ask: What if AI generated the lesson, not the learning surface? I built persistent, domain-specific learning surfaces where the learner and AI tutor can see, act, and continue together. What it does The learner chooses what to learn and how to learn it . The AI teaches inside the existing surface: demonstrating, annotating, asking questions, reacting to learner actions, and guiding the lesson step by step. Chess and an interactive triangle-learning surface are two working examples of the same pattern. Build the learning surface once. Personalize the lesson endlessly. How I built it Each surface exposes structured WebMCP tools for generating lessons, updating the learning state, and acting on the environment. Chess and triangle learning expose different domain actions, but use the same collaboration loop: generate a lesson, demo, or quiz → read state → demonstrate → learner acts → read change → continue The agent works through explicit tools instead of scraping or rebuilding the UI. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was the missing reverse communication path from the learning surface back to the chat . A tutor might ask: “What move would you play to checkmate in one move?” The learner should make the move directly on the board, and the surface should report that action back to the agent so the lesson can continue naturally. Today, that loop is incomplete. The AI cannot truly wait for a learner action and automatically resume when the surface reports it. For the prototype, I generate a prompt describing the learner’s action and ask the user to send it back to chat manually. What’s missing is a native: AI asks → learner acts → surface reports → AI continues That bidirectional communication would make the tutoring flow much more natural. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I built two different learning domains - chess and triangle learning - using the same WebMCP pattern. More importantly, the AI is not just automating an interface. It is teaching through it , while the learner works on the same live state. That turns WebMCP from an automation layer into a collaboration layer. What I learned The biggest lesson was: Generative learning does not require a generative interface. A stable, professional surface can actually give AI more useful freedom, because it provides reliable tools, shared state, and meaningful learner actions. I also learned that truly interactive tutoring needs more than tool calls. It needs bidirectional agent-surface communication so the learner can act directly in the environment and the AI can continue from that action. What's next for Generative Learning Chess and triangle learning prove the pattern. The same idea could apply anywhere learning needs a shared interactive environment - circuits, chemistry, maps, music, and more. These are examples of the broader pattern, not announced products. Longer term, the same surfaces could also support teacher-defined learning goals and measurable outcomes while preserving a fully personalized learning path. title: Agent Arena — Games That Any Agent Can Play
pitch: WebMCP turns an AI agent from an adviser into a real player in a shared game—invited, permissioned, and synchronized with people.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns an AI agent from an adviser into a real player in a shared game—invited, permissioned, and synchronized with people. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Agent Arena — Games That Any Agent Can Play From AI advice to AI participation Most “AI games” connect one model API to a server. Agent Arena explores a more open pattern: a human can invite a compatible agent into a shared browser experience, where it participates under the same rules and state as everyone else. Mini Chess is the first reference game. A person can play against an agent, or invite two independent agents—one for White and one for Black—to play each other while people watch the same live board. What it does Each private invitation grants exactly one role-scoped player seat. The agent uses page-defined WebMCP tools to read the frozen rules, join, inspect shared state, wait for its turn, and submit a move. The server remains authoritative for invitations, identities, permissions, legal moves, turn order, revisions, and results. The visible board and the agent tools operate on one live session. The game is deliberately small so the interaction model is easy to see: humans invite agents, agents identify themselves and act only when permitted, and every move is validated before the shared state changes. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the page offer a small semantic action model instead of requiring an agent to infer a game from pixels or requiring the game to integrate a particular model vendor. The same invitation, identity, turn-taking, permission, synchronization, and action pattern can extend to other games and collaborative experiences. How it was built The private controller registers five tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Their schemas reject unknown properties; read operations are marked read-only. Tool execution and the human interface call the same Express API and SQLite-backed session state. The project uses one-time invitation capabilities, post-join player tokens, rule and revision guards, idempotent action IDs, and a legal-move engine. It is an independent, open-source MIT repository: the live demo is linked from a project gallery, but the application has no dependency on the personal website.
