title: Dabble Me: a simple, private journal that helps you write.
pitch: A journal built for people and their agents: WebMCP tools search, open, and draft journal entries in your signed-in session. Work with the agent to write your entry and submit it together.
about_excerpt: A journal built for people and their agents: WebMCP tools search, open, and draft journal entries in your signed-in session. Work with the agent to write your entry and submit it together. Like Comment Story Updates Drafting a new journal entry for the day. Utilizing the search function. Inspiration I built Dabble Me in 2014 after OhLife shut down . I had been a near-daily user for three years. The trick was that the medium was email: a prompt arrived in my inbox, I replied, and the habit stuck. No extra app or thumbs-only typing. No notification fatigue. It was designed precisely for my sick desire to constantly need Inbox Zero. Dogfooding this app has become my sacred space now: the first dates with my now wife, photos and how I felt seeing my boys grow up, and the personal growth I would've otherwise missed had I not read how far I've come. The daily email bring these private days back to me, the way Timehop does for public posts. What it does Dabble Me is a live, private journal. You can still write by replying to email. PRO users can also search, reflect, and draft in the browser. With WebMCP enabled , a signed-in tab registers structured tools: search_journal_entries / list_journal_entries / analyze_journal — read this session’s journal only open_journal_day / open_search_page / open_write_page — move the UI so the person sees the same screen draft_journal_entry — fill the write form and highlight it get_journal_session — tell the agent whether the tab is signed in and whether PRO tools are available Signup, login, search, and write forms also use declarative toolname / tooldescription attributes so an agent can fill fields without guessing labels. A status banner on the page makes the agent’s action visible. How we built it The product was already a Rails app with a remote, OAuth MCP server at /mcp . WebMCP is a different layer: tools run in the page, with the user’s cookie session, not a headless API token. Discovery so a client that only has https://dabble.me can find the surface: /.well-known/webmcp , /mcp/server-card , /.well-known/ai-catalog.json , plus Link headers and /llms.txt Session JSON at /webmcp/journal/* that reuses the same search/list/analyze logic as remote MCP, always scoped to current_user public/webmcp.js that feature-detects document.modelContext (and the older navigator.modelContext ), registers tools for the current auth state, fills Summernote on draft, and navigates for “open this day” Declarative forms for account and journal UI, without toolautosubmit Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was privacy vs. demo-ability. Journal apps cannot run anonymously. They also cannot require WebAuthn if we want an in-app browser to finish login. The compromise: session cookies, PRO for write/search, and a dedicated demo account...not a real diary. The second was editors. The write box is Summernote, not a plain <textarea> . A declarative form fill would look done and still leave the rich editor empty. draft_journal_entry has to talk to the editor, then leave Create Entry for the human. Accomplishments that we're proud of This is not a toy journal. Dabble Me has been a real, private, email-first product since the OhLife shutdown in 2014. The agent and the user share one interface. When the agent searches or drafts, the page shows it. Writes are cooperative by construction: fill and highlight so the draft is reviewed by a human before submitting ai-only entries. We kept two complementary layers honest: remote MCP for ChatGPT/Claude connectors, WebMCP for the live tab. What we learned WebMCP is not “MCP in a JSON file.” It is a browser API for this document, this session, this user . Discovery helps agents find you. registerTool + execute is what they actually call. We also learned that the best tool for a journal is often the one that refuses to finish. Submission should be human-reviewed...a feature, not a bug. 😁 What's next for Dabble Me More page-state tools: jump to a hashtag, open last year on this day, draft into an existing date the way email replies already append Tighter visual feedback when a tool is running ( toolchange , :tool-form-active ) A first-class “agent draft” review state so a filled form is obvious even after a refresh Keep the remote MCP server for headless clients, and keep WebMCP for the tab where the human is sitting Built With javascript ruby-on-rails Try it out dabble.me Created by Paul Arterburn Like Share this project: Updates Paul Arterburn started this project — Aug 25, 2026 07:32 PM EDT

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. title: NodeCraft
pitch: A shared architecture canvas where humans and AI agents build together. WebMCP lets agents inspect live app state and create, connect, arrange, and review the same workspace humans edit.
about_excerpt: A shared architecture canvas where humans and AI agents build together. WebMCP lets agents inspect live app state and create, connect, arrange, and review the same workspace humans edit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI assistants are getting much better, but I kept noticing the same gap. Most of the time I am still talking to an AI about the application I am using instead of letting the AI actually work with me inside it. I wanted to explore a simple question: what if I and an AI agent could work on the same live application state? I chose architecture diagrams because they make this easy to see. I can move a component myself, ask the agent to continue working, and the agent should be able to understand what is on the canvas now instead of starting from a separate representation. That idea became NodeCraft. What it does NodeCraft is an architecture canvas where a human and an AI agent can work together. I can create, move, remove, and organize components directly on the canvas. At the same time, NodeCraft exposes capabilities through WebMCP that a compatible AI agent can discover and use. The agent can inspect the canvas, create components, connect or disconnect them, arrange the architecture, remove components, and flag something for design review. The key part is that there is no separate AI version of the diagram. My actions and the agent's actions update the same application state. For example, I can ask an agent to add an API service, Postgres database, Redis cache, and payment service. The agent can discover NodeCraft's WebMCP tools and create those components directly on the live canvas. I can then manually change the canvas and the agent can work from the updated state. I also added undo and redo, local persistence, editable human and agent names, an activity feed showing who did what, JSON import and export, and a simple way to start a new canvas. How I built it I built NodeCraft with React and HTML5 Canvas. The application registers seven WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_canvas_state create_canvas_node connect_nodes auto_layout_nodes remove_node disconnect_nodes flag_for_review I tried to make the tools describe useful actions rather than low level UI operations. An agent should be able to ask NodeCraft to connect two components. It should not need to know how I draw the connection on the canvas. The tools that modify the canvas update the same React state used by the normal human interface. get_canvas_state gives the agent a structured view of the nodes and connections that currently exist, and I marked it as read only. This is really the core of NodeCraft. I can make a change manually, the agent can inspect the current canvas, make its own changes through WebMCP, and I can continue working from there. I also added cleanup for registered tools, duplicate connection protection, human and agent action tracking, undo and redo, local browser persistence, and versioned JSON import and export. I experimented with WebMCP's cross origin model too. The flag_for_review tool is set up so that it can be selectively exposed to an authorized reviewer origin. WebMCP is important to the project because I did not want to build another chat box connected directly to an LLM. NodeCraft exposes what the application knows how to do, and a compatible agent can discover those capabilities and use them. The agent and the application do not have to be designed as one tightly coupled system. Challenges I ran into One of the first challenges was deciding what the agent should actually be able to do. I could have exposed low level actions that imitate how a human uses the interface, but that did not feel useful. If the user wants the API connected to Postgres, the agent should express that intent and NodeCraft should handle the visual details. Shared state was another challenge. I wanted agent actions to affect exactly the same state as my manual actions. I did not want to maintain a second representation of the architecture just for AI. There were also a lot of smaller problems that showed up while building: preventing duplicate directed connections, removing connections when a node is deleted, making sure WebMCP handlers have the latest React state, tracking whether an action came from the human or agent, safely importing project files, and cleaning up registered tools correctly. Testing was interesting too. At first I could manually execute individual WebMCP tools, which proved the tools worked, but that was not the experience I was trying to build. I then tested NodeCraft using the Chrome Model Context Tool Inspector with an actual agent. I gave it a natural language request to build part of an ecommerce architecture. The agent discovered the tools exposed by the page and created an API Service, Postgres Database, Redis Cache, and Payment Service directly on the canvas. That was the moment the idea became much more real to me. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am most proud that NodeCraft got beyond simply registering a WebMCP tool and showing that it could be called. Seeing an agent discover the tools from the page and create components on the same canvas I was editing manually was the main thing I wanted to prove with this project. I am also happy with the state reading side of it. get_canvas_state means the agent has a way to understand what currently exists instead of only having actions it can execute. I spent time on the rest of the application as well because I did not want the result to feel like only a tool calling demo. The canvas survives a refresh, actions can be undone, human and agent activity is visible, projects can be downloaded and imported again, and a new canvas can be started without manually clearing browser storage. For a hackathon project, I feel like I ended up with both a WebMCP experiment and something that feels like an actual small product. What I learned My biggest learning was that designing tools for an agent is different from adding AI to an existing interface. The agent does not need the same interface that I need as a human. I care about dragging boxes and seeing connections on a canvas. The agent needs capabilities such as create_canvas_node , connect_nodes , and get_canvas_state . I also underestimated how important reading state would be. Giving an agent actions is useful, but giving it a way to understand what the human has already done makes the collaboration much more interesting. It means the agent can continue from the current application instead of treating every request like a new task. I started the project thinking mostly about WebMCP tool calls. By the end, I was thinking about WebMCP more as an agent facing interface to the application itself. That is probably the biggest thing I will take away from this project. What's next for NodeCraft There is a lot I could take further. For NodeCraft, I would like to explore richer architecture semantics, multiple saved projects, cloud collaboration, architecture validation, and agents that can reason about architectural constraints rather than only manipulate the diagram. I also think the idea applies beyond architecture diagrams. Workflow builders, visual editors, planning tools, dashboards, and other applications already have structured state and actions that humans interact with through a UI. WebMCP creates an interesting opportunity to expose those capabilities to agents as well. NodeCraft is my first experiment with that idea, and I would like to keep exploring what applications look like when humans and AI agents can work inside the same product together. title: Dish Decider
pitch: Everyone’s AI has a seat at the table. DishDecider lets agents coordinate on one shared plan, catch conflicts, and make smarter choices together—with WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Everyone’s AI has a seat at the table. DishDecider lets agents coordinate on one shared plan, catch conflicts, and make smarter choices together—with WebMCP.

 Architectural Diagram 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every group event has the same failure mode: five people bring chips, nobody brings a main course, and somebody blows the budget — and nobody notices until it is already awkward to fix. That is not really a communication problem; it is a coordination problem . Group chats and shared spreadsheets still rely on someone manually cross-checking everyone's plans. 

 WebMCP made us wonder: what if every participant's own AI agent could act on the same live shared plan instead of every assistant working in isolation? Agents could understand what each person wants, see what has already been claimed, and catch conflicts before they are committed. That is the idea behind DishDecider. 

 What it does 

 DishDecider is a shared event planner. One person creates an event with a budget cap; anyone with the link can join with just a name and dietary restrictions — no account required. 

 Participants can claim dishes manually or simply tell their agent what they want in natural language, such as "I'm broke this week" or "I want to impress but only have 20 minutes." The agent turns that request into structured constraints and recommends a specific dish. 

 The core feature is shared-state conflict resolution . If a proposed dish duplicates an existing choice, violates a participant's dietary restriction, or pushes the group over budget, the system detects the conflict, explains why in plain language, and suggests an alternative. Every action is visible in the shared event and recorded in an activity log. After the event, a recap shows computed metrics such as total spending, conflicts resolved, and suggestion acceptance rate. 

 How we built it 

 We built four WebMCP tools, registered through document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 interpret_intent — converts open-ended requests into structured constraints 
 suggest_item — recommends an item using those constraints and the current event state 
 resolve_conflict — validates a proposal against live shared state and identifies conflicts 
 explain_tradeoff — compares valid alternatives and explains the reasoning 
 

 All four route through a consolidated reasoning endpoint backed by an LLM, with Zod-validated structured output and a deterministic fallback so the application remains functional if a model call fails. 

 Event state is stored in Supabase , with realtime subscriptions so every participant sees updates without refreshing. The application is deployed on Vercel . 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our biggest challenge was proving that WebMCP itself actually worked . It is easy to write registerTool calls and assume they are working; it is much harder to verify that a browser-native agent can actually discover them. 

 We tested this directly in Chrome Canary with WebMCP enabled. document.modelContext returned a live ModelContext object, and document.modelContext.getTools() resolved with all four tools and their definitions. That was the point where the project went from "this should work" to "we can prove it works." 

 We also hit a frustrating deployment issue when our LLM provider deprecated the model we were using. The actual fix was small, but a stale deployment initially kept serving old code, making the problem much harder to diagnose. It taught us to verify the actual deployed commit and runtime behavior , rather than assuming a successful push means the newest code is live. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that DishDecider is not just a UI calling an AI API — it is a genuinely agent-native page with a browser-discoverable WebMCP tool registry . 

 We also got real multi-participant conflict resolution working across separate sessions: two participants, two agents, one shared event, and a genuine conflict detected and resolved with a specific explanation. The result is visible to both participants in real time rather than being a scripted demo. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that "does it work?" and "did we verify it works?" are very different questions. With an experimental standard like WebMCP, assumptions can easily look correct until you test the actual browser behavior. 

 We also learned that building an agentic application is not just about getting an LLM to produce a good answer. The interesting engineering problem is connecting that reasoning to structured tools, shared state, validation, and observable actions . 

 What's next for DishDecider 

 The underlying pattern is not specific to potlucks. Multiple people independently contributing to a shared, constraint-aware plan could also apply to roommate expense management, group trip planning, or gift coordination . 

 Longer term, we would like to test DishDecider with a real external WebMCP-aware agent completing the workflow through natural conversation. That would take the project from proving that our tools are technically discoverable to proving the full agent → tool → shared state → resolution loop end-to-end with an independent agent.

title: voice-web-mcp
pitch: Use a full duplex/speech to speech voice agent CLI to control websites via webMCP + naturally learning languages with accents/tones with Anki cards.
about_excerpt: Use a full duplex/speech to speech voice agent CLI to control websites via webMCP + naturally learning languages with accents/tones with Anki cards. Like Comment Story Updates anime-photo Home page Inspiration Customers sometimes need to access tools/websites, but they can’t do it because websites are hard. The websites have bad UX, the customers are older and non technical, or don't speak English. What it does Parts I built two things: A basic webMCP controllable anki website for language learning. A (realtime duplex speech to speech) voice harness CLI that supports WebMCP. Codex voice mode doesn't let you talk to websites, this thing does. Examples Anyways, here's me screwing around with a bunch of people's websites they built (besides the example video): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLPP6FwJZGwUA taboo game - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rqPqUa1mNcA rubiks cube https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fIQoW5sJ65g more of my own anki - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a86MogHEFQA maze solver - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MVpu7fn3kqQ More technical details The website is straightforward, lets you import real Anki apkg files, and have it run on chrome. The agent harness in a similar way to claude code but its streaming speech to speech. It can control your files, your website, chrome tabs/cast controls, etc. Voice wise it supports parsing like Barge in, accents, accoustic event cancellation, noise cancellation, high pass/gain controls, etc. reference codes https://portpowered.github.io/anki-web-mcp/ is the website. https://github.com/portpowered/go-agent-harness is the CLI. Note that you have to have spent like $50+ dollars on OpenAI APIs to get any real usage out of the voice CLI, otherwise you're going to get rate limited, so probably constrained to the webMCP website otherwise. But anyways, it should be able to access whatever website you want. The AI is kind of dumb though. It works on the various webMCP showcases. Recordings: IRL recording: https://youtu.be/G_SsdL5Yqj8 Screen recording: https://youtu.be/811ooWpI0Zw How we built it We built it largely using 1) Codex/Claude 2) An agent factory/orchestrator that wraps luna max/codex workers. I had a Claude agent manage the factory as appropriate. 3) OpenAI realtime API 4) Golang 5) NextJS based static site on github pages. Challenges we ran into The UX of interacting with the MCP is highly fragile. You need to have to have a very strongly defined AGENTS.md and there is no current obvious way to declare WebMCP AGENTs.md/Instructions for each website. Tools that are available on different pages are different, and controlling them is hard for declaring the appropriate context on different pages. audio processing graphs are really actually quite complicated (barge in, accoustic event cancellation, umm/sigh, tool processing), this ended up being a significant time sink since current models aren't able to comprehend audio failures directly (except for like gemini). I don't really understand all the audio tools so was hard to build. Chrome is super flaky for casting and open/close with session controls. Accomplishments that we're proud of its actually really cool to get the agent to just fix the site using your voice. I only recorded it for a second, but I was using it to learn japanese for a few hours since I usually run on my phone. It helps a lot with like coming with phrases and accent help. Helps a lot with korean and chinese as well, since my accent is bad, and I don't understand tones. ~90% of the code was implemented via luna max workers and fixed and dispatched by them. I mostly just left it to run on my laptop at about 50 agents or so. The digital signals processing is more work than I imagined and I was able to figure it out and understand. Understanding accoustic event cancellation, barge in, noise cancellation. Independent of the webMCP functions, the fact that there's now like a generic Anki page that customers can load their deck into is super useful, because installing an app is annoying. What we learned webMCP is super useful actually, i'm probably going to tamper monkey a bunch of websites so that I can just buy stuff off doordash. Audio data signals processing, like how to make the voice robots not echo itself and re-trigger, how to set up the noise clearing, how to set up VAD, etc. Realtime models are much more useful than I anticipated, but they're still kind of flaky. What's next for voice-web-mcp better multi tab handling if you have multiple browser tabs running and you want the agents to focus on a specific one or move between tabs generally. better multimodality input/output is needed for things that can watch/hear/read. better streaming is needed for things that happen over time better connections to payments and authorization is needed for delegated permissions better AGENTS.md/instruction declaration. title: Bankgraph
pitch: Bankgraph lets people and ChatGPT investigate a bank, the U.S. banking system, and the economy on the same live, editable research board.
about_excerpt: Bankgraph lets people and ChatGPT investigate a bank, the U.S. banking system, and the economy on the same live, editable research board. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Bankgraph turns a question about a bank, the banking system, or the economy into a live research board that ChatGPT can build with you. Compare the years before past failures with the reported paths of active banks today. Move from one bank to the banking system and the economy without rebuilding the data first. Start with the condition you care about, even when you do not know which bank to search for. Put bank behavior and economic context on the same working surface without flattening their different time bases. Trace what changed inside a bank, then see where it sits among comparable institutions. ChatGPT reads the exact data behind each view and continues from the board you change by hand. About the project A research surface for open data Bankgraph is my take on a Bloomberg-style research surface for public U.S. banking and economic data. Ask about an institution, the banking system, or the economy, and the work takes shape on a live board that you and ChatGPT can explore together. The data already exists. Every U.S. bank files a detailed quarterly record, while rates, credit, inflation, employment, and banking-system series are published by public agencies. Using that record is harder than finding it. A question such as “Is this bank an outlier?”, “Was deposit growth broad or concentrated?”, or “What tended to change before banks failed?” can still require regulator APIs, quarterly archives, matched institution histories, and series that run on different calendars. Bankgraph does that groundwork once. It brings FDIC institution records and financial filings together with official data from the U.S. Treasury, Bureau of Labor Statistics, and Federal Reserve Board. The reporting period, unit, definition, cohort, source, and coverage remain attached to the analysis. From one bank to the economy You can start with a familiar institution, compare it with a sensible peer group, and zoom out to the banking system. You can then place that behavior beside interest rates, credit, deposits, inflation, and employment. Or you can start without a bank name: describe a financial condition, screen the full population, and let the data determine which institutions belong on the board. The board combines histories, exact tables, peer distributions, reported component changes, metric relationships, headquarters maps, economic context, and written takeaways. Its views share the same banks, measures, periods, and cohort, so a change made in one place carries through the analysis. The same surface can help an analyst compare peers, a reporter test whether a headline trend is widespread, a researcher investigate the years before past bank failures, or someone simply understand what is happening at a familiar bank and in the economy around it. ChatGPT works with you on the screen Through WebMCP, ChatGPT operates Bankgraph directly. It can search institutions, define or revise a cohort, screen banks by financial measures, run multi-period and historical analyses, and arrange the results as charts, tables, maps, comparisons, and short takeaways on the site. The workflow can begin with named banks or with an open-ended question. ChatGPT can compare JPMorgan Chase with its peers, add more banks on request, switch the interface to dark mode, and read the figures behind the updated board. It can also start from a condition such as a high loan-to-deposit ratio, find the relevant banks first, and build the comparison from those results. The result remains a working Bankgraph board. You can change a bank, measure, period, chart treatment, or layout by hand, while ChatGPT reads and changes the same on-screen workspace. Each view provides structured data with reporting dates, definitions, units, cohort context, pagination, and source metadata, so ChatGPT can answer from the underlying values without interpreting a screenshot. How it works Bankgraph uses one workspace model for the visible interface and its WebMCP tools. Human and agent actions therefore operate on the same state and the same analytical vocabulary: institutions, measures, periods, cohorts, and views. The analytical results are deterministic. Change attribution uses reported components and explicit formulas, cohort analysis reports its usable population, and historical series preserve missing values. This keeps quick answers tied to inspectable data while still allowing the board to change freely. The application is built with SvelteKit, Svelte 5, TypeScript, and ECharts on Cloudflare Workers. D1, KV, and R2 support the application and its public-data pipeline. What was difficult, and what I learned The hardest part was making one workspace predictable while a person and an agent could both change it. Every analytical choice needed a visible meaning, every view needed a stable identity, and each agent action had to continue from the board as it stood. Time was the other challenge. A quarterly balance, a year-to-date income field, a reported ratio, and a weekly banking-system series are different kinds of observations. Bankgraph carries their time basis, units, transformations, coverage, and source definitions through ingestion, analysis, display, and export instead of flattening them into one misleading timeline. I also learned that useful WebMCP tools need to express analytical intent rather than mirror individual buttons. The tools can ask Bankgraph to construct a cohort, compare a set of institutions, or publish a result as an appropriate view. The visible interface still provides the controls needed to inspect and revise what the agent produced. What I built during the challenge Bankgraph’s public-data foundation predates the challenge. The product experience shown here—the shared Research board, its visual system, measure-led screens, multi-period and failure-pattern analyses, semantic board composition, structured reads behind every view, and the WebMCP system that connects them—was built during the submission period. Commit b852f9b records the pre-challenge baseline; the public history after it contains the complete extension. Testing instructions for judges Open bankgraph.app in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and keep the site visible beside the conversation. The live application needs no account, provider key, or local setup. Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled also works. Start with: “Compare JPMorgan Chase with Bank of America, Citi, and Wells Fargo.” Once the board appears, say: “Add Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and U.S. Bank. What’s the short version?” Then try a question that begins with the data rather than a bank name: “Start fresh. Which five active banks over $10 billion have the highest loan-to-deposit ratios? Build the comparison here.” Ask ChatGPT to add loan growth or problem loans, change one view by hand, and continue the analysis. The board should reflect both the changes you make and the changes ChatGPT makes through WebMCP. title: Assistant Studio
pitch: A studio where a human and their agent build a customer chatbot together. Publish, share and delete stop at a consent gate enforced outside the model.
about_excerpt: A studio where a human and their agent build a customer chatbot together. Publish, share and delete stop at a consent gate enforced outside the model. Like Comment Story Updates Publish was approved and SPENT. The agent then tried to delete — refused, different fingerprint. Consent does not transfer. The agent asked to publish. Nothing ran. The dialog names the exact action, its fingerprint, and the terms: this action, once, 120s. The studio with four tools registered. Publish, share and delete do not exist yet — there is nothing to act on. A guided flow: teach it, try it, put it live. The reply is composed from the knowledge you gave it, in the tone you chose. Inspiration We published a paper this year about trust in the Model Context Protocol — Whose Stranger Is It? (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20847425). It argues for a deterministic guard: the agent proposes, the policy decides, and the execution happens outside the model. WebMCP sharpened that argument in a way we did not expect. The standard carries two annotations that look like safety metadata — readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint — and both are declared by the page itself , the very party that may be the adversary. There is no signing, no revocation, no audit levels. That is exactly where the paper's assumptions fail in a browser tab. So we stopped writing about the guard and built one. What it does Assistant Studio is where you build the chatbot that answers your customers. You give it a purpose, teach it what it should know, try it the way a customer would, then put it live on a channel. The whole studio works for a person alone, with no agent anywhere. WebMCP is an enhancement on top of a working product, never a precondition for it. When an agent is present it drives the same studio through seven tools. Four run freely. Three — publish, share, delete — are seen by other people or cannot be undone, and those three do not execute on the agent's say-so. Why this use case fits WebMCP. Building an assistant is long, iterative, unglamorous work: write a purpose, paste knowledge, test, notice the tone is wrong, fix, test again. An agent is good at that loop; a person has the taste to judge the result. What makes it the right demo is what happens at the end of the loop: the output gets published to customers, shared with colleagues, or deleted. The collaboration is genuinely useful and the boundary genuinely matters. Most agent demos have one or the other. How it improves the experience. Before: four screens and about ten clicks per assistant. After: one sentence to the agent, and the interface moves in front of you — an assistant appears in the list, knowledge lands in its panel, a test reply comes back. You are not reading a transcript of what an agent claims it did; you are watching your own application change. The agent does not replace the interface, it shares it. At the boundary the experience inverts on purpose. When the agent asks to publish, the studio stops and shows the exact action in plain words — Publish "Cafe Bot" to the whatsapp channel — composed by the application from the arguments, never phrased by the model. The friction is the feature, and it appears at precisely three places out of seven. What is now possible that was not. An agent that builds another agent, with a person watching it happen live rather than reviewing it afterwards, and with a limit that holds regardless of what the model decides. Publish, share and delete cannot occur without a click made at that moment, on that action, with those arguments. One approval never becomes two. An approval for one assistant never moves to another. An approval to publish never becomes a deletion. How we built it Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind v4. State lives in memory: no database, no auth, no API keys in the repository. Test replies are composed deterministically from each assistant's own knowledge and tone, because the subject here is the consent gate, not the wording. The WebMCP implementation. Seven tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , each with a precise JSON Schema and enum constraints wherever the value space is closed, so the model guesses less. Lifecycle. Registration is bound to component lifetime with AbortSignal . State-dependent tools. The three sensitive tools are registered only while at least one assistant exists. They appear on the first create and unregister when the last is deleted, emitting a real toolchange event. A tool with no valid target does not exist. The guard. Every execute is wrapped by guarded() . It reads sensitivity from a build-time manifest — never from the arguments, never from the model — and for sensitive tools it requires a consent bound to the tool name and to SHA-256(tool ‖ NUL ‖ canonical(args)) . Missing consent means the function is never called, and the agent receives a refusal explaining that a dialog is now open and that it cannot grant this itself. The ledger. In memory, single-use, 120-second TTL, no localStorage: yesterday's approval must not be usable today. grant has exactly one call site in the whole repository — the onClick handler in the confirmation dialog. You can verify that with a single grep, and the README tells you how. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP registry is a single global keyed by tool name, which means two concurrent registrations do not compose: the second overwrites the first, and then the first one's teardown unregisters the survivor. React StrictMode's double mount is exactly that race. It presented as tools that registered and then silently vanished. Registration is refcounted per document now. A subtler one: useSyncExternalStore requires a referentially stable server snapshot. An inline () => [] allocates a fresh array every render, and React threw "Maximum update depth exceeded" on first paint. Frozen module-level constants fixed it — and the same hazard was hiding in the consent ledger's entries() , which rebuilt and re-sorted on every read. Accomplishments that we're proud of Eighteen tests, run with pnpm test . Four are the invariants from §7.4 of the paper: a sensitive action without consent is dropped; the same action with matching consent executes; consent for one action does not pass another; a consumed consent does not replay. Ten more assume a hostile model rather than a careless one: twenty hammered calls yield one dialog rather than twenty (flooding a person with modals until one is clicked is itself an attack), reordered argument keys cannot buy a second execution, expiry is checked at the millisecond on both sides, a guessed hash fails without burning a legitimate consent , and sensitivity passed as an argument changes nothing. All four invariants were also verified end-to-end in a real browser against the live domain, not only at the unit level. What we learned Honestly, and this matters more than anything else in this submission: it does not solve prompt injection , and the paper it comes from says so explicitly. A compromised model still chooses which action to propose and how persuasively to propose it. The guarantee is deliberately narrower and worth stating exactly: a sensitive action never happens silently, and consent is contemporaneous, single-use, and non-transferable. The guarantee holds outside the model, which is the only place it can hold. We also learned that the interesting failures are not in the cryptography. They are in the plumbing — a global registry that silently drops registrations, a render loop that eats the answer you just asked for. The gate was the easy part. What's next for Assistant Studio Where the standard's page-declared annotations fail, and how an agent behaves when it meets a refusal it cannot talk its way past, becomes material for the next version of the paper. The repository stays public and MIT-licensed as a citable reference implementation. Built With next.js react tailwindcss typescript vercel webmcp Try it out studio.jack-ai.net github.com doi.org Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Designed and built the whole project: the consent gate and its test suite, the WebMCP tool layer, the interface, and the submission materials. title: MCP VisionQuote
pitch: MCP-based AI estimator that instantly calculates camera coverage, cable length, BOM, labor, and drafts commercial proposals for video surveillance & structured cabling projects.
about_excerpt:
MCP-based AI estimator that instantly calculates camera coverage, cable length, BOM, labor, and drafts commercial proposals for video surveillance & structured cabling projects.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 After 22 years installing CCTV, access control, and structured cabling, I kept hitting the same wall: turning floor plans and site walkthroughs into reliable, itemized quotes still 
 took hours of manual counting and spreadsheet work. MCP VisionQuote was born from that friction — an AI estimator that combines Model Context Protocol (MCP/WebMCP) with domain 
 knowledge from real-world low-current projects. Every surveillance or cabling quote starts with the same questions: how many cameras, how much cable, which conduits, how many man-hours? Experienced integrators can estimate a site in
 minutes, but clients still wait days for a polished proposal. I wanted to capture that expertise in a tool that reads project context through MCP tools, reasons about layouts and 
 requirements, and returns a quote an installer can trust. 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 MCP VisionQuote exposes domain-specific tools through MCP/WebMCP: estimate_project , get_bom , generate_proposal , and suggest_camera_placement . The backend is Python 3.12 + 
 FastAPI, with a lightweight SQLite store and a seed price catalog. A FastAPI web UI lets users enter site parameters and instantly see a BOM, labor estimate, and commercial proposal. I 
 used YOLOv8-nano for optional photo-based placement suggestions, and Render + Cloudflare Tunnel for the public deployment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was not the code — it was encoding field reality. Camera counts change when a hallway has no ceiling access. Cable lengths explode when plenum routes are blocked. I 
 had to balance AI speed with installer-grade accuracy, so every recommendation includes assumptions that a human can review and override. Trust, not full automation, became the real 
 goal. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 Domain experience is the differentiator. Generic LLMs can write a quote; only a system grounded in low-current installation practice knows why a quote is wrong. MCP proved to be the 
 right glue: it keeps project data separate from reasoning, making the estimator easier to audit, extend, and connect to other tools. 

 What's next for MCP VisionQuote 

 MCP VisionQuote is a practical step toward AI-assisted field estimating — built by someone who has pulled the cable, mounted the cameras, and argued about the labor hours.

 I built MCP VisionQuote end-to-end as a solo developer, from the initial idea and architecture to the Python/FastAPI backend, WebMCP tools, user interface, testing, and deployment. I implemented project estimation, bill of materials generation, proposal creation, and camera placement suggestions.

title: WebOps Commander
pitch: An agent-native incident response command center where AI agents investigate outages through WebMCP, simulate safe fixes, and execute production-changing actions only after explicit human approval.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native incident response command center where AI agents investigate outages through WebMCP, simulate safe fixes, and execute production-changing actions only after explicit human approval.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Modern websites are designed primarily for people. When AI agents need to interact with those applications, they often have to interpret pages visually, reason about buttons and forms, and reproduce workflows that were never designed for machine interaction. 

 WebMCP suggests a different future: websites can expose intentional, structured capabilities directly to AI agents while continuing to provide rich interfaces for humans. 

 That idea inspired WebOps Commander . 

 We wanted to explore a question: 

 
 What would an incident-response application look like if it were designed for humans and AI agents from the beginning? 
 

 Instead of building another chatbot or allowing an agent to blindly click through an operations dashboard, WebOps Commander gives the agent structured operational capabilities through WebMCP while preserving explicit human control over consequential actions. 

 What it does 

 WebOps Commander is an agent-native incident-response command center built around a deterministic simulated production outage. 

 A fictional e-commerce platform experiences a severe checkout incident shortly after a new version of checkout-service is deployed. 

 The human operator sees a visual operations dashboard containing: 

 
 live service health 
 checkout error rate 
 p95 latency 
 order throughput 
 estimated revenue impact 
 service dependencies 
 logs 
 distributed traces 
 deployment history 
 incident status 
 agent activity 
 

 At the same time, a compatible AI agent receives structured WebMCP tools that allow it to investigate the same system directly. 

 The agent can: 

 
 inspect the active incident 
 inspect service health 
 query metrics 
 search logs 
 inspect traces 
 inspect service dependencies 
 inspect recent deployments 
 compare releases 
 search operational runbooks 
 estimate customer impact 
 simulate a rollback 
 request a production-changing action 
 wait for explicit human approval 
 execute an approved rollback 
 observe system recovery 
 update and resolve the incident 
 

 The core workflow is: 

 Observe → Investigate → Correlate → Simulate → Request Approval → Human Approves → Execute → Recover 

 Why WebMCP? 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent interacting with an operations platform may need to determine which page contains deployment information, interpret charts, find buttons, understand forms, and infer what actions are safe to perform. 

 That approach can be brittle. 

 With WebMCP, WebOps Commander intentionally exposes structured capabilities such as: 

 query_service_metrics 

 search_logs 

 search_traces 

 get_recent_deployments 

 compare_deployments 

 simulate_rollback 

 request_rollback 

 execute_approved_action 

 The agent does not need to guess how the user interface works. 

 The website tells the agent what capabilities are available, what inputs they accept, and what actions are permitted. 

 The human interface and agent interface operate on the same application state, so WebMCP actions are immediately visible inside the command center. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 WebOps Commander is intentionally not designed around full autonomy. 

 Investigation is safe for the agent to perform independently. 

 Consequential actions are different. 

 For example, the agent can determine that a rollback is likely to resolve the incident and simulate its expected impact, but it cannot immediately change the simulated production environment. 

 Instead, it creates a pending action: 

 Rollback checkout-service from v2.18.4 to v2.18.3 

 The human sees the proposed action together with: 

 
 the agent's reasoning 
 expected recovery 
 current error rate 
 expected post-rollback error rate 
 estimated risk 
 

 The human can then approve or reject the action. 

 Only an approved action can be executed. 

 This creates a clear separation between: 

 Agent investigation 

 Agent recommendation 

 Human authorization 

 Agent execution 

 Every WebMCP interaction is also recorded in the visible agent activity timeline. 

 The Incident 

 The demonstration focuses on one deliberately small but polished scenario: Checkout Meltdown . 

 A deployment of checkout-service v2.18.4 introduces stricter payment-token issuer validation. 

 Shortly afterward: 

 
 checkout failures increase from approximately 0.6% to 18.4% 
 p95 checkout latency increases from approximately 620 ms to 4.7 seconds 
 completed orders fall by approximately 38% 
 estimated revenue exposure reaches approximately $21.4K per simulated minute 
 

 Other services remain healthy. 

 Through metrics, logs, traces, deployment history, and release comparison, the agent can correlate the incident with v2.18.4 . 

 It can then simulate a rollback to v2.18.3 , request authorization, and—after human approval—execute the remediation. 

 The command center visually shows the system recovering. 

 How we are building it 

 WebOps Commander is intentionally scoped as a focused hackathon demonstration rather than a production observability platform. 

 The application uses a deterministic simulation instead of real cloud infrastructure so that every judge can reproduce the same incident without accounts, API keys, external services, or unreliable dependencies. 

 The planned architecture consists of: 

 
 Next.js 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Tailwind CSS 
 shadcn/ui 
 WebMCP 
 Zod 
 Zustand 
 Recharts 
 Vitest 
 Playwright 
 GitHub Actions 
 

 Operational state, telemetry, logs, traces, deployments, and recovery behavior are simulated locally. 

 WebMCP is the primary agent interface. 

 The project does not require an embedded chatbot or external LLM API—the compatible AI agent interacting with the website is the agent. 

 Challenges 

 The most interesting challenge is not simply exposing functions to an AI agent. 

 It is deciding what an agent should be allowed to do. 

 Read-only investigation tools should be easy to invoke. 

 Simulation should be safe. 

 Production-changing operations should be protected. 

 That led us to design a small capability model with separate categories for: 

 
 read operations 
 simulations 
 approval requests 
 consequential actions 
 

 Another important challenge is making agent activity understandable to the human operator. WebOps Commander therefore visualizes WebMCP invocations in an audit timeline so users can see what the agent inspected, what it concluded, and what it attempted to change. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes the way a web application can be designed. 

 Instead of treating AI agents as external automation systems that must reverse-engineer a user interface, the application can expose a deliberate machine-facing capability layer alongside its human interface. 

 The result is not simply easier automation. 

 It enables a different interaction model: 

 
 Humans provide intent and authority. Agents investigate and execute structured workflows. Websites provide the contract connecting them. 
 

 What's next 

 After the hackathon, WebOps Commander could be expanded to explore: 

 
 multiple incident scenarios 
 richer permission policies 
 tool-level access control 
 real observability integrations 
 real deployment systems 
 multi-agent operational workflows 
 reusable WebMCP patterns for infrastructure products 
 

 For this challenge, however, the focus remains intentionally narrow: 

 one incident, one excellent human-agent workflow, and a clear demonstration of why WebMCP matters. 

 

 
 Built With

title: Conversion Lab
pitch: Make products easier for buying agents to choose. Conversion Lab uses WebMCP to turn verified evidence into tested storefront copy, Shopify update previews and PAUSED OpenAI Ads projections.
about_excerpt: Make products easier for buying agents to choose. Conversion Lab uses WebMCP to turn verified evidence into tested storefront copy, Shopify update previews and PAUSED OpenAI Ads projections. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A product can be right for a shopper and still lose the recommendation. Most commerce pages are written for people, who can infer meaning from photography, brand language and scattered specifications. Buying agents need something more explicit: product facts they can discover, verify and connect to the shopper's actual constraints. That creates a new growth problem for merchants. Optimising the human-facing page is no longer enough. Merchants also need to understand whether an agent can identify the right product, explain why it fits and carry the same approved product truth into organic discovery and paid preparation. Conversion Lab explores that problem as a real merchant workflow. WebMCP supplies the missing interaction layer: the website can expose purpose-built tools to an agent while the merchant and agent work with the same visible page state. The result is more than a chatbot or a generic automation. It is an evidence-led conversion lab for agent-mediated commerce. What it does Conversion Lab begins with a fictional Shopify-style merchant, Fieldwork Supply, and a £159 modular commuter backpack. The generic listing contains too little explicit information for our frozen buyer-intent battery and scores 0/8 . Through ten page-scoped WebMCP tools, an agent can: inspect eight merchant-controlled product and policy facts; audit organic and paid-channel readiness; create an evidence-bound product representation; test it against eight deterministic buyer needs; move the result from 0/8 to 8/8 , with no unsupported claims; stage the exact variant at a visible review checkpoint; publish the approved representation to the demo storefront; prepare a Shopify Admin update preview; generate a locally validated OpenAI product-feed CSV and a PAUSED Ads projection with £0 spend ; export a content-addressed optimisation receipt linking the evidence, evaluation, approval and channel projections; answer a shopper need constraint by constraint and update a bounded shared cart. Approval and reset are deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool surface. The public browser can record a digest-bound demo approval, but the app states clearly that this is not authenticated merchant authority. There is no live Shopify write, Ads upload, campaign activation, checkout or payment path in the public build. How we built it The reference application is built with React 19, TypeScript and Vite and deployed as a credential-free static application on Vercel. The interface contains a merchant growth studio and a shopper view backed by one shared workspace, so WebMCP actions and visible browser state remain consistent. The WebMCP layer registers ten narrowly scoped tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Inputs reject unexpected properties, read-only operations declare their intent, and every result reports what changed, what authority was used and the safest next action. Browsers without WebMCP still receive a useful human interface and an honest fallback message. Under the interface, versioned commerce contracts preserve product identity, evidence provenance, lifecycle state, evaluation results, approval and channel projections. A versioned SHA-256 digest binds the exact product target, commercial snapshot, representation and complete evidence content before publication or export. Inputs are captured as immutable canonical snapshots so caller mutation cannot change an output after verification. The Shopify spine includes a version-pinned Admin GraphQL read adapter, product identity checks and an exact productUpdate preview. The OpenAI Ads spine derives every exported field from the approved product snapshot, validates the product-feed row locally, serialises deterministic CSV and keeps the campaign projection paused. A portable optimisation receipt packages the mutually consistent workflow into content-addressed JSON. We supported the build with unit, contract, infrastructure, adversarial and Playwright browser tests, plus change-aware and complete GitHub Actions gates. Tests cover lifecycle legality, evidence provenance, contradictory shopper constraints, approval substitution, asynchronous mutation, feed-schema boundaries, tool-registration failure and the absence of prohibited external effects. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was preserving useful agent autonomy without quietly widening authority. An agent should be free to inspect, propose, test and explain. It should not be able to turn a readable product ID, a browser click or a provider credential into merchant approval or paid spend. That led us to separate representation approval from future external-effect authorization and to make the demo's current authority limitation visible rather than hiding it behind optimistic language. Product fit created another subtle problem. A keyword match is not a recommendation. A request for a waterproof bag for a 17-inch laptop must not pass because the product is waterproof when the evidence says it fits only a 16-inch device. We changed the shopper evaluator to classify each material constraint as supported, contradicted or unknown and to return an overall match only when every required constraint is supported. Cross-channel consistency was equally demanding. Copy, SKU, price, availability, URLs, brand and evidence all need to belong to the same approved product truth. We moved money to exact GBP minor-unit precision, bound every feed-bearing field to approval and independently recomputed validation results before producing receipts. Finally, WebMCP is not present in every browser environment. We kept the complete merchant workflow usable without it, then ran the deployed application in a WebMCP-enabled ChatGPT browser to verify native discovery of all ten tools and the end-to-end shared-state workflow. Accomplishments that we're proud of A live, repeatable WebMCP product experience rather than a collection of disconnected tool calls. A measurable 0/8 → 8/8 improvement using the same frozen buyer-intent battery and eight verified evidence records. Ten discoverable site tools spanning audit, drafting, evaluation, review, publication, paid preparation, portable proof, shopper fit and cart state. A visible authority boundary: the agent can stage an exact variant but has no approval tool. One digest-bound product truth reused across the demo storefront, Shopify preview, OpenAI Ads projection and optimisation receipt. A deterministic, downloadable CSV and JSON receipt without credentials, activation, spend, checkout or payment. A public Vercel deployment, native ChatGPT WebMCP acceptance run and a comprehensive automated quality gate. We are especially proud that the safety model is part of the product experience. The demo does not merely avoid external effects; it explains which effects are absent, which validations are local and what additional authority a production integration would require. What we learned Agent conversion optimisation is less about generating more persuasive copy and more about organising product truth. The strongest representation is the one whose claims can be traced to current, product-bound evidence and tested against concrete buyer needs. We also learned that WebMCP is most powerful as a collaborative surface. The agent is not operating in a hidden automation layer. It works inside the merchant's live page, over the same evidence, lifecycle and cart state the user can see. Approval, execution and observed outcomes are different claims. Approving a representation does not automatically authorize a Shopify write or an Ads operation. A production system must bind each external effect to the exact channel, destination, payload, limits, budget, expiry and replay policy. Later conversion observations must retain the representation and effect lineage that produced them. Most importantly, Conversion Lab is larger than this website. The website is the first reference host for a reusable optimisation capability. What's next for Conversion Lab The next bounded step is to extract a DOM-free Conversion Lab core and prove that the web application, a TypeScript SDK and a read-only CLI produce equivalent audit, evaluation and receipt-verification results from the same input. From there, we plan to add Shopify OAuth, multi-product ingestion, durable tenant workspaces, authenticated merchant approvals and controlled publication with rollback. OpenAI Ads delivery would follow the same governed model: explicit account authority, feed acceptance, a PAUSED default and separate authorization before activation or spend. The longer-term product is one core delivered through several surfaces: a standalone SaaS workspace, a Shopify embedded app, SDK/API and CLI integrations, MCP/WebMCP adapters and a module for larger age

title: Paper Trail
pitch: Say it once - one sentence about your life event, and every agency, insurer, and employer form gets filled, cross-checked, approved by you, and receipted.
about_excerpt: Say it once - one sentence about your life event, and every agency, insurer, and employer form gets filled, cross-checked, approved by you, and receipted. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every big life event arrives with a hidden invoice: not money, but paperwork . A birth triggers 15–40 separate actions scattered across the Social Security Administration, the health insurer, and the employer's HR portal — each with its own login, its own forms, its own deadlines (add a dependent within 30 days or wait for open enrollment), and its own ways of spelling the same name. Humans have always been the integration glue between these portals: re-typing identical data, making format mistakes, missing windows. When we read the WebMCP spec, one sentence rewired how we think: websites can hand agents structured capabilities instead of forcing them to screenshot pixels. The paperwork layer is the biggest unclaimed prize for that idea — so we built the app we wished existed: say it once, and the whole bundle gets done, with the human still sovereign. What it does Type one sentence — "We had a baby girl on June 3rd at General Hospital." One interview , no forms: the hub derives the facts and materializes an action bundle across three independent portals, with deadline math computed live (DOB June 3 + 30 days → insurer window closes July 3). Each portal owns a tool surface : walking into a page dynamically registers its tools and walking away unregisters them ( AbortController ). The agent only ever sees the tools for the page it's on. Drafts fill from one canonical profile — and a reconciliation engine catches cross-portal conflicts (the hospital's "Okafor-Reyes, Amara" vs. the profile's "Amara Okafor-Reyes"; "Jun 03, 2026" vs. "2026-06-03"), explains them in plain language, and standardizes only on the human's say-so. Nothing files without a human click. Every write tool is a two-call gate: the first call opens an on-page dialog showing every field about to be filed; the second call executes only if the human actually approved — enforced in code, not in a prompt. Replay a confirmation id → unknown_confirmation_id . Let the agent approve itself → human_approval_missing . File twice → already_submitted . Everything ends in a receipt ledger : payload digest → confirmation number → timestamp → human-approval flag. The showpiece : pt_cascade_update . The family moves mid-flow; one call re-derives the whole situation — deadlines recomputed, every pending draft re-filled across all three portals — while filed actions stay untouched, because receipts preserve what was actually submitted. How we built it A zero-dependency, zero-build static SPA — classic scripts, no framework, no backend, deployable anywhere (it even runs from file:// ). mcp.js — the WebMCP layer: registerTool with readOnlyHint annotations, per-portal AbortSignal lifecycles, and a guarded executor (activity-rail logging, ~1.5K output budgets, throws → typed errors agents can self-correct from). portals.js — three fictional portals (SSA, Meridian Health, employer HR) with schemas, strict in-code validation whose errors are written for the agent, the two-call ConfirmGate , and the reconciliation engine. hub.js — the one-sentence interview resolver and the hub tool surface ( pt_start_life_event_interview , pt_get_action_bundle , pt_reconcile_field_conflicts , pt_get_receipt_ledger , pt_cascade_update ). store.js / bundle.js — canonical profile, dependency-aware bundle, deadline math, event-sourced receipts — plus a store subscription so the page the human is watching re-renders live when the agent mutates state through the protocol. 26 tools across 4 surfaces; 13 annotated read-only; 3 gated writes. A /diag.html page probes the runtime (API presence, live registration, getTools() visibility, abort lifecycle) — 11/11 checks pass in Chrome 150 with #enable-webmcp-testing . Challenges we ran into The runtime diverges from the spec text. In the real Chrome build, modelContext.registerTool() returns undefined , not a Promise — our .then() chain silently died at boot. We caught it only by testing against the actual enabled runtime, and now handle both styles. That bug alone justified building a diagnostics page. Tool identity is page-scoped. Re-entering a portal risks a synchronous Duplicate tool name throw; abort-then-re-register had to be proven clean (it is — verified via getTools() ). The "shared live app" requirement is real work. When the agent conducts the interview through the protocol, the human's screen must react — we wired store-driven re-rendering so the bundle materializes on screen as the tool call lands. Timezones and dates. "Jun 03, 2026" vs. "2026-06-03" needed part-wise date comparison, not toISOString() gymnastics that silently shift days across UTC offsets. Making the gate genuinely binding. The tempting shortcut is a confirm dialog the agent can talk its way past. We made approval a server-side-of-the-page fact: the finalize call checks the human's actual click in code, and we proved the negative paths on camera. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full judge experience runs through the runtime's own executeTool : interview → surface swap → gated filing (pending → human approval → submitted) → reconciliation → cascade → ledger. Not a scripted path — the protocol path. Receipts as evidence : every filing carries a payload digest and confirmation number; the ledger reads like an audit trail, because that's what it is. Honest degradation : without a WebMCP runtime the chip says so, the human buttons drive the same code paths, and the app still demonstrates every flow. A dark, full-height activity rail that narrates every tool call — the human and the agent visibly share one live artifact. What we learned Protocol depth is a design material, not a checkbox. Dynamic surfaces, annotations, and elicitation-shaped gates changed the architecture, not just the API calls. Human-in-the-loop belongs in code. A prompt saying "ask first" is a suggestion; a gate that physically cannot finalize without the human's click is a guarantee. Test in the real judging environment early. The single most dangerous bug we fixed was invisible in every browser except the one with the flag enabled. Agents need agent-legible errors : strict in-code validation with messages written for self-correction turns failures into progress. What's next for Paper Trail Move and bereavement event packs — the bundle engine takes new event types without architecture changes. Native requestUserInteraction elicitation as a progressive enhancement of the two-call gate. An accessibility operator mode — the same tool surfaces are a better substrate than the visual DOM; narration and pacing ride the protocol for free. Handoff export — the remaining human-only actions (notary visits, in-person verifications) as a calendar file, because a good agent knows what it can't do.
