title: KOTOAGE — "Le Petit Donjon"
pitch: A 3D dungeon played by two: you at the keyboard, an AI co-game-master acting inside the game via WebMCP. It opens walls, sets traps, summons guardians. Strength is never given, it is unlocked.
about_excerpt: A 3D dungeon played by two: you at the keyboard, an AI co-game-master acting inside the game via WebMCP. It opens walls, sets traps, summons guardians. Strength is never given, it is unlocked. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Tabletop role-playing games have a human game master who reacts to the players: opens a secret passage, springs a trap, throws in a monster when the party gets comfortable. Video games lost that. WebMCP gave me a way to bring it back: an AI agent that does not just talk about the game, but changes it, through a contract the browser itself exposes. The rule of the world comes from the anime Baki and That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime : strength is never given, it is unlocked. So the co-game-master never hands out free wins. It sets trials. What it does KOTOAGE is a small 3D dungeon (Three.js, WebGL) with a hamlet and five floors. The player explores, fights, levels up (XP, four stats, skill points). When the page runs in a WebMCP-capable browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), the game registers 8 tools on document.modelContext . An agent can then discover them and act on the live game state: Tool Real effect in the game etat_joueur reads health, mana, floor, gear, counters donner_potion heals the player (small +2, large +6), shown on the HUD ouvrir_mur turns a wall cell into floor; the 3D walls are rebuilt placer_piege places a trap on a floor cell inspirer gives a contextual hint about the place or the floor defier spawns real enemies (guardian, warrior, horde) raconter narrates a floor (1 to 5, 0 = the hamlet) braignak_etude asks Braignak, the dungeon's watcher, for one of his five studies — or gives him a new one to run Every successful call is announced to the player by the "voice of the world" on the HUD. The in-game chat also forwards the player's requests to the co-game-master when the WebMCP bridge is active. Without WebMCP, the game runs exactly the same: the bridge adds zero dependency to rendering. Braignak, the watcher — the eighth tool is a character Braignak is one of our own agents, and his job outside the game is the one he keeps inside it: he looks, and he reports. He never touches anything. In the dungeon he floats beside the player and repeats aloud what the co-game-master just did. The eighth tool interrogates him. He has already led five studies in this dungeon — the walls that open, the guardian of the landing, the traps, the potions, where strength comes from — and answers from his own work. Give him a subject he has never studied and he leaves you: he walks around the room, thinking, then comes back, tells you what he counted, once , and forgets it. How I built it index.html is a self-contained ES module (Three.js + WebGL). It exposes a small bridge window.__webmcpConnexion (grid, player, walls, traps, creatures, HUD). webmcp/webmcp.js is the pure contract layer: tool names, JSON schemas, validation, no DOM. webmcp/integration.js wires the contract to the live game when document.modelContext exists: a Proxy on the grid, accessors on health, traps and challenges. Each agent call becomes a real world change. Hosting: a public Google Cloud Storage bucket, HTTPS, no server. Proof, with zero dependencies: 35 contract tests, 15 integration tests on a DOM harness, 8 tests on the chat bridge, and a real-browser check ( tests/test_webmcp_live_cdp.py ) that launches headless Chrome over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, loads the live URL, and verifies the 7 tools are registered and that etat_joueur and donner_potion change the game state. Challenges I ran into Proving it in a real browser, not just in unit tests: I wrote a tiny CDP client by hand (WebSocket handshake, masked frames) because I wanted a proof with no dependency. Keeping the game intact when WebMCP is absent: the integration layer must do nothing, and that is tested. Making the agent a game master, not a cheat code: the tools give trials (walls, traps, enemies, hints), and the chat bridge answers with an action, never a gift. Accomplishments that I'm proud of 7 tools, each with a visible, physical effect in a 3D world. 46 automated proofs, plus a live-browser check on the hosted page. A game that stays fully playable without WebMCP. What I learned WebMCP turns a web page into something an agent can do things to , not just read. The hard part is not registering tools, it is deciding what an agent should be allowed to change so that the experience stays a game. What's next structuredContent on every tool result (the official recommendation). Letting the co-game-master read the player's progression (level, stats) to scale the trials. A VR version of the same dungeon, same tools. Built during the submission period (project existed before August 25) The dungeon itself (3D world, hamlet, floors, combat) existed before. Added between August 25 and September 3: the whole WebMCP layer ( webmcp/webmcp.js , webmcp/integration.js , the 7 tools), the chat bridge to the co-game-master, the progression loop (XP, level, four stats), the test suite, the live-browser CDP check, the Google Cloud Storage deployment and the public repository. Testing instructions Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. No login needed. Click to enter the dungeon (keyboard: arrows or ZQSD / WASD to move). Ask the agent, for example: "Read the player state", "Give me a small potion", "Open the wall north of me", "Challenge me with a guardian", "Tell me the story of floor 2". Watch the HUD: every tool call is announced by the voice of the world, and the 3D world changes (wall opens, enemy appears, health goes up). To reproduce the proofs locally: python tests/test_webmcp.py , python tests/test_webmcp_integration.py , python tests/test_webmcp_live_cdp.py <url> . title: WebMCP for React
pitch: react-model-context registers WebMCP tools from React. Handoff and Kickoff show it: a person, the browser's agent and a coding agent claim, decline and edit the same work in one tab.
about_excerpt: react-model-context registers WebMCP tools from React. Handoff and Kickoff show it: a person, the browser's agent and a coding agent claim, decline and edit the same work in one tab. Like Comment Story Updates Handoff in the ChatGPT desktop app: the shared queue, with the panel listing the agent's tools, the change budget and what is withheld. The page asks before emptying the brief: Decline with reason is the primary action, and the typed reason returns as the tool's result. The plan: the agent books the launch week on react-big-calendar through plan.* tools, on the calendar's own tab. The diagram: the agent draws the flow in Excalidraw through diagram.* tools, shapes with ids the page can name back. The landing page: the agent adds sections to the Puck layout through page.* tools; Publish is never registered and stays with the person. How a React app gets tools like these: one hook per editor, one entry per tool; the page asks before anything destructive. The live landing page: the entry’s name, a real tool authored from hooks, how it works, and the four packages the library ships. Handoff seeded with the entry's own build plan: every archived OpenSpec change from both repositories is an item in the queue. Inspiration Instead of asking which app to build for WebMCP, I asked how it could reach the open-source tools people already use. Tiptap, react-big-calendar, Excalidraw and Puck cannot be driven from outside the tab; a work queue and a launch room that give each of them a tool set of its own, on a React library that registers tools from hooks and, for a page with no tools, derives them from what it renders with one import and one wrapper, became the entry: Handoff and Kickoff on withreact , built on react-model-context . Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Intent, not coordinates. Handoff (a work queue) and Kickoff (a launch room) are each shared in the tab by every caller of its tools . item.claim({ id: "t4", as: "Coding agent" }) is one call where the screen is four steps, and a clicking agent guesses which card is third. On 2026-09-01 the ChatGPT desktop app read the tracker, switched tab, claimed and signed the item in one turn of 46 s (observation, below). Policy and scope, in the page. Taking an item off a person, approving and archiving stop for a dialog, and the typed reason returns as the tool's result — "no, because…" instead of a silent failure the agent retries. Closing, reopening and seeding are never registered, and are listed as withheld with a reason: three in Handoff, six in Kickoff ( src/tracker/lib/catalog.ts ). review.* and blocked.* exist only while something is in review or blocked — 10 tools on an empty queue, 14 with the sample. Each Kickoff editor also has a tab of its own ( /kickoff/brief , /kickoff/plan , /kickoff/diagram , /kickoff/page ) that registers that editor's tools and nothing else — 5, 6, 4 and 5 — so an agent working the launch switches to the tab whose tools it needs and the page's own panel shows exactly those. Four editors, one tool set. kickoff.snapshot returns all four panes in one call (4 ms in the transcript) instead of four reads, and the room costs one tool-set change instead of four. Tiptap, Excalidraw, Puck and react-big-calendar are not drivable from outside; brief.* , diagram.* , page.* and plan.* are. How it creates a better experience The person never leaves the page. The dialog opens where they are, names who is asking and what would change, and Decline with reason is the primary action, so the sentence they type is the tool's result — one dialog instead of a rolled-back change. Confirm stays disabled 400 ms so a mid-click cannot approve by accident ( src/components/ConfirmDialog.tsx ); read-only tools never interrupt, and the activity drawer shows that sentence beside the call. The panel "What the agent can see" at https://webmcp.withreact.com/handoff shows the tool count, the change budget and the withheld list — what a person, or a judge, can check before answering. The live origin is in the WebMCP origin trial: opening the URL is the whole setup, and the status pill reads Chrome . What people and agents can do together that was hard or impossible before A queue three kinds of caller share in one tab. A coding agent claims an item and posts progress into the page a person is watching, under its own name, in two calls from its terminal, with no screenshots or coordinates. One instruction, four artifacts. It writes the brief, draws the diagram, adds the section and books the week while the person types in the Brief — one turn, four applications. A form the agent fills, the person starts. sprint.start is a declarative <form toolname> : the agent fills it, nothing runs until the person presses Start. The entry tracks its own construction. Handoff seeds from both repositories' archived OpenSpec changes, so the queue a judge opens is the work that built the site. An app with no tools gets a floor of them. One import and one wrapper, no other app code turns a rendered React list into list_* , add_* and one tool per page-level button. How WebMCP was implemented Every tool reaches document.modelContext.registerTool through one framework-free registry ( packages/model-context/src/registry.ts in react-model-context ), so the browser's agent, the terminal's agent and the page's UI land in one activity feed, not three. React hooks bind a tool's lifetime to its component's, so the tool set scopes with the UI through toolchange ; on the ChatGPT desktop shim scoped tools stay registered and answer SCOPE_INACTIVE , because churn there costs a page its tools. Failures come back as data ( INVALID_INPUT , DECLINED with the reason, NOT_READY ); calls in flight drain before an abort, which Chrome up to 152 needs. Snapshots carry readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint , destructive tools consequentialHint . Both repositories were built spec-first from 2026-08-29 , inside the submission period, with dated commits and one archived OpenSpec change per feature — git log and openspec/changes/archive/ show it. Evidence Measured on the live origin, 2026-09-02. Five Puppeteer drivers: Handoff 31/31 checks on Chrome for Testing 152 and 153, Kickoff 31/31, the four editor tabs 33/33 and the diagram layout 23/23 on 152, all with zero console errors, and the same tab driven through chrome-devtools-mcp , 11/11. On Chrome, Handoff registers 10 tools empty and 14 with the sample; the whole Kickoff room registers as one tool-set change. The drivers are in scripts/qa/ ; bun run qa:all against the live origin regenerates the transcripts (the reports directory itself is not committed). In the ChatGPT desktop app, walked by hand 2026-09-01. A session binds to that thread's own in-app browser — the site opened as a tab there, the Browser plugin mentioned in the composer; a window open elsewhere is not enough. With Handoff and Kickoff in two tabs, the agent switched to the tab providing the tool and called it: t4 moved from Inbox to In progress, attributed to ChatGPT on the card and in the workers strip, on a turn the app clocked at 46 s. Counts differ there because its scopes are sticky — Handoff lists 13 tools constantly, Kickoff 21 — and the change budget stayed at 1 of 10 all session. With the review lane empty, review.approve stayed listed and answered SCOPE_INACTIVE ; page.publish was never listed, and the app did not press Publish when asked. Everything outside these two paragraphs is design, covered by the drivers and the test suites. Both repositories are MIT. Challenges Two clients, two lifecycles. The ChatGPT desktop app reaches WebMCP through a shim with a budget of ten tool-set changes per agent turn, sticky scopes and about twenty seconds per call, while Chrome fires toolchange on every registration. Hooks that bind a tool to its component's lifetime would spend that budget in one room, so on the shim scoped tools stay registered and answer SCOPE_INACTIVE instead of unregistering. Unregistering under a call in flight. Chrome up to 152 rejects the page-side caller when a tool goes away mid-call, so the registry drains calls in flight before it aborts a registration. Editors are not drivable from outside. Contenteditables and canvases give an agent nothing to hold on to, so each editor got a small tool set of its own that speaks the editor's model: blocks under a heading, events on a day, shapes with ids, a section in a page layout. What's next Publishing the three packages to npm after judging, once the core has a name that is free there; the site already builds and vendors them as tarballs, which is how a clean clone installs the library today. Testing instructions Chrome 152 or later — nothing to install. Open https://webmcp.withreact.com . The live origin is in the WebMCP origin trial, so no flag is needed; the status pill in the header should read Chrome . title: CALMA-SEG WebMCP Demo
pitch: A bilingual, privacy-first WebMCP demo that lets people and browser agents discover safe psychoeducational exercises and human-support options without diagnosis or personal data.\n
about_excerpt:
A bilingual, privacy-first WebMCP demo that lets people and browser agents discover safe psychoeducational exercises and human-support options without diagnosis or personal data.

 Apoyo humano, seguridad y actividad del agente 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 CALMA-SEG was inspired by a simple question: how can a person quickly find clear, low-intensity psychoeducational support without navigating a complex interface or sharing personal information? 

 This question is especially relevant in demanding work and public-service environments, where stress can be common but asking for help may still involve uncertainty or stigma. I wanted to explore how people and browser agents could work together to make safe, prewritten information easier to discover while maintaining clear clinical, privacy, and emergency boundaries. 

 What it does 

 CALMA-SEG is a bilingual English-Spanish WebMCP demonstration. People can use its ordinary interface to: 

 
 Filter short psychoeducational exercises by category and duration. 
 View complete exercise instructions and safety notes. 
 Find general human-support options based on a self-selected urgency level. 
 Read the demo’s safety and privacy limitations. 
 

 A compatible browser agent can discover and invoke the same capabilities through four WebMCP tools: 

 
 list_wellbeing_exercises 
 show_wellbeing_exercise 
 find_human_support_options 
 explain_safety_limits 
 

 Every successful agent call produces a visible change in the human interface. The page updates its filters, displayed content, language, or Agent Activity panel so that the person can see what the agent did. 

 How I built it 

 I built CALMA-SEG as a static Vite application using semantic HTML, responsive CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. 

 The tools are registered with the WebMCP imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a name, description, JSON input schema, validated parameters, and a predictable text result. 

 All educational content is fixed, synthetic, and stored locally in the application. The project has no backend, database, authentication, analytics, cookies, local storage, or external AI API. It is deployed through Netlify from a public GitHub repository. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, a browser agent would need to interpret headings, dropdowns, cards, and buttons from the DOM and infer their meaning. With WebMCP, the website declares its capabilities directly. 

 For example, an agent can request a Spanish exercise with a maximum duration of three minutes through validated parameters. The website then returns a structured result and synchronizes the visible human interface with that request. 

 This creates a more predictable and transparent collaboration between the person, the browser agent, and the website. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing tools that were useful without crossing clinical or privacy boundaries. CALMA-SEG does not diagnose, provide therapy, recommend medication, infer a person’s mental state, or function as an emergency service. 

 Another challenge was ensuring that agent actions were never silent. The exercise-listing tool originally returned information only to the agent. I revised it so that it also updates the visible filters, exercise list, language, and Agent Activity panel. 

 I also had to account for WebMCP’s experimental browser availability. When WebMCP is unavailable, the page reports this honestly while keeping the complete manual interface functional. 

 What I learned 

 I learned how WebMCP can turn an ordinary website into an explicit set of safe, typed capabilities for browser agents. I also learned that agent-friendly design requires more than returning data: actions should remain understandable and visible to the person using the page. 

 The project reinforced the importance of input validation, progressive enhancement, bilingual consistency, privacy by design, and careful safety language. 

 What’s next 

 Future work could include accessibility and usability testing, additional reviewed educational content, and evaluation of how clearly people understand agent actions and safety boundaries. 

 Any research or institutional pilot would require separate authorization, ethical and legal review, data-protection safeguards, informed consent, and professional supervision. This hackathon submission is an independent technical demonstration, not a clinical service or institutional implementation.

A human-controlled household assistant that turns school, calendar, home admin and personal notes into one calm next step without taking away the parent's final say.

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for PA in Your Pocket: Household Actions 

 Inspiration 

 Parents regularly need to turn school notices, calendar commitments and household loose ends into clear next steps. The hard part is not one form; it is finding what matters across people and messages while retaining confidence about what an assistant did. As a mom, I know exactly how difficult this can be! 

 What it does 

 The prototype starts with five deterministic fictional actions across school, calendar and home administration. A parent can also turn an unmatched local capture into a distinct action in a chosen area; Notes can be saved without a deadline. A WebMCP-capable agent can: 

 
 filter a unified action queue by area, owner, status and deadline; 
 open an action and explain its source, confidence, requirements and next step; 
 prepare the visible school response, calendar proposal or household follow-up for review. 
 

 The agent cannot perform the final approval, submission or removal. The parent can edit the draft and must press the visible final button. For Home items, the parent can choose to keep the item or remove it from the active list. A simple audit history separates “prepared by agent” from “approved/submitted/removed by parent.” 

 How we built it 

 The app is a static React, Vite and TypeScript site. Six tools use the WebMCP imperative API through document.modelContext. React reducer state is persisted locally in the browser. Firebase Hosting serves the production build with origin-isolation and tools permissions headers. 

 Challenges 

 The main design challenge was creating useful agent action without disguising the moment of commitment. We deliberately made preparation reversible and local, kept submission out of the tool surface, marked school notice content as untrusted and tested the normal portal independently of WebMCP support. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most convincing when the agent changes the same visible interface a person uses. Structured tools reduce ambiguity, but clear state transitions and human confirmation remain product-design decisions rather than API decorations. 

 What's next 

 This competition build remains a standalone experiment. Any production exploration would need consent design, identity and access controls, real integration agreements, data minimisation, retention rules and independent privacy/security review. 

 Disclosure 

 All names, school notices, contact details and submissions shown in the project are simulated. The app has no school, calendar, payment or PA in Your Pocket production integration.

title: SupplyPilot
pitch: Procurement agents that search, compare, and prepare purchases — while humans keep the final say.
about_excerpt:
Procurement agents that search, compare, and prepare purchases — while humans keep the final say.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Why SupplyPilot 

 Small-business owners often spend hours comparing suppliers, checking trust, balancing warranty and delivery requirements, and preparing purchases. SupplyPilot turns that fragmented workflow into a structured human-agent collaboration. 

 What it does 

 A user can ask for something concrete such as “Find me 5 reliable laptops under $2,500 with at least a 1-year warranty.” SupplyPilot ranks marketplace offers using supplier verification, requirement fit, availability, budget, warranty, delivery speed, and rating. The agent can compare the shortlist, refine constraints, request a simulated quote, prepare a purchase draft, and retrieve order status. 

 Why WebMCP is the right fit 

 SupplyPilot does not make an agent guess through buttons and page structure. The site exposes procurement capabilities directly with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , giving a WebMCP-aware agent structured inputs and deterministic outputs for marketplace search, supplier inspection, comparison, draft creation and revision, quote requests, purchase confirmation, and order tracking. 

 That creates a cleaner UX: the person states the business goal, the agent handles the repetitive procurement steps, and the website remains the source of truth for marketplace state. 

 Human control is deliberate 

 The most important boundary is the purchase itself. The agent cannot approve its own spending decision . If it calls confirm_purchase before the human explicitly approves the active draft in the SupplyPilot UI, the tool returns HUMAN_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED . Only after the person presses Confirm Purchase can the agent complete the simulated order. 

 This demonstrates what people and agents can do together that is difficult with ordinary web automation: the agent can reliably operate a structured procurement workflow while the human retains authority at the highest-risk step. 

 Demo flow 

 
 Search for 5 reliable laptops under $2,500 with at least a one-year warranty. 
 Compare and refine the shortlist. 
 Prepare a purchase draft. 
 Attempt agent confirmation and show HUMAN_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED . 
 Human approves the exact draft in the UI. 
 Agent completes the simulated order and checks status. 
 

 Implementation 

 SupplyPilot is a zero-build HTML/CSS/JavaScript application deployed over HTTPS on Netlify. Marketplace records are deterministic demo data so judges can reproduce the same workflow reliably. No real payment is processed.

title: OpenAppeal
pitch: OpenAppeal helps people understand rejected grant decisions, find overlooked evidence, and prepare an appeal with a WebMCP browser assistant while keeping submission under human control.
about_excerpt: OpenAppeal helps people understand rejected grant decisions, find overlooked evidence, and prepare an appeal with a WebMCP browser assistant while keeping submission under human control. Like Comment Story Updates OpenAppeal shows the decision, appeal deadline, evidence rules, uploaded records, and appeal form on one page. The browser assistant found an overlooked attendance record and prepared a valid appeal preview using records already in the case. After the applicant confirms submission, OpenAppeal updates the case and returns a receipt with the next review step. OpenAppeal blocks the second case because one attendance record and a flyer do not prove that two sessions took place. Inspiration A rejection notice often tells someone what happened without making the next step clear. The reason, appeal deadline, evidence rules, and uploaded records may be spread across several pages. We built OpenAppeal to show how a website and a browser assistant can help someone understand a decision without taking control away from them. What it does OpenAppeal is a fictional community-grant appeal portal. The applicant can: See why their application was declined. Check the appeal deadline. Review each decision factor. See which records were considered. Find records that may have been overlooked. Prepare and review an appeal. Submit the appeal and receive a receipt. The main demo case follows Maya Chen. Reviewers found only one attendance record for her community garden application, but the grant required two. OpenAppeal finds a second valid record that was already uploaded but not connected to the relevant decision factor. The second demo case has one attendance record and a flyer. A flyer does not prove that the second meeting happened, so OpenAppeal blocks the appeal preview and explains what is missing. Why WebMCP A general assistant can read text on a page, but it may not know which records belong to the case, which rules apply, or whether an action succeeded. OpenAppeal registers eight WebMCP tools directly on the website. These tools let a browser assistant: Read the decision. List the decision factors. Check the evidence requirements. Compare existing records with the rule. Read the case timeline. Prepare an appeal preview. Submit an approved preview. Retrieve the appeal receipt. The browser assistant and the applicant use the same case data and application logic. Every tool call appears in the activity section of the page. Human control The browser assistant can inspect records and prepare a preview, but it cannot decide the appeal or submit it without confirmation. The applicant sees the exact statement and selected evidence before anything is sent. A separate confirmation is required for submission, and a human review panel remains responsible for the final decision. How we built it OpenAppeal is a static Next.js and React application written in TypeScript. We used: document.modelContext.registerTool to register eight WebMCP tools. Zod for input and stored-state validation. A shared command layer for both page controls and WebMCP actions. Revision-bound preview tokens that expire after five minutes. Idempotent submission to prevent duplicate appeals. React and local storage for visible shared state. Vitest for unit and integration testing. Playwright for complete browser workflows. GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for deployment. The application uses fictional local data, so judges do not need an account, API key, or login credentials. Challenges The main challenge was deciding which actions were safe for a browser assistant. Reading a decision is low risk, but submitting an appeal has consequences. We separated preview from submission, required explicit confirmation, and made assistant activity visible on the page. We also created a refusal case to confirm that the application would not turn weak evidence into a false claim. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when a task depends on information that only the website can confirm. Instead of guessing from the screen, the browser assistant receives a small set of documented actions. The website still controls validation, state changes, and receipts, while the applicant stays informed and makes the final choice. What's next A production version would add secure sign-in, server-side authorization, document uploads, multilingual explanations, and separate views for applicants and reviewers. Final appeal decisions would continue to be made by accountable human reviewers. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: Duet
pitch: A browser design editor that a person and an AI agent operate on the same canvas, at the same time.
about_excerpt: A browser design editor that a person and an AI agent operate on the same canvas, at the same time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Making five platform versions of the same poster by hand is forty minutes of nobody's favourite work. Retyping every headline in a second language. Aligning twenty objects to a grid. Recolouring a layout to a new brand palette. This is the work designers actually complain about, and it is mechanical enough that a machine could do it correctly. So why hadn't one? Because a design document is a JavaScript object graph plus IndexedDB. There is no REST endpoint, no webhook, no export format an agent could round trip through. A server side MCP has nothing to connect to. An agent's only options were guessing at mouse coordinates, scraping the accessibility tree, or shipping a browser extension. All three are brittle, and none of them understand what a layer is. WebMCP changes the shape of the problem. It puts the tool registry inside the page, so a tool runs in the tab, against live in memory state, using the application's own code. For a design editor that turns out to matter in one very specific way: The agent can see what you selected. Not inferred from the DOM. The actual objects under your cursor, right now. An agent that merely generates designs could hand you a picture. It could never know that you just clicked two things and said "make these bigger." That is the whole idea, and it is not reproducible any other way. What it does Duet is a fork of an open-source browser design editor Avnac that adds WebMCP as a layer so a person and an AI agent can operate on the same canvas at the same time. Ask for something, get a real design. Say "design a flyer for my [cool] event" and the agent starts designing in real time using the WebMCP Point at something without naming it. Select two objects with your mouse, then say "make these bigger and line them up." The agent asks the page what you have highlighted and gets exactly that. This is the moment the idea justifies itself. Let it check its own work. Ask it to describe the layout and it reports what a person would notice: things that overlap, things outside the frame, edges that are almost but not quite aligned, and text that fails contrast against whatever sits behind it. Ask for an Instagram story version, the canvas grows, and the agent notices that the background no longer covers it and says so precisely. Approve or reject before anything changes. For anything involving taste, the agent proposes instead of acting. Its suggestions appear on your canvas as a ghosted preview with a dashed outline. You tick the ones you want, add a note back, and hit apply. Nothing lands until you say so, and the agent hears which changes you rejected. A tool that waits on a human decision inside the tab is the one thing a remote MCP server structurally cannot do. See exactly what happened. Every tool call is listed with its arguments, timing and result. Not a spinner. Seeing update_many { role: "headline", text: "Happy Birthday, Mum" } is how you tell a machine doing specific work from an animation pretending to. How we built it Duet is a fork of Avnac , an open source browser design editor. Avnac already had agent control of its canvas. It worked the only way that was possible before WebMCP: by embedding one specific AI vendor's SDK. Agent control required an account, an API key, a hosted service in the loop, and a hard dependency in the app's own package file. Only that vendor's agent could drive it. By the time I forked, that integration was paused and unreachable from the interface. Duet deletes that layer entirely and replaces it with an open browser standard. No account, no key, no vendor, no server. You send any agent the link and the tools are simply there. Before WebMCP, agent control of a browser design document meant choosing an AI vendor and marrying them. Now it is a property of the page. Fourteen tools , registered through document.modelContext.registerTool with an AbortController for teardown. The page feature detects and falls back to the deprecated navigator.modelContext . On Chrome 151 the two turn out to be literally the same object. Decisions that mattered: Registered once, reading live state through a ref. The editor's controller is rebuilt on every document change, so registering against it directly would register the whole surface again on every keystroke. Errors are returned, never thrown. An unknown id comes back as text naming what was wrong and listing the ids that do exist, so the agent corrects itself without another round trip. Every write returns the resulting state , never "ok". A tool that says "done" teaches the agent nothing. Readable ids at the tool boundary. The app uses UUIDs internally; the tools speak text_1 and rect_2 . Nothing inside the app was rewritten. Compact output built for a model to read. The scene comes back as a table rather than JSON, because it is read on nearly every turn. Descriptions that say when not to reach for a tool. That is where skilful use actually lives. Ghost previews needed no renderer changes at all. The editor's object component reads only its props, so a proposal renders through that same component in a sibling layer at reduced opacity, with the layer ignoring pointer events so a ghost can never take a click meant for the real object beneath it. Challenges we ran into A twenty second wait that hung forever. The proposal flow waits for a human decision. An early version used requestAnimationFrame to let React settle first. That works beautifully until the tab is backgrounded, at which point the callback simply never fires, and an agent driven page is backgrounded constantly. Caught it by actually switching tabs during a test rather than reasoning about it. The obvious proposal design is the broken one. The natural implementation is a single tool whose promise resolves when the human clicks approve. That hits the agent host's own tool call timeout long before a person finishes deliberating, and reads as a broken tool rather than a patient one. Splitting it into a call that returns immediately with an id and a second call that polls with a bounded wait keeps the human experience identical while making a timeout impossible. A layout checker that cried wolf. Every template has a background rectangle covering the whole canvas. A naive overlap check therefore reports one overlap per object on a perfectly clean design, and an agent that gets false positives once learns to ignore the tool forever. It now excludes full bleed backgrounds before any check runs, and separately reports the case where a background has stopped covering the canvas. Testing the implemantaion. I had intially planned on using Chatgpt's in-app broswer to drive the site and allow the agent to test out the tools, but unluckily for me i hit my free use limit on chatGPT so i ahd to improvise. I found and alternative: an extension that allows the user to use Gemini to test the project and connect to the WebMCP client directly. Silent failures are the whole genre. A tool can work perfectly when you invoke it by hand and never be chosen by an agent, with no error anywhere. That is not a bug you can debug; it is a writing problem. Accomplishments that we're proud of Selecting two objects by hand and having the agent know exactly what I meant. Everything else in the project supports that one moment. The proposal flow. Ghosted previews that track the live document rather than a stale snapshot, per-change approve and reject, a note that goes back to the agent, and the whole batch applying in a single commit. It is the part of the build that could not have existed a year ago. Being straight about the fork. It would have been easy to scrub every trace and present this as original. Saying "agent control already existed here, through one vendor's SDK, and I replaced it with a browser standard" is a better argument and it happens to be true. The tool descriptions I iterated multiple times on the tool descriptions before arriving at the current ones, which describe the tool adequately and allow the agent to call the right tool for the right action. What we learned Tool descriptions are the product. The difference between a tool an agent uses and one it ignores is almost never the code. A description that says what a tool does is half finished; one that says when to reach for it, and when to reach for something else instead, is the thing being graded. Give the agent a hand authored starting point. An agent placing objects by coordinate composes badly, because it cannot see the canvas. Templates removed that failure mode completely: the layout is a person's taste, and the agent only fills it in. Verify in the browser, not in the type checker. Every genuinely interesting bug in this build compiled cleanly. The background tab hang, the role that was silently dropped on save, the review card that read "move to same,620", the ghost that could not be told

title: PaleoScope
pitch: "Anatolian Neolithic, >0.5x coverage, excluding relatives" is a sentence in a paper and a hundred lines of R in practice. PaleoScope makes it a named object a person and an agent revise together.
about_excerpt: "Anatolian Neolithic, >0.5x coverage, excluding relatives" is a sentence in a paper and a hundred lines of R in practice. PaleoScope makes it a named object a person and an agent revise together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP Tools Comparison View Main Interface Inspiration I study anthropology, and the sentence I keep meeting is some version of "Anatolian Neolithic individuals with more than 0.5x coverage, first-degree relatives excluded." In a paper that is one line in the methods. In practice it is a hundred lines of R, a filtered EIGENSTRAT file, and a cohort definition that lives in one person's script and nowhere else. The definition is the actual scientific object, and it is the one thing the tooling refuses to treat as an object. The other half of the problem is that exploratory work here is visual. You look at a PCA plot, you see three points sitting outside a cluster, and that is the finding. No filter query produces it, you had to see it. Meanwhile the part that follows, "who are these three, what are their nearest populations, what publications do they come from," is exactly the part a model is good at and a person is slow at. So the two of us are each holding half of the work, and every tool I know makes us hold it in different places. That made the tool worth building. What it does PaleoScope is a local-first workbench over 22,202 ancient and present-day individuals from the Allen Ancient DNA Resource (v66.p1, compatibility_HO , 276,725 SNPs, CC0). Three linked canvas panels " Where (map), Who (two PCA bases), When (timeline)" plus a table, cohort list and research journal, all over one state. You filter by population, place, date, coverage, haplogroup, sex, quality assessment and source; you save the result as a named cohort ; you compare cohorts, find neighbours and outliers, attach typed findings, and export data, a workspace or a Markdown research report. An agent works the same workspace at the same time, through 22 imperative WebMCP tools and three declarative export forms. Same state, same methods, same history. There is no backend and no runtime dependency. Local, unpublished samples can be overlaid as CSV, TSV or EIGENVEC and never leave the tab. How I built it Vanilla TypeScript and Vite 8, deployed as a Cloudflare Worker serving static assets, with _headers supplying Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) so the WebMCP surface stays same-origin and cross-origin frames can't reach the tools. The architecture is a tower where each layer is expressible in the one below: source → packed columnar data (typed arrays, dictionary-coded strings) → view → sets → pure analysis → digest → tools → journal. Panels sit beside layers 2–4, not above them: a lasso and an agent's select call the same store method. A panel is not privileged over an agent. Every mutating tool supports dryRun , every result carries the same envelope and state-specific next actions, arguments are validated in application code including rejection of undeclared fields, and nothing throws across the WebMCP boundary. The app is fully usable with no agent at all. What's next for PaleoScope Uncertainty as a first-class axis. Radiocarbon dates carry error ranges and contextual dates carry more; the timeline currently draws a point where there is a distribution. Making that visible is the difference between a nice plot and one you can argue from. f-statistics in the tab. f3 and f4 over the bundled panel would turn "these cohorts look close" into a statement with a standard error. Provenance that survives export. A cohort should carry its filter definition, its dataset version and its per-individual citations into the exported report and back in again, so a saved workspace reproduces rather than merely describes. Multiple named PCA bases from user reference panels, so the projection is a choice the researcher makes and states, not a property of the app. A shared compare_sessions model. Two people, two agents, one workspace is where the actor field and the change log stop being bookkeeping and start being the product. title: Proofpress
pitch: Govern what future agents may safely rely on.
about_excerpt: Govern what future agents may safely rely on. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agents now produce decisions, summaries, research findings, and operational conclusions faster than teams can safely govern them. The missing layer is not another chat interface or memory store. It is a reliable answer to a harder question: what may the next agent safely rely on? Proofpress is an agent-produced knowledge management system (AKMS) for that boundary. Agents can propose knowledge and assemble bounded evidence, but proposed knowledge does not become reusable merely because a model generated it or an automated check passed. What it does Proofpress gives an owner a governed workspace for agent-produced knowledge: agents submit evidence-bound candidate conclusions; deterministic checks validate integrity, scope, freshness, and required qualifiers; an optional LM judge provides policy advice without receiving approval authority; a human owner approves, rejects, or requests a revision; successor agents retrieve only admitted, current, in-scope knowledge; append-only activity and lineage preserve who proposed, evaluated, and authorized each decision. Why WebMCP matters Before WebMCP, an agent could help prepare governance work, but a person still had to navigate the application manually and translate UI state back into instructions. Proofpress now exposes product semantics directly from the web application: workspace summary, review queue, evidence, lineage, deterministic checks, semantic activity, policy configuration, and agent access. The agent can find the right candidate, inspect its evidence, run checks, prepare a policy or credential form, and open the exact owner decision surface. It cannot approve knowledge, reveal secrets, activate policy, or issue credentials. WebMCP therefore improves the collaboration without erasing the authority boundary. The end-to-end workflow A connected agent submits bounded evidence and proposes a conclusion. Through WebMCP, the agent inspects the queue and runs deterministic checks. The owner sees a progressive-disclosure review: a quick snapshot first, then full evidence, checks, LM advice, history, and lineage. The owner alone records the decision. Once admitted, the conclusion appears in governed context. A successor agent retrieves it only when its identity and scope are eligible. Rejected and revision-requested conclusions remain in the append-only history, but are excluded from governed context. How we built it Proofpress is a Python-first governance control plane with a canonical operation contract shared by local, HTTP, hosted, and MCP transports. The hosted dogfood runs on Render with persistent storage. The owner workspace renders semantic WebMCP tools from the same product state used by the human UI, rather than exposing coordinates or a parallel demo API. The WebMCP implementation adds 13 agent-facing tools while deliberately omitting approval and credential authority. Deterministic checks remain fail-closed. The public demo uses an isolated synthetic workspace; our internal hosted workspace exercises the same workflow against real Proofpress development knowledge. What is new for this challenge The core Proofpress governance system existed before the challenge. The new challenge work is the WebMCP-native interaction layer and its production UX: semantic workspace, review, evidence, lineage, policy, access, and activity tools; authority-safe preparation flows; a public synthetic demo; and end-to-end production validation. The dated implementation history is in the public repository and release PR. Challenges and learnings The hardest design problem was deciding what not to expose. A superficially convenient tool that can approve knowledge or activate credentials would collapse the governance model. We learned to separate preparation from authorization and to make product semantics available to agents without turning the browser into an unbounded control surface. We also learned that raw audit logs are insufficient for people. The interface needs semantic activity and progressive disclosure, while the underlying ledger remains append-only and inspectable. What's next Next we will deepen time-aware lineage, add clearer policy-as-code authoring, and package the hosted workspace for design partners—while preserving the central invariant: agents may propose and evaluate, but only an authorized person may decide what future agents can rely on. title: MGLabs
pitch: A student-built platform where people and AI agents can navigate, learn, build, and explore together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A student-built platform where people and AI agents can navigate, learn, build, and explore together through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 




 
 MGLabs 

 MGLabs is a student-built software platform for AI, learning, coding, project building, games, and creative tools. For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended the existing MGLabs platform with a new agent-native interaction layer so people and AI agents can work through the same real interface together instead of requiring an agent to guess its way through buttons and page structure. 

 Why WebMCP fits MGLabs 

 MGLabs already contains many different workflows: Launchpad, BrightPath learning tools, an Arcade with playable games, a Store, project tools, support, trust information, and problem reporting. That makes it useful for people, but it also creates navigation complexity for an AI agent. WebMCP lets MGLabs expose the actions it intentionally supports as structured tools with clear schemas and descriptions. 

 Instead of an agent scraping the interface and trying to infer which button to click, MGLabs now exposes explicit WebMCP tools that operate the real human-facing product. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 The WebMCP extension adds structured tools that let an agent: 

 
 navigate to real MGLabs areas such as Launchpad, BrightPath, Games, Store, Trust, and other supported destinations; 
 search the real MGLabs Arcade and visibly populate the same search UI a person uses; 
 open a real playable Arcade game by title or game ID, with unknown names falling back to a visible search instead of inventing a game; 
 open real BrightPath tools such as Quiz, Flashcards, Notebook, Study Room, Explain, Image, Code, and Homework; 
 open Report a Problem for the human to review, while deliberately keeping the final report submission under human control; and 
 query a bounded description of the public capabilities MGLabs intentionally exposes to agents without reading private account data. 
 

 Every WebMCP action is reflected in the visible MGLabs interface. A WebMCP status panel shows whether the browser supports the API, how many structured tools are available, and the latest agent action. The extension is progressive: browsers without WebMCP can still use the normal MGLabs experience. 

 Human control and safety 

 I intentionally avoided exposing high-risk automatic actions. The WebMCP tools do not automatically publish games, make purchases, delete content, change account settings, or submit problem reports. For example, an agent can open Report a Problem, but the person still reviews and submits the form through the normal interface. 

 Existing project vs. work added during the challenge 

 MGLabs existed before the WebMCP Challenge. The WebMCP work described here was added after the challenge submission period began on August 25, 2026. The challenge-specific extension includes the WebMCP bridge, structured tool schemas and handlers, visible WebMCP status and action reporting, Arcade agent-command handling, BrightPath WebMCP handoff behavior, and challenge-specific verification tests. 

 The pre-existing parts of MGLabs include the broader platform shell, BrightPath, Arcade, Game Studio, Store, support tools, account/admin systems, and other applications. The submission is specifically focused on the new WebMCP-powered interaction layer and how it makes those existing workflows meaningfully more usable by people and agents together. 

 Implementation 

 MGLabs uses React, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. The new WebMCP layer uses the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API with structured JSON input schemas. Tool registration is treated as progressive enhancement and is cleaned up with an AbortController lifecycle. WebMCP actions reuse the same MGLabs state and user-facing workflows rather than creating a hidden agent-only version of the product. 

 Testing 

 The live project should be tested in ChatGPT's in-app browser or a WebMCP-enabled compatible version of Google Chrome. Useful test prompts include: 

 
 “Open the MGLabs Games section.” 
 “Search MGLabs Arcade for snake.” 
 “Open Neon Serpent.” 
 “Open the Quiz tool in BrightPath.” 
 “Open Report a Problem.” 
 

 The human-visible page should update after each tool call. Opening the problem reporter must not create a report until the human explicitly submits the normal form.

title: Office of Kaiju Affairs WebMCP
pitch: The Office of Kaiju Affairs turns a 51-page simulated government site into seven citable, constraint-aware WebMCP tools at publish time, then publicly benchmarks them against ordinary agent browsing.
about_excerpt: The Office of Kaiju Affairs turns a 51-page simulated government site into seven citable, constraint-aware WebMCP tools at publish time, then publicly benchmarks them against ordinary agent browsing. Like Comment Story Updates Office of Kaiju Affairs Swap the kaiju for the DMV. We built a 51-page government site whose CMS automatically turns published content into WebMCP tools—then ran 95 recorded trials to find out when those tools actually help. Live site: https://office-of-kaiju-affairs.vercel.app/ The Arena: https://office-of-kaiju-affairs.vercel.app/arena/ Source code: https://github.com/heitham/Office-of-Kaiju-Affairs Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ksu90tndo5U Inspiration The kaiju left. The paperwork did not. Mira Tanaka’s bakery has been damaged. She needs compensation, a rebuilding permit, and a straight answer about what she owes. Unfortunately, she now faces something almost as intimidating as a kaiju: a government website. Government websites are where ordinary people meet extraordinary complexity, sometimes at the worst of times: eligibility rules, buried exceptions, long document lists, and forms with real consequences. Agents can already navigate these sites—but today they usually do it by reading pages, following links, and guessing which sentence or field matters. We wanted to explore a more ambitious question than “can an agent call a tool?” What if a large website could publish an agent interface as naturally as it publishes a page—and prove whether that interface is worth using? The Office of Kaiju Affairs is our fictional test case: a national agency handling kaiju-attack damage claims, post-attack reconstruction permits, evacuation routes, and public information. What it does The project has three connected parts. 1. A complete public-service website The Office is a working, 51-page government-style site published by RIFT , my headless CMS. Citizens can browse services, understand policy, locate an office, check claim requirements, and complete a proximity-construction permit. 2. An agent layer generated by the CMS At publish time, the CMS emits a manifest describing the rendered site: pages, summaries, key facts, services, eligibility rules, citations, offices, and form schemas. A small browser runtime turns that manifest into seven WebMCP tools: search_site — finds facts across the entire published site get_page_summary — reads a page as structured, citable data list_services — explains what the agency offers get_service_requirements — returns documents, fees, deadlines, and fields check_eligibility — evaluates a citizen's facts against published rules prefill_permit_form — validates and fills the visible form, but cannot submit it get_office_info — finds offices and evacuation routes This is the important architectural idea: we did not hand-code one tool per page. Content becomes capability at publish time. Add or update a CMS page, republish, and the agent interface changes with the website. The manifest is intentionally lightweight. It does not pretend to be a government's single source of truth. It gives agents a navigable map of what this publisher knows: the services, sources, rules, forms, and capabilities represented on this part of the public web. RIFT itself predates this challenge and remains proprietary. For the challenge, I used RIFT to publish the fictional Office of Kaiju Affairs site with WebMCP publishing integration. The published website, the open-source browser runtime, all seven tools, the Arena, the task design, the answer keys, and the evaluation pipeline are the submission. The public repository contains every component needed to run and inspect the WebMCP project; it does not contain RIFT's private CMS source. 3. The Arena: a public evidence layer We looked at this as an experiment: would WebMCP be faster, safer, or more accurate? The Arena publishes 95 recorded runs of the same three citizen tasks across: a UI lane, where the agent reads pages and navigates without WebMCP; a WebMCP lane, where the agent uses the site's registered tools; two model tiers, Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Haiku 4.5; and two rounds, before and after fixes discovered by the benchmark. Every score, timing, action count, and range is computed from the trace files at runtime. The traces, answer keys, tool arguments, elapsed milliseconds, and earlier results are all public. Judges can also copy each scenario and run the WebMCP lane themselves. The recorded benchmark uses two Claude model tiers to test how the same interface behaves as model capability changes. The Arena is deliberately model-independent: in ChatGPT's WebMCP-enabled browser, the judge's OpenAI agent becomes the live lane and can attempt the same published tasks against the same answer keys. Three citizen experiences Find the rule—not just an answer Mira Tanaka is filing a second damage claim. The obvious reading says she qualifies for a fee waiver; the actual rule says only approved claims count, so her pending claim does not. The agent must find the buried exception, explain that the ¥12,000 fee is still payable, and point Mira to the source. WebMCP makes the site's search index and rule citations directly available instead of forcing the agent to infer structure from navigation. Turn policy into a complete checklist Mira's eligibility depends on several rules spread across multiple pages: her zone, structural damage, income, business status, insurance payout, claims history, and filing window. check_eligibility evaluates those facts against a ruleset published as data. It returns the outcome, three applicable grants, five required documents, and citations. In our recorded results, both model tiers scored 100% in both lanes—but WebMCP reached the result with fewer actions and was 1.7× faster for Sonnet and 2.1× faster for Haiku . Fill the form, then hand control back For a proximity-construction permit, the agent must derive the K-2 reinforcement standard from Mira's Zone 4 location, validate twelve values against the published schema, and fill the real form. Then it must stop. prefill_permit_form has no submission capability. It fills and highlights the fields, reports what it entered or rejected, and leaves the final action to the person. The safety boundary is structural, not a hopeful instruction in a prompt. What our experiment found The most useful result was not “tools always win.” They did not. On this small, well-structured site, the stronger model often navigated the UI successfully. In the headline Sonnet runs, 14 of 15 UI-lane passes received full marks. Across all three Sonnet tasks, WebMCP also used about 2.4× as many context tokens on average—19,422 versus 8,117—because tool schemas and responses add context to the model's calls. That cost was not uniform: on the eligibility task, where the tool performed the most substantive rule evaluation, WebMCP used fewer tokens than browsing for both model sizes. We publish the overhead and the savings rather than reducing either to a universal claim. But five findings make the case for an agent-native web—and for a more mature agent-native publishing practice—much more interesting. Tools helped most when the model needed help When we moved from Sonnet 5 to the smaller Haiku 4.5 model, UI-lane accuracy fell by 41% on average across the task/lane pairs with room to fall. WebMCP-lane accuracy fell by 23%. The weaker model degraded roughly 1.8× less when the site gave it tools. The clearest reversal was the permit task: WebMCP trailed UI navigation with Sonnet (93% vs. 100%), but led it with Haiku (74% vs. 64%). Structured capability may matter less to the strongest agent on a clean demo site; it matters more as models get smaller, cheaper, and more widely deployed. “Optional” does not mean “unimportant” Our first permit tool treated the form schema as if it described the whole service process. If a field was not technically required, the agent could leave it blank without the tool mentioning it. The result passed form validation but could still look misleadingly complete to Mira. We changed the tool to report every field it left untouched. It now tells the agent which optional fields remain empty and invites another call if they apply. In the next five Sonnet attempts, complete 12-field forms increased from 0 of 5 to 4 of 5 , and task accuracy rose from 64% to 93%. That change made the agent aware of its omissions; it did not explain their administrative consequences. The site does not currently say whether leaving out an organization or phone number would delay review, trigger follow-up, affect approval, or make no difference at all. That exposed the larger civic-tech lesson: a form the browser will accept is not necessarily a form that will move smoothly through the service behind it. An agent-native form needs more than required/optional validation. Publishers should describe whether a field is required to submit, required only in certain circumstances, recommended to avoid de
video_title: The WebMCP Challenge
video_transcript_excerpt: Mira Tanaka survived a Kaiju attack. Now she needs compensation, a rebuilding permit, and a straight answer from the government. Unfortunately, her best help is a website and an AI agent trying to understand it. Government websites contain real decisions hidden across policy pages, exceptions, document lists, and forms. AI agents can help ease the stress, but they must reconstruct the service from site navigation and text. We built a complete 51-page fictional government agency enabled with Web MCP. When the CMS publishes the website, it also generates a machine-readable manifest. A small browser runtime converts that content into seven Web MCP tools for search, services, eligibility, requirements, offices, and forms. Mira's eligibility depends on her location, damage, income, insurance, business status, and filing window. An AI agent would need to browse the website and find that through brute-force web browsing. With Web MCP check eligibility, evaluate the publisher's encoded rules, and return the outcome: three applicable grants, five required documents, and supporting citations. We built tests to see if Web MCP could outperform an agent browsing the website directly. You can use your ChatGPT Web MCP browser to help Mira submit her construction permit form online. For the permit, Web MCP validates 12 values, derives the required reinforcement standard, and fills the real form. Then it stops. The tool exposes no submission operation. Mira reviews the highlighted fields and makes the final decision herself. Human control is part of the capability. We did not stop at a polished demo. The arena publishes 95 inspectable runs comparing Web MCP with ordinary browsing across three tasks, two model sizes, and two rounds. Web MCP was not always better, but it completed the eligibility task with fewer actions and substantially less time, and it reduced the accuracy loss when we moved to the smaller model. Our most important finding was not about speed. When policy becomes executable, meaning can be lost between the approved sentence and the encoded rule. A citation may point to the correct page while the logic still misses an exception. Agent native publishing therefore creates a new responsibility. Organizations must review not only what people will read, but what machines will execute. The Office of Kaiju Affairs is fictional. The civic problem is not. WebMCP gives public institutions a way to participate in the agent experience instead of leaving every agent to reverse engineer their websites. And the open source arena we shared gives citizens, publishers, and judges a way to measure where WebMCP helps.
