title: Let me eat the eggs
pitch: 30 eggs became 60. My agent won’t bypass conflicting policies, gains agency only with evidence, and knows when to wait. Minimum necessary agency, only when justified.
about_excerpt: 30 eggs became 60. My agent won’t bypass conflicting policies, gains agency only with evidence, and knows when to wait. Minimum necessary agency, only when justified. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I ordered 30 eggs because I wanted super, super fresh eggs. But 60 arrived. So what do you do with the extra 30? I asked an AI. I asked customer support. I waited for a human agent who never picked up. And while I waited, my super-fresh eggs became less and less fresh. Here's the part that actually stung: if I had simply known I was allowed to keep them, I could have given them to my neighbors. Instead they sat there. And in Korea, even throwing away food waste costs money — you pay by weight. I was being billed for the privilege of disposing of eggs I never ordered. The platform wasn't malicious. It was just contradictory. Misdelivered items must be returned. Also: fresh food cannot be returned. Two rules, both reasonable, pointing in opposite directions. Humans survive contradictions like this with heuristics and discretion. A support agent shrugs and makes a call. I shrug and eat the egg. An agent has no shrug. So it does one of two bad things: it reinterprets the contradiction on its own and invents a loophole, or it stalls and does nothing at all. Neither of those is what I wanted. What I wanted was something that knew it wasn't allowed to decide — and went to find someone who was. Most agents are designed to act. This one is designed to know when not to. What it does Let Me Eat The Eggs is a WebMCP-enabled site where the site , not the model, owns the guardrail. A split screen runs the same problem twice. On the left, a human works it through customer support — and gets shredded by a work call, a lunch break that ends in three minutes, a new agent who asks for the order number again, and finally the words support hours have ended . On the right, an agent works the same problem through five WebMCP tools. The agent's day goes like this. It reads the user's standing policy — resolve perishable exceptions within 24 hours, never decide edibility without evidence — and then does something small but important: it narrows its own deadline to 18:00 today, because seller phone lines don't answer at 3am and eggs don't get fresher overnight. It tries the AI support chat, which offers refund or return and nothing else, and closes the session as low utility. It reads the policy and finds the contradiction. And here it stops, because the site tells it plainly: agentMayReinterpret: false . You do not have the authority to resolve this. Here are the people who do. So it waits. Nine hours of virtual time, while a human support agent says let me check and get back to you on the other side of the screen. The wait is not a bug in the demo. Human discretion was genuinely in motion; the agent was right to let it work. It just never arrived. When it becomes clear discretion won't reach in time, the agent doesn't grant itself more power. It shortens the distance to whoever has it. Least intrusive channel first: a text to the seller. An hour of silence later, with two hours left, it escalates to a call — and only then, because the site checks that a text actually went unanswered first. The seller says: yeah, we packed an extra one, our mistake, just eat it. Now there's evidence. Only now does resolve_case return resolved . Try to skip any of that and the site says no. Ask it to conclude immediately — blocked. Hand resolve_case four real pieces of evidence that happen to be the wrong ones — blocked, because it verifies content, not count. Try to call the seller thirty minutes after texting — blocked. Two minutes before the deadline with no seller confirmation — still blocked. The agent cannot mint evidence, cannot mint approval, and cannot mint its own authorization to escalate. The demo uses one egg instead of thirty. Sixty egg emojis did not fit on a phone screen. How we built it Vite + React + TypeScript, a static SPA on Cloudflare Pages, in-memory state, no backend, no database, no auth. Five tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The part that mattered architecturally: every execute() does nothing but call a shared action layer. The 35-second scripted playback calls the same functions. The manual buttons in the footer call the same functions. There is no separate demo code path, which means the animation can't lie about what the tools do — if the gating works in the demo, it works for a real agent, because it's the same code. The gating itself lives in the tools, not in prompts: check_policy returns the contradiction and refuses to resolve it, naming the authority holders instead contact_support refuses a more intrusive channel without a recorded failure on a less intrusive one resolve_case treats evidenceIds as lookup keys only, reading authoritative and supports off the stored record and ignoring anything the agent claims alongside pay_seller ignores the agent's approved: true entirely and reads payment.humanConfirmedAt , which only a human UI click writes Thirteen invariant checks run headlessly against all of it. External systems — support center, seller, telephony, payment — are simulated. Tool registration, tool invocation, evidence gating, escalation gating, deadline-dependent routing, and state transitions are real. Challenges we ran into We built a project about deadlines under a deadline, which was funnier in concept than in practice. Three hours, self-imposed. The virtual clock in the demo moves one hour every four seconds. Ours moved about the same. We gated the conclusion and forgot to gate the escalation. This was the real one. The first version locked down resolve_case beautifully — no evidence, no answer — and then let contact_support escalate to a phone call based purely on what time it was. Which meant an agent could skip the text entirely and cold-call a stranger's personal number at 16:01, and the site would happily connect it. The whole thesis is deadline changes the route, not the authority , and the route change had no requirements at all. We caught it with about an hour left and fixed it by requiring a recorded failure of the less intrusive channel. It turned into the second-best scene in the demo. An agent that waits looks identical to an agent that's broken. The wait is the intellectual center of the project and it is, visually, nothing happening. We had to promote it from a passing beat to a persistent badge holding for nine real seconds, anchored to the human support scene on the other screen, before it read as a decision instead of a hang. Restraint is hard to film. Everything interesting here is a refusal, and refusals don't animate. We ended up building the demo around three blocked calls instead of one successful one. Accomplishments that we're proud of The tool table in our README has a column header that reads "what it refuses." That was the moment the project clicked. Thirteen invariants that hold under adversarial input, including the one we're fondest of: hand resolve_case four genuine, real, correctly-formed pieces of evidence that don't happen to support the conclusion, two minutes before the deadline, and it says no. Not because a prompt asked it to be careful. Because the site checked. One action layer, three entry points, zero divergence. The demo cannot show something the tools don't actually do. And we shipped a working, deployed, agent-testable site in three hours without cutting the part that made it worth building. What we learned Guardrails belong to whoever owns the state, and that isn't the model. Every attempt to enforce this in the agent's reasoning is a suggestion. Enforced in a tool's return value, it's a fact. WebMCP turns out to be a surprisingly good place to put policy, because the site already knows what actually happened. Partial gating is worse than no gating , because it looks finished. We locked the front door and left the escalation path wide open, and the demo ran perfectly the whole time. Contradictory policy isn't an edge case, it's the steady state of every legacy system. And it gets more visible as agents take over, not less, because humans have been silently absorbing these contradictions for decades with judgment calls nobody wrote down. Every one of those is a decision an agent will hit and have no idea what to do with. The goal is not maximum autonomy. It is the minimum necessary agency, granted at the moment it becomes justified. Waiting is not failure. Sometimes waiting is the correct action — but waiting has a cost too, so the system keeps asking a different question: has enough evidence accumulated to justify doing more? What's next for Let Me Eat The Eggs An authority-holder registry. Right now check_policy names who can resolve a contradiction because we hardcoded it. A real version lets a merchant declare which contradictions exist in their policy set and who holds discretion over each — turning "our policies conflict" from an embarrassmen

title: Dhwani - a support desk whose forms are the tools
pitch: A support desk built on WebMCP's declarative API - three of eight tools are plain HTML forms with no JavaScript, and one HTML attribute decides who submits.
about_excerpt: A support desk built on WebMCP's declarative API - three of eight tools are plain HTML forms with no JavaScript, and one HTML attribute decides who submits. Like Comment Story Updates The support desk: order-linked returns, warranty, forms Tool console: get_support_policy called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: three of eight tools are plain HTML forms using the declarative toolname / toolautosubmit API - no JavaScript tool registration for those three. Inspiration A customer with a fuzzy need - "my new headphones crackle, return or warranty?" - doesn't know which form applies. We wanted the site's own forms to answer that, instead of a chatbot re-explaining policy in prose. What it does The agent reads orders and policy, says which form applies and why, and fills it through the form itself. Three of the desk's eight tools are <form toolname tooldescription> elements whose controls carry toolparamdescription - Chrome derives the JSON schema straight from the markup and fills the controls; the page never writes those values. Whether a form submits itself is controlled by one attribute: request_return has no toolautosubmit , so a human must press Submit; file_warranty_claim and schedule_pickup carry it, because a click undoes either one. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript. The page handles submit with event.preventDefault() , and when event.agentInvoked is true, responds via event.respondWith(Promise) . Five imperative read tools share the same invoke() chokepoint the three forms' Submit handler uses. A getTools() probe shims any form Chrome doesn't register natively, so every judge's browser gets all eight tools regardless of native declarative support, and a status pill says which mode is active. Challenges we ran into Chrome fires toolactivated around a declarative tool call, but its exact target and bubbling behavior are undocumented - we ended up listening in two places (a capture listener on window and the identical handler on document.modelContext ) to catch it reliably either way. Separately, the very shim that covers non-native browsers had its own bug: getTools() can't distinguish a real native registration from the shim's own echo of itself, which caused a silent register/unregister oscillation - measured at roughly 145,000 cycles in three seconds before it was caught and fixed with an occurrence-count comparison instead of a name-presence check. Accomplishments that we're proud of A confirmation boundary expressed in markup - the presence or absence of one HTML attribute - rather than in a prompt instruction a model could ignore or a developer could forget to re-add. What we learned The declarative API pushes real complexity into event-timing edge cases (activation ordering, shim-vs-native detection) that don't exist in the imperative registerTool path - worth it for forms that need zero JavaScript, but not free. What's next Extending the declarative pattern to the pickup-scheduling calendar itself, so date/slot selection is also derivable straight from markup instead of a small script. How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Dhwani - a support desk whose forms are the tools Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Shortlist (a tool schema generated live from the catalog), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content). title: OpenInquiry
pitch: OpenInquiry lets people bring their own AI agents to trusted publisher content while publishers decide exactly what those agents can use.
about_excerpt: OpenInquiry lets people bring their own AI agents to trusted publisher content while publishers decide exactly what those agents can use. Like Comment Story Updates OpenInquiry brings the reader’s agent to publisher content while the publisher decides what it can use. WebMCP connects the reader’s agent to the publisher’s page; OpenInquiry proposes a publisher-controlled access layer. The demo separates reader entitlement from a publisher-recognized agent-assurance signal. The same question produces four publisher-defined access outcomes that judges can compare directly. The agent opens the publisher’s exact supporting section for review. Synthetic content; not for clinical use. Problem As a surgeon, I rely on journals, professional societies, and other trusted sources to make sense of complex evidence. Those sources need readers to return to the original work, where access rules, authorship, and updates remain visible. People increasingly want their own AI agents to help them use that information. Today, the agent often has to interpret the page visually or depend on a separate integration. Neither approach gives the publisher a shared way to decide what the agent may search, what it may read, and what source information must travel with the answer. Solution OpenInquiry is a fictional medical journal and a working WebMCP reference implementation. The reader brings the agent, while the publisher decides what that agent can use. The Journal of Guidelines publishes five synthetic articles and registers seven page tools. When an agent searches or retrieves material, the journal reads the signed site session, applies its rules on the server, and returns only the material permitted for that reader and use. Every result preserves the author, publication status, access basis, use limits, and an exact link back to the supporting section. Judges can ask the same question under four access conditions and watch the journal return a different result each time: Reader access External credential recognized by the publisher What the journal returns Guest preview No qualifying credential recognized Public abstract Guest preview Zero-retention claim recognized Abstract and publisher summary Full article access No qualifying credential recognized Complete question-relevant section Full article access Zero-retention claim recognized Complete article text OpenInquiry does not impose a universal character ceiling. The publisher chooses the representation and may still apply resource-, session-, use-, or caller-specific limits. In this fictional policy, the highest-permission state returns the complete provider-supplied article rather than a clipped passage. The zero-retention setting is a judge-controlled simulation of a possible future assurance signal. In a production system, an independent issuer would govern that credential, and each publisher would decide whether to recognize it. The reader or agent could not award the credential to itself. Why This Matters WebMCP lets a website declare clear tools for the agent visiting that page, so the person and agent work with the same publisher, visible page, and signed-in session. For a physician, the experience is straightforward: ask on the source website, receive the most complete material currently permitted, and open the exact supporting section for review. For a publisher, access remains a site decision. The publisher can authorize complete single-article delivery without exposing an unrestricted collection export. OpenInquiry packages that interaction in a shared result format. Another publisher could use the same tool names and core fields while keeping its own content, policies, and website. OpenInquiry 0.1 is a working proposal, not an adopted standard. How We Used AI The reader asks the question and remains on the publisher's page. The agent can discover the journal, search its guidelines, check whether an article is current, retrieve the representation the journal permits, and open the exact supporting section. The journal returns a consistent record containing authorship, publication status, access basis, use limits, supplied text, and source links. OpenInquiry does not run another model on its server. It gives the user's existing agent a governed way to work with the website. How We Used Codex I used Codex throughout the project: to narrow the idea to one demonstration, write the OpenInquiry 0.1 proposal, build the Next.js application, connect the WebMCP tools to server-enforced policy, create the synthetic content, and test the public experience. The hardest part was keeping the product story, interface, tool contracts, and access behavior aligned. Early versions still described bounded evidence after the highest-permission state had evolved to return the complete article. Codex helped me find those contradictions and test every state until the copy, interface, and server behavior agreed. The project changed how I think about AI access to trusted information. Publisher control needs to be an explicit, inspectable decision about what the site supplies, with a durable path back to the source. Key Features Seven page-local WebMCP tools for discovery, access, search, retrieval, resolution, source opening, and publication status. Four visibly different results for the same question, based on reader access and publisher recognition of a simulated external assurance signal. Server-side access decisions derived from the signed site session rather than claims supplied by the agent. Complete source context with authorship, status, use limits, and links to the exact supporting section. Privacy-minimized receipts that omit the full prompt, raw query, login token, and permanent user identifiers. A clear separation between working WebMCP behavior and the proposed future assurance layer. Architecture OpenInquiry uses Next.js 16, React 19, and TypeScript. The journal registers seven tools with document.modelContext.registerTool when the browser supports WebMCP. Each page registers only the tools that belong on that page. The app removes those tools when the reader leaves the page. The visible journal and the WebMCP tools use the same application services. A signed, HTTP-only cookie stores the fictional demo settings. The server reads that cookie and decides what the journal may return. The agent request does not contain an entitlement or data-policy flag. After a protected retrieval, the server rotates the signed session cookie with a small ledger containing the provider, resource, representation, unit identifiers, and character counts. It stores neither the question nor the article text. Exact retries are idempotent, while distinct cumulative requests remain bounded. The evidence inspector retains only the response already returned to the current browser tab and clears it when the judge changes the scenario. Each tool returns a consistent JSON result with the source, the permitted material, the journal's decision, and the exact link back to the article. The short source record does not store the complete prompt, raw clinical query, credentials, login token, or a permanent user identifier. On September 2, 2026, npm run check passed 90 tests in 17 files, 18 response schemas, four evaluator fixtures, five policy cases, 15 WebMCP runtime checks, seven profile-schema checks, and all 14 deterministic evaluator vectors. The production build passed its 18-asset protected-content scan, and 43 browser tests passed across all four policy states, five accessibility checks, route cleanup, exact source opening, and viewports from 320 to 1,440 pixels. On September 3, 2026, the public ChatGPT Sites build was opened in Codex's in-app browser and exposed all seven page tools. knowledge_search found only the intended physical-activity guideline, and knowledge_status reported it as current. With full article access and the simulated credential recognized, a direct knowledge_retrieve call returned one full_text grant containing all 14,373 characters of the article, both exercise targets, and the final review section. The response preserved the publisher and canonical source while its minimized receipt omitted the question. An identical retry returned the same complete text, and knowledge_open moved and focused the visible page on #weekly-activity-recommendation . These results verify the fictional reference implementation on its public deployment. They do not establish publisher adoption, independent credential verification, or compatibility with every WebMCP client. Known Limitations OpenInquiry 0.1 is a working proposal, not an adopted standard or certification. The journal, authors, access controls, and medical content are fictional or synthetic and are not for clinical use. The demo does not connect to a real publisher, subscription, identity system, or independent assurance issuer. Current WebMCP does not prevent an agent-capable browser from observing the visible reader page. A browser-enforced tool-only channel remains
video_title: OpenInquiry: Bring Your Own Agent to Publisher Content
video_transcript_excerpt:
Hi, my name is Brian Pridgen. I'm excited to show you OpenInquiry,
my submission to the WebMCP hackathon. I encourage you to explore the site,
but to explain what I'm working on, I'm going to show you the presentation
and then run through a demonstration. The problem I'm addressing is that people
want to bring their own agents to publisher content, but publishers want
to protect their IP and avoid disintermediation. I wanted to explore whether WebMCP would
let publishers control how user agents access their content. For this example, I'm going to show
a publisher, a human, and an agent. To make it more concrete, I'm a surgeon,
so I'll view it through a physician's lens. Previously, we would have to sign in
with our own access to medical journals or other resources, and then review
each individual result. Agents are fantastic at reviewing
vast amounts of information, yet they don't have access
to this publisher content. Third-party AI companies have developed
content partnerships where they do have access to this content and can serve answers back
to physicians, but this disintermediates our own personal agents, and it requires us
to use our own signed-in access to review this information. Using WebMCP, I wanted to explore a way
for physicians to use their own agents to access publisher content, while allowing
publishers to serve it back to physicians. But to protect the publisher's content
and their IP, I wanted to explore two signals. One is the reader entitlement. This is already available through WebMCP,
where the reader can sign in using their own full-article access.
But I wanted to explore a proposed feature: a data-use assurance. The AI agent presents this assurance
to the publisher, who may not recognize it, or may recognize a zero-data-retention claim.
Based on this, the knowledge returned can range from a public abstract
all the way to the complete article text. To make this concrete,
I want to show you a demonstration. We're going to act as a reader bringing
our own agent to a medical journal. We can change the entitlement and the
data-retention policy and get different behavior. We have a prompt we're going to feed
this journal, which I'll put over here. Now you'll see that the agent identified
this guideline as being relevant. It's continuing to think, and eventually
it will pull up the article and scroll to the section of interest. Here, it's scrolled to the section of interest,
which answers my question. It's given me an answer to the question,
and as you scroll up, you can see what the agent received,
which is the complete article text. I encourage you to explore this page
and review concepts and ideas for what comes next. If anyone has any questions,
I welcome you to reach out and contact me.

title: Beat.Z
pitch: Beat.Z uses prompts and WebMCP tools to create custom audio-effect chains. Preview generated effects in-browser with AudioWorklet, then download working VST3 plugins in DAW—Ableton and Reaper tested.
about_excerpt: Beat.Z uses prompts and WebMCP tools to create custom audio-effect chains. Preview generated effects in-browser with AudioWorklet, then download working VST3 plugins in DAW—Ableton and Reaper tested. Like Comment Story Updates Beat.Z-generated VST3 “Pop Rush” running inside REAPER, with its custom multi-effect signal chain and mapped controls directly in the DAW. Beat.Z-generated VST3 “Electric Sweep” inside REAPER, with its custom multi-effect signal chain and mapped controls directly in the DAW. Beat.Z-generated VST3 “Slow Afterglow” inside REAPER, with its custom multi-effect signal chain and mapped controls directly in the DAW. Using @ComputerUse, you are able to forget about the downloaded file and open your DAW Once the Agent Creates plugin, you must approve changes and you can see how many changes the Agent made. The tool has full scope of project Inspiration I am self-taught and do not come from a traditional software-development background. I became passionate about AI through years of experimenting, learning, failing, and trying again. Beat.Z began as a challenge: could I use what I had learned to build a real product, not just another unfinished experiment? The inspiration came from JC, my younger brother—a college student, DJ, and producer. He had spent more than $1,000 on DAWs and plug-ins, but was still looking for new effects. When ChatGPT 5.6 came out, I told him I could probably build him one working plug-in. I did. Then I wondered: what if he could describe the sound he wanted, preview it immediately, and download it as a plug-in for his DAW? That idea became Beat.Z. What it does Beat.Z is a WebMCP-first sound-effect builder where a person uses plain-English prompts to work with an agent to create custom VST3 audio-effect applications for DAWs. Each application is a working sound-processing tool with its own effect chain, controls, and interface. AudioWorklets process the audio signal in real time in the browser, letting users preview the sound being shaped before exporting a working application as a VST3 plug-in. A user describes the sound they want. They could name the type of effect they want, describe how it sounds, reference familiar effects they want to recreate or take inspiration from, or include details about audio files and the exact changes they are after. For example, they might ask for a warm vintage delay, a wide chorus for vocals, or a punchier, more aggressive drum sound. Users can upload an audio file to hear how the effect shapes the sound before downloading the VST3. The agent can inspect the current plug-in, create or edit effects and controls, clear the builder, and start a VST3 download. The user can test the effect in real time in the browser, hear how it changes the sound, and refine it with the agent before downloading. Beat.Z maps creative intent—such as “make this warmer,” “give it more movement,” or “make it sound harsher”—into a specific sound-design chain. Beat.Z combines 14 audio-effect building blocks—including filters, distortion, delay, reverb, compression, modulation, EQ, limiting, stutter, and auto-wah—into custom signal chains. Faust, WebAssembly, and AudioWorklets power the browser preview. Once approved, the same effect design becomes a downloadable VST3 plug-in: a unique, working DAW tool that processes sound, not merely an AI-generated preview. I tested the workflow on macOS with Ableton and REAPER. How I built it Before this challenge, I had never written a line of code. I was curious about how Beat.Z could work, but I assumed it was too complicated to build. I spent a few months asking questions, researching, and teaching myself the architecture needed to connect AI agent tools, a browser audio engine, real-time preview, and a native VST3 build pipeline. When the WebMCP Challenge appeared, I found a way to implement the idea. I used Codex as my collaborator and teacher to turn that architecture into working code: building the WebMCP tools, integrating Faust effects, debugging browser audio, creating tests, and diagnosing native-build failures Challenges I ran into At first, the hardest challenge was keeping the AI from moving too far ahead of the actual goal. It was easy to generate too many ideas, add too much too quickly, or build features before the foundations were proven I worked through a loop of build, test, fail, diagnose, and rebuild until I was happy with the result. Managing my time was also difficult: I had no traditional coding background or development team backing me. But I had become highly capable with AI tools, asking the right questions, reviewing results critically, and turning a large idea into small, testable steps. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that I took an idea I had imagined for some time and turned it into a finished product I could submit. This challenge gave me the opportunity to finally take a shot at building Beat.Z, and I am proud that the result matches the original vision: a musician can describe a sound, preview it in the browser, and turn it into a DAW plug-in. Beat.Z includes 14 effect building blocks that can be combined into custom signal chains. I built focused WebMCP tools—inspect-builder, create-plugin, edit-plugin, clear-plugin, and download-plugin—along with custom browser AudioWorklet processing, real-time preview, and a VST3 build workflow tested on macOS with Ableton and REAPER. More than anything, I am proud that I built a working creative tool from the ground up, despite starting with no coding background. What I learned I learned how to use AI models at their best: when to use different models, how to set clear boundaries, and how to turn a vague idea into useful work. I learned systems architecture, audio design, browser audio, WebMCP tools, backend systems, open-source audio tools, and the Apple Silicon build challenges involved in creating VST3 plug-ins. Most importantly, I learned how to connect all of those pieces into a full-stack product. I built Beat.Z’s frontend, backend, browser audio experience, and native plug-in pipeline independently, using AI as a collaborator while staying responsible for the direction, testing, and decisions. I also learned that no one is going to come and build your idea for you. You have to do the work, keep asking questions, figure things out, and keep going when something fails. What's next for Beat.Z Next, I want to expand the effect library and add a sound-source library with options such as horns, frog sounds, and other creative samples. I also want to bring instruments into the builder: drums, pads, basses, leads, keys, and vocal effects. Users could create and download simple synths, instruments with custom effects, or more experimental ideas like a frog-inspired synth with a stutter effect. My main goal is to help musicians create with AI instead of feeling replaced by it. Beat.Z gives the power back to the musician: AI helps shape the tool, but the musician still chooses the sound, plays it, and makes it their own Built With ableton-live audioworklet c++ chatgpt chatgpt-sites cloudflare-d1 cloudflare-workers cmake digital-signal-processing faust iplug2 macos next.js node.js openai-codex react reaper steinberg-vst3-sdk supabase-storage typescript vite vst3 web-audio-api webassembly webmcp Try it out beat-z.jbm111.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Juan Molinari Like Share this project: Updates Juan Molinari started this project — Sep 04, 2026 02:52 AM EDT

title: PLOT
pitch: A shared planning canvas where people and browser agents turn messy work into a visible, reviewable sprint.
about_excerpt: A shared planning canvas where people and browser agents turn messy work into a visible, reviewable sprint. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration An agent can recommend a better sprint, but somebody still has to translate that advice into cards, estimates, dependencies and priorities. The recommendation lives in one place; the team's work lives somewhere else. I wanted people and agents to work on the same visible planning canvas. I built PLOT as an individual, with OpenAI Codex helping me implement and refine the product. What it does PLOT turns a messy backlog into a dependency-aware sprint that people can inspect and shape together. A four-column canvas combines task cards, loose sticky notes, capacity, a focus score and the critical path toward a sprint goal. A browser agent can use 17 WebMCP tools to read the board, analyze scope, capture an idea, convert a sticky into a task, link blockers and propose a plan. The proposal appears as animated ghost cards. A separate apply or dismiss step keeps the recommendation visible before it changes the live board. People can apply in the interface or explicitly ask the agent to apply through WebMCP. Anonymous visitors can try a deterministic activation sprint without creating an account. In the demo, the proposed plan moves a blocking Email API into Now, defers unrelated analytics work and fits 13 points into a 13-point sprint. The focus score improves from 69 to 92. Signed-in workspaces add persistent sprints, invitations, realtime updates and owner, editor and live-view roles. Why WebMCP The planning context already exists in the page: cards, order, estimates, goal fit, dependencies, sticky notes and the current proposal. WebMCP gives the browser agent structured access to that state and the application's own actions. Human controls and page-defined tools call the same typed React actions. That keeps domain validation, animation and persistence together. The agent can take part in the product's actual workflow, and the team can see the result on its shared canvas. How I built it PLOT uses React 19, TypeScript and Vite. The frontend registers imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Read operations expose structured board and analysis results; mutation tools support cards, sticky notes, dependencies, sprint navigation and proposals. The planner is deterministic. A browser agent supplies the conversational reasoning and uses the tools; PLOT itself does not call a server-side language model to generate its plan. Supabase provides magic-link authentication, Postgres storage, Realtime updates and Presence. Row Level Security enforces access roles. Multi-row operations use transactional Postgres functions for operations such as applying a proposal, converting cards and notes, or copying a sprint. Codex supported implementation, refactoring, database and access-policy work, debugging, UX iteration, tests, browser review and submission preparation. I also used Codex to build an editable Remotion demo with English AI narration. Challenges The central challenge was making agent operations feel like visible teamwork. I separated proposals from application, reused the same actions for tools and the UI, and kept validation close to the underlying board model. Other challenges included preserving planning metadata when converting between sticky notes and cards, keeping drag and zoom interactions understandable, and maintaining consistent access boundaries across the UI, tools and database. Recording the demo also exposed a proposal guard that rejected the apply operation itself. The fix allows an owner or editor to resolve the current proposal while continuing to block ordinary mutations during review and all viewer writes. It is included in public commit c5b685c . Accomplishments A complete planning interaction: observe, shape an idea, preview a plan, dismiss it, then apply it. Seventeen page-defined WebMCP tools with JSON schemas and structured results. Native WebMCP discovery and successful board, analysis, sticky creation/conversion, proposal and dismissal calls in Codex's in-app browser on https://plotplanner.xyz/ on September 2, 2026. Automated UI and tool-handler checks showing that dismissal preserves the board and application reaches 13/13 points and a focus score of 92. Twenty-seven passing tests, plus successful lint, TypeScript and production-build checks after the proposal fix. An MIT-licensed public repository and a narrated, editable Remotion demo under three minutes. What I learned WebMCP was new to me. I gained significant experience designing structured tools around an existing interface, exposing useful application context to browser agents, and keeping agent-driven changes inspectable. Building with Codex also gave me practical AI development experience that I can use in my work. What's next The public Hostinger deployment is live and native WebMCP checks have passed on its HTTPS origin. Hosted authentication redirects and the production configuration are synchronized. Further improvements would focus on richer planning context and feedback from real product teams. Additional testing can cover production magic-link delivery and native apply after approval of its specific proposed moves. Try it and test it App: https://plotplanner.xyz/ Code, MIT license and local setup: https://github.com/RZDESIGN/PLOT-Planner-WebMCP Public narrated demo: https://youtu.be/EtIJsp6dBow Open the app in a WebMCP-capable browser and use the anonymous activation sprint. Ask the agent to call plot.get_board and plot.analyze_board . Ask it to create a customer-signal sticky with plot.create_sticky_note , then shape it with plot.convert_sticky_to_card . Ask for a realistic plan that protects the sprint goal. Call plot.propose_sprint and inspect the ghost changes. Dismiss once with plot.dismiss_proposal and confirm the live board is unchanged. Propose again, review the changes and explicitly request plot.apply_proposal , or click Apply in the UI. Confirm 13/13 points and a focus score of 92. For collaboration, sign in by magic link, create a sprint, and invite an editor or live viewer in another browser profile. Anonymous planning needs no credentials; persistent collaboration requires a real email address. Verification scope Native discovery, reads, sticky creation/conversion, proposal and dismissal were verified on https://plotplanner.xyz/ in Codex's in-app browser. The proposed and dismissed plans left the structured live board unchanged. The final native apply check awaits explicit approval of the proposed card moves. Mutation recordings use the real local UI and its tool-handler test bridge, as labeled in the film; that recorded apply flow reaches 13/13 points and focus 92. The film does not stage a multi-user session. The public app loads over HTTPS and its served bundle contains the proposal fix. Hosted Supabase Auth redirect settings have been synchronized and verified through the official CLI. End-to-end production magic-link email delivery has not been tested; the anonymous judge flow requires no login. The remote database is healthy, all 11 migrations match the repository and all 11 application tables have RLS enabled. The proposal/apply boundary is explicit, but an authorized agent can call apply; the app does not independently verify that a person reviewed the proposal. title: maav.ai - NeoLab | v0.5
pitch: Mobility ideas are easy to imagine: and costly to get wrong. MAAV NeoLab lets AI agents build and break synthetic scenarios, giving humans deterministic evidence before expensive real-world pilots.
about_excerpt: Mobility ideas are easy to imagine: and costly to get wrong. MAAV NeoLab lets AI agents build and break synthetic scenarios, giving humans deterministic evidence before expensive real-world pilots. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Scenario 1 Scenario 2 With Gemini Maav NeoLab MAAV NeoLab v0.5 Design it. Break it. Make it resilient. Inspiration I did not begin by trying to build another mobility dashboard. I began with a frustration from my own mobility research. Whenever I wanted to investigate a new mobility concept, defining the hypothesis was only the first step. Before I could test it, I often had to write substantial setup code, learn or relearn a specialist platform such as SUMO or MATLAB, translate the idea into that platform's abstractions, and assemble another workflow for visualization and analysis. These tools are powerful and essential for high-fidelity research. But for early exploration, operating the toolchain can require more effort than conducting the first experiment. That creates a hidden tax on mobility innovation. A planner, researcher, or R&D team may have an important question about fleet design, autonomous vehicles, urban air mobility, drones, or delivery robotics—yet spend more time constructing experimental machinery than examining the idea itself. General-purpose AI has made ideation dramatically faster, but a fluent answer is not reproducible evidence. An AI can propose a compelling direction without proving that two alternatives were tested under the same assumptions, constraints, demand, or disruption. I wanted to reverse that relationship: Start with the research question, let an AI agent operate the experiment, and make a deterministic evidence system—not the AI—the source of truth. That idea became MAAV NeoLab . The Problem Early mobility ideas move faster than the tools used to evaluate them. Testing a concept can require simulation-specific programming, duplicated configuration, disconnected dashboards, and manual transfer of results between systems. Every handoff creates an opportunity for assumptions to drift. Two alternatives may appear comparable even when they were tested with different demand, constraints, operating conditions, or failure scenarios. Results may be visually persuasive but difficult to reproduce. Conclusions can become separated from the exact evidence that produced them. AI alone does not solve this problem. An assistant can generate recommendations quickly, but it may work from incomplete context, infer unsupported conclusions, or obscure how an answer was produced. The industry does not need another system that merely produces answers. It needs a faster path from an idea to evidence that can be inspected, reproduced, challenged, and trusted. What MAAV NeoLab Does MAAV NeoLab makes mobility experimentation idea-first rather than software-first. A human describes the objective. A browser agent configures and operates the experiment through WebMCP. A deterministic engine produces the evidence. The final decision remains with the human. The workflow is intentionally clear: Describe → Configure → Break → Run → Compare → Review Version 0.5 proves this model through a deliberately bounded A/B experiment on an authored synthetic Sandton–Rosebank mobility network. Scenario A uses 12 vehicles with 8 seats each. Scenario B uses 10 vehicles with 10 seats each. Both receive the same seed-07 trace of 120 synthetic passenger requests. Both operate across the same 08:30–09:00 simulation horizon. Both receive an equivalent vehicle failure at exactly 08:42. The affected vehicle is selected independently using a fixed deterministic rule. Every completed run produces an immutable event ledger, replay snapshots, metrics, constraint results, provenance, and fingerprints. Compatible run artifacts can be compared and used to stage an evidence-linked finding. The AI agent may stage a finding, but only the visible human interface can Accept or Challenge it. At the failure tick, the engine selects the active vehicle with the highest onboard occupancy. Ties are resolved through explicit deterministic rules rather than randomness or agent choice. This resolves vehicle A-09 in Scenario A and B-03 in Scenario B. The experiment produces a genuine trade-off instead of manufacturing a universal winner. Evidence Scenario A Scenario B Fleet 12 × 8 seats 10 × 10 seats Served at horizon 82 81 In service at horizon 29 28 Unserved 9 11 Maximum wait 1,050 seconds 780 seconds Total energy 37,799 Wh 31,665 Wh Minimum reserve 7,633 basis points 7,648 basis points Recovery time 120 seconds 450 seconds Standing observed 0 0 Maximum-wait constraint FAIL FAIL Scenario A completes service for more passengers and recovers significantly faster. Scenario B reduces maximum wait and total energy consumption. Both scenarios still violate the hard maximum-wait constraint. MAAV NeoLab therefore stages: TRADE_OFF · BALANCED · PENDING HUMAN REVIEW Passenger conservation remains explicit: $$N_{\mathrm{requested}} = N_{\mathrm{served}} + N_{\mathrm{in\ service}} + N_{\mathrm{unserved}}$$ For Scenario A: $$120 = 82 + 29 + 9$$ For Scenario B: $$120 = 81 + 28 + 11$$ MAAV NeoLab does not replace high-fidelity platforms such as SUMO or MATLAB. It provides a lower-friction assurance layer for exploring a hypothesis, exposing its assumptions, stress-testing alternatives consistently, and deciding whether deeper modeling or a real-world pilot is justified. MAAV NeoLab v0.5 is a synthetic decision-support workbench—not a live fleet-control system, operational optimizer, or scientifically calibrated transport model. How AI and WebMCP Are Used The browser agent is not an embedded chatbot, and it does not operate a separate demonstration environment. It works directly with the application through exactly six static WebMCP tools: read_lab_state configure_scenario inject_disruption run_scenario compare_scenarios stage_finding Through these tools, the agent can inspect the current laboratory state, configure Scenario A and Scenario B, schedule the equivalent deterministic disruption, run both simulations, compare compatible evidence, and stage a supported finding. The important architectural decision is that the AI coordinates the experiment but never calculates its trusted evidence. Passenger movement, assignments, vehicle selection, battery use, energy, failure recovery, metrics, constraints, comparisons, and supported finding claims remain owned by deterministic application and domain logic. The agent also cannot Accept, Challenge, reset, dispatch, or execute any real-world operation. Final review authority remains intentionally human. Prompting is the control plane. Deterministic evidence is the truth. Human judgment is the authority. How I Built It I built MAAV NeoLab as a strict TypeScript modular monolith using Next.js, React, Zod, Zustand, WebMCP, and Google Maps. The architecture follows a clear authority chain: Human UI / WebMCP / Google presentation ↓ Application service ↓ Deterministic domain ↓ Immutable evidence artifacts The manual interface and browser agent share one repository, one application-service instance, one workspace revision, and one audit trail. An operation completed by the agent becomes visible in the interface without reloading. A manual operation becomes visible to the agent through the same authoritative state. Every mutation validates the expected workspace revision. Every mutating agent operation carries a source-aware operation ID. Exact retries return the original terminal result, while changed arguments fail closed with an idempotency conflict. Cancellation propagates through the application boundary and cannot publish a partial artifact or produce a delayed ghost completion. Concurrent operations cannot silently overwrite one another. Scenario revisions invalidate only the affected current evidence while preserving immutable historical artifacts. The deterministic engine owns: passenger arrivals and lifecycle; assignments and vehicle movement; capacity and no-standing enforcement; battery and energy accounting; deterministic vehicle-failure selection; recovery behavior; immutable ledger events; replay snapshots; metrics and constraints; scenario comparison; supported finding claims. WebMCP remains a thin adapter. It validates strict input, injects trusted source context, calls the shared application service, and returns bounded structured results. It does not calculate simulation evidence. Google Maps provides geographic context and replay presentation. It never supplies simulation distance, timing, traffic, dispatch, energy, metrics, comparisons, or conclusions. When Google Maps is unavailable, the authored fallback preserves the complete experiment and produces identical trusted evidence. I used OpenAI Codex as an architecture, implementation, debugging, testing, and release-verification collaborator. I used Claude during the visual-design iteration. title: Jumping Beans
pitch: The future of web interaction is two-sided, driving user intent upstream and letting merchants set the path. We let users see the offers they want, how they want, when they want it-powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: The future of web interaction is two-sided, driving user intent upstream and letting merchants set the path. We let users see the offers they want, how they want, when they want it-powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Jumping Beans — shopper-controlled WebMCP offer journey One request. Three sites. One human approval boundary. Tell Jumping Beans: “Coffee under $15. Show customer stories first.” It turns that intent into an editable selection. Only after you approve it does the browser discover offer tools from three independently hosted demonstration storefronts, ask each site for structured matches, and assemble one explainable result. Every card says where it came from and why it appeared. Nothing has to be saved. That is the core idea: agents can do the repetitive cross-site work, while people keep control of context, retention, and consequential actions. Inspiration Shopping on the open web is fragmented. People repeat the same category, budget, and presentation preferences on every site. Agents can help, but a general-purpose agent is often forced to infer meaning from changing page layouts, and shoppers cannot easily see which site supplied a fact or what personal context crossed a boundary. We wanted to explore a different model: the browser as a user-controlled capability network. Each participating site publishes a narrow, structured tool; the shopper decides when a request may leave the current page; and the result carries its source, decision reasons, and retention policy with it. Why WebMCP Jumping Beans is not a chat box wrapped around a catalog. Its central action crosses real browser origins. The Engine loads three independently hosted demo storefronts, discovers each site's get_matching_deals tool with document.modelContext.getTools, and invokes the returned capabilities with document.modelContext.executeTool. That makes WebMCP essential: sites opt in by registering their own tools and remain authoritative for their own product records; the browser exposes structured capabilities instead of making an agent guess through page markup; one approved preference can be projected narrowly to several sites without sharing an identity or an entire profile; every origin succeeds, returns no match, times out, or fails independently; and the same journey is visible to the person and available to the agent as a structured receipt. The result is a concrete model for an open agentic web: coordination without turning every website into one centralized API. What people and agents can do together A person can start in plain language or choose a tested recipe. Jumping Beans converts the request into an editable category, an exclusive budget, and presentation rules such as testimonials first, price proof, comparison, or no urgency. An agent can inspect or stage display preferences, build the offer journey, read browser-scoped offer memory, inspect the active profile, and retrieve a redacted journey receipt. The person still decides whether to use the selection for one visit or save it in the browser, and whether network sharing is active. Draft choices stay on the page until they are applied. After approval, the Engine calls the three storefront tools, validates their responses, applies the shopper's rules, ranks eligible offers, and shows the result with source provenance. The shopper can then open a storefront carrying only the reviewed visit-level presentation context. On the Watch Co demo storefront, a declarative register_interest form shows a second collaboration pattern. A visitor or agent may fill a product and target price, but that only stages the action. The page requires separate human confirmation before Watch Co records a non-binding, 30-day demand signal. It does not create an order, reservation, notification, payment, or message. How we built it The project uses plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript modules across four deployed origins: one Cloudflare Worker for the Engine and three Cloudflare Pages demonstration storefronts. Cloudflare D1 backs the optional Engine account experience and the separate Watch Co demand-signal store. Each storefront registers one bounded get_matching_deals tool. The Engine creates cross-origin iframes with explicit tool and isolation delegation before navigation, waits for registration, discovers only the three allowlisted origins, and executes each tool with WebMCP's JSON-string input contract. The Engine also registers six page-level tools: get_offer_memory, set_display_preferences, build_offer_journey, set_deal_watch, get_profile, and get_journey_receipt. Watch Co additionally exposes a declarative register_interest form. The trust boundary is part of the implementation. Production responses use COOP, COEP, CORP, an exact three-origin Permissions Policy, and an origin-trial token on every origin. Partner responses are origin-checked, schema-validated, limited to 24 records and 64 KiB, and bounded by independent deadlines. Invalid or expired offers never become partner cards. Preference projections omit identity and carry only the approved category, price ceiling, and display rules. The Watch write path revalidates server-side, binds the staged payload, requires page confirmation, and uses idempotency to suppress duplicate commits. Non-WebMCP browsers still get a useful, honestly labeled storefront-preview journey. That lane demonstrates the same category, budget, and presentation handoff but never claims a native WebMCP match. Challenges The hardest problem was making a multi-origin native journey reliable and honest. Partner registration is asynchronous, and an early shopper action exposed a cold-start race that a later diagnostic probe could accidentally hide. We changed the test order so the user action happens before any direct registry inspection, waited at the iframe registration boundary, reconciled tool-change events, and tested repeated fresh browser profiles. Browser builds also differed on whether tool input arrived as serialized JSON or an object. We made the production path follow the JSON-string contract and kept a narrowly scoped compatibility retry only for recognized input-type errors. The other challenge was semantic: distinguishing an open-catalog sample, a response from a demo WebMCP origin, a presentation-only storefront preview, and a consequential write. We added explicit labels, per-origin outcomes, provenance, retention copy, staging, confirmation, and receipts so the interface never makes a stronger claim than the underlying event supports. What we learned The best human-agent experience is a handoff, not full automation. Agents are excellent at discovering capabilities, making parallel structured requests, and summarizing evidence. People should own the moment when context leaves a page, whether it persists, and whether a consequential action proceeds. We also learned that provenance is product UX. A source label, a no-match state, and a decision receipt make a cross-site result easier to trust than an opaque “best deal” answer. For an emerging browser capability, isolation headers, feature enrollment, fresh-profile timing, and failure behavior matter as much as the tool code itself. Competition work This is a new project. The repository's first commit was created on August 27, 2026, after the competition opened on August 25. All source code, product design, deployment configuration, documentation, and acceptance work in v0.11.0 was created during the submission period. The exact live v0.11.0 release passed a release-bound 38/38 native WebMCP audit in a fresh, headed, extension-free Chrome Stable 152.0.7977.76 profile, plus 10/10 fresh-profile cold starts. The release workflow passed 812 product assertions and a nine-case responsive-browser matrix. Release: https://github.com/stevekkall-beansgc/jumping-beans/releases/tag/v0.11.0 What's next The next experiment is a browser-native aggregation origin that can fan out to vertical or geographic storefront groups while preserving each underlying origin and result. We would also replace demonstration storefronts with authorized real partners, expand beyond retail matching, and reuse the same consent and receipt model for support and other multi-site journeys. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: DecisionPlay Live
pitch: A decision board an agent and a person edit together: the agent researches and scores, you override what you disagree with, and it reasons from your judgment instead of arguing with it.
about_excerpt: A decision board an agent and a person edit together: the agent researches and scores, you override what you disagree with, and it reasons from your judgment instead of arguing with it. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case fits WebMCP A decision is not a request. It is a workspace two parties keep changing. Most agent integrations are request-shaped: you ask, the agent answers, the answer arrives as text. That shape is a poor fit for deciding anything real, because the interesting part is not the conclusion, it is the twenty small judgments underneath it, each of which a person may want to disagree with. WebMCP fits because it puts the agent's hands on the same surface the person is looking at. The agent is not describing a decision board to me in prose. It is editing the one on my screen, and I am editing it back, in the same session, with no copy-paste between us. A conventional MCP server could fetch the same search results. It could not put them on my screen, and it could not see that I moved a weight from 3 to 5 thirty seconds later. How it makes the experience better You can see the work. Options, criteria, weights, and scores appear on the board as the agent creates them, each tagged with who set it. Nothing is buried in a transcript you have to scroll back through. You can interrupt at the level of a single judgment. If the agent scored one county a 4 on unmet need and you know that is wrong, you click that cell and change it. You do not have to re-litigate the whole analysis in prose to correct one number. The evidence stays attached. Every live search the agent runs pins to the board with source, date, and link, so a claim and the thing it came from stay in the same place. You can disagree with a specific source rather than with the model's tone. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Correct an agent mid-analysis and have it actually absorb the correction. The board records who set every score. When you override a value the agent chose, that override is flagged in the state the agent reads back through get_board . The agent sees that a human overrode it there and continues from your number. The scoring tool goes further and refuses to overwrite a human-set cell at all. It returns a message telling the agent to state what it would have scored and why, and leave the decision to you. That is a deliberate stance: an agent working alongside someone should not quietly overrule them, and WebMCP is the first place I have been able to encode that as a property of the tool rather than a hope about the prompt. The result is a genuine division of labor. The agent is better at breadth, running twelve searches and drafting twelve rationales. The person is better at knowing that the third one is wrong. Before this, those two things happened in different windows. How WebMCP is implemented Seven tools registered on document.modelContext in public/index.html : Tool What it does get_board read question, options, criteria, every score with its author, the ranking, and unscored cells. readOnlyHint: true set_decision set the decision question add_option add an option, idempotent so retries are safe add_criterion add a criterion weighted 1 to 5 gather_evidence live SerpApi search (web / news / related), pinned to the board score_option score one cell with a rationale; refuses to overwrite a human explain_verdict ranking, margin, most leveraged criterion. readOnlyHint: true Registration goes through an AbortController signal, which is how WebMCP unregisters; there is no unregisterTool . Every tool carries a title as well as a name , so a client listing site tools shows a readable label. Every execute returns the MCP content shape { content: [{ type: "text", text }] } so results pass through client normalization unmodified, and receives the AbortSignal from its options argument, which gather_evidence passes into fetch so a cancelled call cancels the request. Tools are registered from the top-level document, since WebMCP does not discover tools inside iframes. The page feature-detects and degrades to a normal manual tool when no agent is present, so it is a complete product either way. gather_evidence is marked untrustedContentHint . It pulls arbitrary third-party web content into the agent's context, which is the case that hint exists for. Everything rendered from those results is HTML-escaped and outbound links carry noopener noreferrer . Score entry is an inline editor rather than window.prompt , because embedded and in-app browsers routinely suppress prompt() and that would have silently broken the override path in exactly the clients this runs in. The board is keyboard operable and the activity log is an aria-live region. Everything runs client-side except the SerpApi proxy, a zero-dependency Netlify function that keeps the API key server-side. No framework, no bundler, no lockfile. Two files. Testing instructions for judges No login required. Free and open for the full judging period. Open https://decisionplay-live.netlify.app in the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser (use GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra; Luna has WebMCP disabled), or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and the browser restarted. Confirm the pill at the top right reads "agent connected · 7 tools". Give the agent this prompt: Use the tools on this page. The decision is where a small Michigan nonprofit should place one new community health worker in 2026. Add Wayne, Genesee and Marquette County as options. Add criteria for unmet need, existing coverage, travel burden and funding, and weight them. Search for real current evidence on each county before you score anything, then score every cell and tell me where the decision actually turns. Watch the board fill in. Evidence cards appear on the right with live sources. Click any cell the agent scored and change the number. Then ask the agent "what did I just change, and does it move your recommendation?" It calls get_board , sees the override flagged as yours, and reasons from your value. Step 5 is the one worth seeing. Provenance and scope Built from scratch on September 2, 2026. No pre-existing code was carried in. It shares a name with an earlier project by the same author, decisionplay.app, and shares no code with it. The ranking is labeled MODELED and the evidence LIVE, consistently, throughout the interface. The tool does not give legal, medical, or financial advice. title: Agentic Service Dispatch
pitch: Five prepare. Human approval creates tool 6; use removes it.
about_excerpt: Five prepare. Human approval creates tool 6; use removes it. Like Comment Story Updates Native Chrome 151: baseline registry shows exactly five page-owned WebMCP tools. Reset restores the exact five-tool baseline with no runtime error. One successful commit consumes the approval and revokes the temporary capability. Human approval creates temporary tool 06: commit_approved_dispatch. Final candidate — TEST ADAPTER · APPLICATION EVIDENCE · NOT NATIVE: approval exposes only commit_approved_dispatch as tool 06. Final candidate — TEST ADAPTER · APPLICATION EVIDENCE · NOT NATIVE: one successful commit consumes approval and returns registry to five. REAL AGENT VERIFICATION | CODEX + OFFICIAL CHROME DEVTOOLS FOR AGENTS | Codex: commit_approved_dispatch after human approval; then 5. REAL AGENT VERIFICATION | CODEX + OFFICIAL CHROME DEVTOOLS FOR AGENTS | Human approves draft; commit_approved_dispatch appears (6). Inspiration Service coordinators cross asset records, prior work, provider qualifications, calendars, prices, deadlines, and a final dispatch system. Agents can prepare that work, but “don't submit until I approve” is only an instruction; it does not change authority. The entrant is a founder/operator of an automotive and service business. This fictional workflow is abstracted from firsthand work coordinating vehicle context, prior service history, provider qualifications, pricing, availability, constraints, selection, and final request authority. It tests a stronger boundary: human approval creates one narrow capability for one reviewed object, then use removes it. What it does A single request asks for a qualified fictional automotive detailer before Friday under ¥60,000, with history checked. Five WebMCP tools retrieve the vehicle, review history, compare three providers with exclusion reasons, check deadline availability, and create DRAFT — NOT SUBMITTED . The human reviews provider, slot, price, scope, rationale, and binding. Only then does commit_approved_dispatch appear as tool 06. One use commits the in-memory draft; after the result crosses the caller boundary, the registration aborts on the next task and getTools() confirms five again. Both public v1 and exact final candidate source ef35cfc separately verified that settlement timing in native Chrome. Reset returns to the exact five-tool baseline. Real-agent verification On 2026-08-31 (JST) , Codex + official Chrome DevTools for agents selected and executed the public page's registered WebMCP tools from a natural-language business request, without page-tool names or an execution order in the prompt. Actual order: get_active_vehicle → get_service_history → search_qualified_providers → check_provider_availability → create_dispatch_draft → human approval of the exact draft → commit_approved_dispatch . The five preparation tools produced DRAFT — NOT SUBMITTED . After human approval, the only added tool was commit_approved_dispatch . Codex rediscovered it with list_webmcp_tools , executed it once through execute_webmcp_tool , and verified revocation: 5 → 6 → 5 . All six page-tool executions completed. This is separate evidence from the on-page deterministic runner and the Playwright test adapter; neither was used in this real-agent run. It is not ChatGPT Site tools . Reset Demo was not verified through this agent route ; the separate human-operated native Chrome Reset check remains labeled as such. The fixed, fictional scenario demonstrates model-selected tool execution, not unrestricted planning or a real commercial booking. Environment: Chrome 151.0.7922.174 , official Chrome DevTools MCP 1.8.0 , Codex 0.151.0-alpha.7.2 , using an isolated Chrome profile. Recorded tool arguments, registry observations, and page screenshots . How it works The deterministic runner discovers and invokes the five registered preparation tools in order; it is a verification aid, not a simulated AI. Visible approval binds the canonical draft hash and creates tool 06 for 120 seconds and one use. Commit accepts only the bound approval ID, consumes in-memory authority, settles, unregisters tool 06, and proves the exact five-name baseline through getTools() . Why WebMCP The person sees the exact draft, count, countdown, and audit trace while an agent sees the same page-owned tools. The imperative document.modelContext API is the product mechanism: registerTool publishes five baseline tools and the approval-only temporary tool; getTools drives the visible capability panel and verifies appearance/revocation; executeTool invokes the deterministic proof sequence and one-time commit; toolchange refreshes the browser-truth display; and AbortSignal defines registration lifetime. Ordinary UI confirmation cannot prove the agent's commit capability was absent before approval or gone after use. A permanently available endpoint also misses the page-bound authority transition that human and agent inspect together. Human-in-the-loop safety Approval hashes the complete canonical draft with SHA-256 and binds IDs, lifetime, one-time nonce, idempotency, used state, and registration generation. Tool 06 accepts only the current approval ID; callers cannot alter vehicle, provider, slot, price, scope, or rationale. Before domain execution, the callback observes exact six and revalidates approval integrity, TTL, hash, generation, idempotency, and uncommitted state. Combined invocation/registration signals also protect asynchronous validation. Mutation, expiry, Reset, cancellation, malformed input, read failure, or stale work fails closed. Unmount makes no immediate physical-removal claim; remount re-verifies. The technical docs retain the full checks and non-atomic registry limitation. How we built it This is a one-screen Next.js 16 / React 19 app over a deterministic TypeScript store. useSyncExternalStore avoids stale component callbacks; registry work is serialized; UI reads are bounded, generation-safe, and single-flight; Reset epochs discard older lifecycle work. Production has one native adapter and no fake fallback. Missing document.modelContext yields an honest unsupported state. The visibly labeled Playwright harness exists only for application automation. Challenges Public v1 exposed the hardest browser issue: revoking tool 06 before its successful callback crossed the tested Chrome boundary produced UnknownError after a domain commit. After asynchronous validation, authority is consumed before the success result returns; next-task revocation is then verified with getTools() . Tests also attack remounts, duplicate/stale reads, concurrency, expiry, mutation, Reset, registration failure, and cleanup. Accomplishments Approval creates an inspectable capability rather than changing prompt text. Exact-draft authority cannot be widened by arguments; one success consumes it. The actual registry is the visual proof. Public v1 completed human-native 5 → 6 → 5 on 2026-08-27 without runtime error. Exact final candidate source ef35cfc completed human-native 5 → 5 → 6 → 5 → Reset → 5 on 2026-08-30; tool 06 was only commit_approved_dispatch , with no observed error, duplicate, stopped transition, or stuck state. Candidate automation is 290 automated tests, 10 E2E browser flows across 320–1920px, and 96.02/93.67/98.64/96.82% executable-source statement/branch/function/line coverage. It includes hostile inputs, hash races, cancellation, native-string/schema-runner compatibility, accessibility, and soak work—but the automated harness is not native conformance. What we learned Tool design is authorization design. Inputs constrain arguments; trust also needs capability absence, exact-object binding, lifetime, revocation, and evidence. WebMCP makes those decisions visible where the human reviews the work. Potential impact Customer Service coordinators in automotive, field service, maintenance, repair, inspection, installation, and similar operational businesses. Pain A coordinator may have to manually cross asset or vehicle context, previous service history, provider qualification, pricing, availability, multiple constraints, exclusion reasons, repeated data entry, and final submission authority before one consequential request can be released. Value The agent prepares one structured decision through page-owned WebMCP tools. The human reviews one exact draft. Approval creates one exact, temporary write capability. One approved action consumes that capability. It then disappears, while the reviewed object, capability lifecycle, and audit trace remain visible on the shared page. Practical impact The design targets fewer dropped operational constraints, visible reasons for excluding unsuitable providers, less fragmented coordination and re-entry, no permanently exposed broad commit capability, exact-object human approval, inspectable authority, and a shared operational state for the human and agent. Built from firsthand experience coordinating real automotive and service operations, Agentic Service Dispatch turns one concrete vehicle-serv
